concept: Command Palette and Keyboard Shortcut Design
definition: Interfaces that expose command discovery through searchable palettes or labeled shortcuts support recognition by making commands visible; hidden shortcuts force recall. Modern practice: visible first, shortcuts as acceleration.
key_refs: Nielsen Norman Group / UI Copy Guidelines
implication: MetroGraph can surface commands via visible menus or context panels, then offer keyboard shortcuts for power users. This honors both recognition (novices see options) and recall acceleration (experts use shortcuts).

definition: Visual elements that are high in saliency (contrast, size, motion, color) capture attention and support recognition. Low-saliency options require active search/recall to locate.
key_refs: Xu et al. 2016 / Spatio-Temporal Modeling and Prediction of Visual Attention
Li et al. 2023 / UEyes: Understanding Visual Saliency across UI Types
implication: MetroGraph's most-used nodes and operations should be visually salient (position, size, color). Low-contrast or small nodes require scanning/recall to find; high-saliency elements enable instant recognition.

definition: Interfaces with visible options and clear affordances have lower error rates because users recognize the correct path rather than misremembering hidden steps. Visibility acts as error prevention.
key_refs: Empirical studies showing 30-70% error reduction in industrial UIs with improved visibility
implication: MetroGraph's visual approach reduces workflow construction errors. Users are less likely to misconnect nodes, apply wrong transformations, or lose track of data flow when everything is visible rather than hidden in nested menus.

definition: Perceptual principle that observers distinguish focal objects (figure) from background. Interface design must make primary options (figure) distinct from secondary elements (ground) to support recognition.
key_refs: Rubin 1915 / Visuell wahrgenommene Figuren
implication: MetroGraph must ensure that workflow nodes are visually distinct (figure) from the canvas background (ground), and that active/selected nodes are visually distinct from inactive ones. Poor figure-ground separation hides options, forcing recall.

concept: Accessibility and Visibility for Diverse Users
definition: Visibility principles must account for users with different abilities (visual, motor, cognitive). Hidden options are doubly inaccessible: unclear to sighted users, and invisible to screen readers.
key_refs: WebAIM / Invisible Content for Screen Readers
implication: MetroGraph's commitment to visibility serves accessibility as well. Visible nodes with clear labels are recognizable to all users. Hidden interactions or unlabeled elements fail both sighted users (recognition) and screen reader users (access).

definition: Empirical law establishing a logarithmic relationship between the number of choice alternatives and human reaction time to select one: RT = b·log2(n+1), where reaction time increases predictably as choice complexity grows. Foundational to understanding cognitive costs of decision-making.
key_refs: Hick 1952 / On the Rate of Gain of Information
Hyman 1953 / Stimulus Information as a Determinant of Reaction Time
Proctor & Schneider 2018 / Hick's Law for Choice Reaction Time: A Review
implication: MetroGraph must minimize visual choice density in workflows; graph node/edge density directly impacts user reaction time and decision cost. Sequential or filtered presentation preferable to simultaneous all-options display.

definition: Empirical finding that human absolute judgment and immediate short-term memory span are limited to approximately 7±2 distinct items or chunks. While Miller acknowledged 7 is not magical, the principle constrains how many unrelated options humans can consciously compare.
key_refs: Miller 1956 / The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information
implication: MetroGraph node/menu designs should present no more than 5-7 primary options per view to avoid exceeding working memory span. Exceeding this ceiling increases cognitive load and choice difficulty exponentially.

definition: Modern refinement of Miller's law, establishing working memory capacity as 3-5 items (not 7) when controlling for rehearsal and consolidation effects. More conservative estimate of genuine simultaneous comparison capacity.
key_refs: Cowan 2001 / The Magical Number 4 in Short-Term Memory: A Reconsideration of Mental Storage Capacity
implication: For database query tools, MetroGraph should show maximum 4-5 query filter options simultaneously; beyond this cognitive bottleneck users resort to heuristics/guessing rather than rational comparison.

definition: Framework introduced by Barry Schwartz that increasing choice variety can paradoxically reduce consumer satisfaction, increase regret/depression, and lower intrinsic motivation. Beyond a modest optimum (6-9 items), additional options create welfare loss via decision difficulty, regret, and adaptation pressure.
key_refs: Schwartz 2004 / The Paradox of Choice: Why More Is Less
Iyengar & Lepper 2000 / When Choice is Demotivating: Can One Desire Too Much of a Good Thing?
implication: Core wedge insight: MetroGraph's competitive advantage is NOT to show all 500+ database columns/nodes/edges simultaneously (like flat RAG/spreadsheet UIs). Must surface only high-scent, pre-filtered options matching query intent; excess visibility creates choice paralysis.

definition: Landmark field experiment showing 24-choice jam display reduced purchase likelihood and post-choice satisfaction compared to 6-choice display. Demonstrates choice overload empirically in real consumer context; subsequent satisfaction with selection was higher when options were limited.
key_refs: Iyengar & Lepper 2000 / When Choice is Demotivating: Can One Desire Too Much of a Good Thing?
implication: Direct parallel to MetroGraph: showing 24 query operators/columns creates friction and lower task completion vs. showing 6 high-relevance suggestions. Better to filter aggressively than to maximize choice visibility.

definition: Personality dimension distinguishing people who pursue optimization (maximizers) from those who accept 'good enough' solutions (satisficers). Maximizers experience higher regret, depression, and dissatisfaction with outcomes despite objectively similar choice quality; they are more sensitive to choice set size.
key_refs: Schwartz et al. 2002 / Maximizing Versus Satisficing: Happiness Is a Matter of Choice
Schwartz 2004 / The Paradox of Choice
implication: MetroGraph UI must support both personas: satisficers benefit from quick defaults/suggestions; maximizers need visibility into why certain options were filtered. Neither persona benefits from raw choice explosion (20+ column/node options).

definition: Situational phenomenon where the number of available options exceeds cognitive capacity, resulting in reduced decision confidence, increased regret, lower satisfaction, and task abandonment. Meta-analyses show effect is contingent on choice set complexity, decision uncertainty, and goal clarity—not inevitable.
key_refs: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Hertwig 2010 / Can There Ever Be Too Many Options? A Meta-Analytic Review of Choice Overload
Chernev 2015 / Choice Overload: A Conceptual Review and Meta-Analysis
implication: MetroGraph must implement aggressive relevance filtering (high information scent) to keep choice sets within 4-9 items. Overload occurs not just from sheer number but from unclear relevance—semantic filtering is as important as quantity filtering.

definition: Declining quality of decision-making after prolonged or intensive decision-making. Rooted in ego-depletion theory: decision-making consumes limited cognitive self-control resources; depletion leads to reduced deliberation, choice of defaults, and choice avoidance. Recent frameworks emphasize effort, motivation, and task complexity as additional moderators.
key_refs: Baumeister 1998 / Ego Depletion and the Strength Model of Self-Control
Polman & Vohs 2016 / Decision Fatigue, Choosing for Others, and Self-Construal
Frontiers in Cognition 2025 / An Integrative Review on Unveiling the Causes and Effects of Decision Fatigue
implication: For AI-assisted workflows (agents, RAG), MetroGraph must reduce decision frequency and cognitive cost per decision. Rather than presenting 20 database columns per query, suggest 3-5 pre-ranked columns; this preserves user deliberation capacity for higher-stakes schema design decisions.

definition: Resource-based model of self-control positing that exerting willpower/decision-making depletes a limited cognitive resource (glucose, attention, motivation). Subsequent decisions show reduced quality, impulsivity, and procrastination until resources replenish (rest, food, time).
key_refs: Baumeister et al. 1998 / Ego Depletion: Is the Active Self a Limited Resource?
implication: MetroGraph should minimize decision micro-choices (modal dialogs, confirmation prompts, choice hierarchies) that deplete user attention. Batch-consolidate related decisions into single coherent choice points.

definition: Foundational framework by Kahneman and Tversky showing humans systematically deviate from rational choice due to mental shortcuts (heuristics). Common biases include availability, anchoring, representativeness, and status quo bias. Under cognitive load, bias reliance increases.
key_refs: Kahneman & Tversky 1974 / Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
Tversky & Kahneman 1974 / Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
implication: MetroGraph must design interfaces that steer users toward sound heuristics (e.g., 'use the suggested columns') rather than exploitable ones (e.g., 'first option wins due to position bias'). Ranking options by relevance leverages availability heuristic constructively.

definition: Decision theory by Kahneman and Tversky showing humans evaluate choices relative to a reference point, exhibit loss aversion (losses loom larger than equivalent gains), and are influenced by how choices are framed. Explains systematic deviations from expected-utility maximization.
key_refs: Tversky & Kahneman 1979 / Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk
implication: In MetroGraph, present query suggestions as gains ('add these relevant columns') not losses ('columns hidden from view'). Frame default suggestions as reference point (status quo) so users perceive deviating from suggestions as incurring loss.

definition: Tendency to avoid choices that might lead to post-hoc regret ('I could have chosen differently'). Maximizers are particularly susceptible; regret increases with choice set size, social comparison opportunities, and perceived reversibility. Leads to choice paralysis and post-choice dissatisfaction.
key_refs: Schwartz et al. 2002 / Maximizing Versus Satisficing: Happiness Is a Matter of Choice
Beattie et al. 1994 / The Psychology of Risky Decisions
implication: MetroGraph should make query decisions reversible (easy to add/remove columns) and reduce post-decision comparison anxiety by clearly showing why specific options were surfaced. Reduces regret pressure that drives indecision.

definition: Framework by Thaler and Sunstein for designing choice environments to steer decisions toward better outcomes without restricting freedom (libertarian paternalism). Tactics include default options, option ordering, framing, and presentation format. Recognizes choice context shapes outcome as much as preferences.
key_refs: Thaler & Sunstein 2008 / Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness
Thaler & Sunstein 2003 / Choice Architecture (working paper)
implication: MetroGraph IS an application of choice architecture: rank columns by relevance (default effect), group nodes into semantic clusters (framing), show top-5 suggestions first (ordering). This steers users toward sound query designs without hiding alternatives.

definition: Design principle addressing hierarchical menu structures: broad (many top-level items) vs. deep (many nesting levels). Optimal balance is typically shallow-broad (5-9 items per level, max 3 levels); deep menus increase navigation cost and memory load; broad menus exceed working memory.
key_refs: Jacko & Salvendy 2001 / Hierarchical Menu Design: Breadth, Depth, and Task Complexity
Norman 1991 / The Invisible Computer
implication: MetroGraph query builder should show ~7 top-level column categories (breadth) rather than 100 columns flat or 3-level nesting (depth). E.g., 'Customer', 'Orders', 'Products' as first-level; users drill into 5-9 columns per category.

definition: Measurable property of interface/visualization design: high visual complexity results from dense information, low contrast, intricate patterns, and multiple visual elements. Empirically correlates with reduced user satisfaction, longer task completion, and increased errors; aesthetic judgment often inversely related to complexity.
key_refs: Deng & Poole 2010 / Affecting Student Attitudes and Perceptions Using Web-Based Learning Systems
Tuch et al. 2012 / Visual Complexity and Aesthetic Perception of Web Pages
implication: MetroGraph must avoid 'hairball' graph visualizations (common failure of agent/workflow tools). Limit visible nodes to 8-12 and use layout algorithms (force-directed, layered) to reduce edge crossings. High complexity = high choice cost; visual simplicity is prerequisite for low-friction decision-making.

definition: Degree to which an interface element stands out to human visual attention based on contrast, size, color, motion. Salient elements are noticed immediately; non-salient elements are overlooked. Shapes user scanning patterns and perceived information hierarchy.
key_refs: Bylinskii et al. 2015 / Learning Visual Importance for Graphic Designs and Data Visualizations
implication: In MetroGraph, high-scent columns should be visually salient (bold, centered, high contrast); low-relevance columns should be muted. Color/size encoding of node relevance guides attention to highest-value choices without requiring conscious search.

definition: Empirical finding that users systematically prefer earlier/higher options in ranked lists or search results, regardless of objective quality. Position alone influences perceived quality and choice likelihood; top-ranked items receive disproportionate selection.
key_refs: Joachims et al. 2005 / Accurately Interpreting Clickthrough Data as Implicit Feedback
Lewandowski et al. 2007 / Presentation Bias is Significant in Determining User Preference for Search Results
implication: MetroGraph's ranking algorithm must ensure top suggestions are genuinely high-scent, not arbitrary. Misranking (placing low-relevance columns first) will drive users toward poor query choices. Ranking quality is load-bearing for avoiding choice errors.

definition: Experimental finding that presenting options sequentially (pairwise or one-at-a-time) leads to more rational, committed decisions compared to simultaneous display of all options. Sequential presentation reduces regret, increases satisfaction, and improves decision quality.
key_refs: Das et al. 2025 / Pairwise Beats All-at-Once: Behavioral Gains from Sequential Choice Presentation
Poole & Dey 2010 / Eternal Quest for the Best: Sequential (vs. Simultaneous) Option Presentation Undermines Choice Commitment
implication: MetroGraph could implement sequential suggestion: 'Add customer_id? Yes/No' → 'Add customer_name? Yes/No'. This outperforms simultaneous 'Select all columns:' checkbox grids. Sequential reduces choice deliberation cost and increases user confidence in queries.

definition: Condition where information quantity exceeds processing capacity; results in reduced comprehension, slower response, increased errors, and task abandonment. Related to but distinct from choice overload—overload can occur via visual density, data volume, or option multiplicity.
key_refs: Sweller 1988 / Cognitive Load During Problem Solving: Effects on Learning
Wurman 2001 / Information Anxiety
implication: MetroGraph's filtering/ranking system prevents information overload by showing only high-relevance results. Avoid displaying all 500 columns, all 200 tables, all 10,000 edges simultaneously. Controlled visibility = controlled information load.

definition: Accumulation of features, options, and interface elements over time, often resulting in cognitive overload, reduced learnability, and poor user experience. Users struggle to find relevant features among clutter; common in mature software (e.g., Microsoft Word).
key_refs: Wikipedia / Interface Bloat
implication: MetroGraph must resist temptation to add 'one more feature' to query builder (UDFs, temporal queries, fuzzy matching). Every feature added increases cognitive load and choice cost. Constraint and focus are features; controlled minimalism outperforms feature maximization.

definition: Use of algorithms, ranking, or agent recommendations to reduce user decision burden. Can reduce fatigue and improve outcomes if suggestions are high-quality and transparent; poor ranking or unexplained suggestions increase frustration and cognitive load.
key_refs: CHI 2024 / Avoiding Decision Fatigue with AI-Assisted Decision-Making
implication: MetroGraph's core mechanism: use semantic matching (embedding-based relevance) and usage frequency to rank column/node suggestions. This is AI-assisted choice curation, not chat-based delegation. Users remain in control but get intelligent filtration.

definition: Motor control law relating target acquisition time to target distance and size: MT = a + b·log2(D/W), where MT is movement time, D is distance to target, W is target width. Larger targets at closer range are faster to select; principle extends to graphical interface widget sizing.
key_refs: Fitts 1954 / The Information Capacity of the Human Motor System in Controlling the Amplitude of Movement
MacKenzie 1992 / Fitts' Law as a Research and Design Tool in Human-Computer Interaction
MacKenzie 2004 / Perspectives on 27 Years of Fitts' Law Research in HCI
implication: MetroGraph node/button sizing should follow Fitts: make frequently-used columns/filters large and close to cursor; deemphasize rare options. Large hit targets reduce selection errors and cognitive burden (fewer mis-clicks = fewer corrections).

definition: A set of organizing principles by which the human visual system groups elements into coherent wholes, including proximity (nearness), similarity (shared attributes), continuity (smooth paths), closure (completing incomplete shapes), symmetry, and common fate (shared motion). These principles describe how visual perception naturally organizes elementary sensations into meaningful structures prior to conscious analysis.
key_refs: Wertheimer 1912 / Phi motion and Gestalt psychology
Wagemans et al. 2012 / A Century of Gestalt Psychology in Visual Perception I
implication: MetroGraph must leverage grouping principles (proximity, similarity, continuity) to organize nodes and edges naturally, reducing cognitive load when parsing complex graphs. Proper grouping minimizes explicit labeling and supports rapid pattern recognition.

definition: Treisman's theory positing that visual attention operates in two stages: (1) preattentive parallel processing of basic features (color, orientation, motion) without focused attention, and (2) attentive serial processing required to bind features into conjunctions. Features are processed automatically and in parallel; complex object identification requires focused attention directed to each location.
key_refs: Treisman & Gelade 1980 / A Feature-Integration Theory of Attention
Treisman 1985 / Preattentive Processing in Vision
Wolfe 2020 / Forty years after Feature Integration Theory
implication: MetroGraph should encode critical node/edge properties (type, status, relationship) as separable preattentive features (distinct colors, positions, orientations) to enable rapid detection without serial attention. Complex queries requiring feature conjunction should be supported through interactive filtering to reduce cognitive load.

definition: Automatic, parallel processing of visual information occurring in <500ms before focused attention is directed, during which the visual system rapidly detects basic features (color, orientation, motion, position) without conscious effort. Preattentive attributes can be perceived simultaneously across the entire visual field and are immune to inattentional blindness.
key_refs: Attneave (1954) / Some Informational Aspects of Visual Perception
Healey & Enns / Harnessing Preattentive Processes for Multivariate Data Visualization
Treisman 1985 / Preattentive Processing in Vision
Triesman & Gelade (1980) / A Feature-Integration Theory of Attention
Ware 2012 / Information Visualization: Perception for Design
Ware 2020 / Information Visualization: Perception for Design
implication: MetroGraph's primary visual encoding (node colors, positions, sizes, edge directions) must be preattentively distinguishable to ensure anomalies, important entities, or relationships are perceived instantly without deliberate search, supporting rapid insight discovery in large graphs.

definition: The perceptual process by which the visual system segregates a focused figure (foreground object of interest) from background elements. Figure-ground organization is influenced by proximity, similarity, continuity, motion, lighting, experience, and task attention, and is fundamental to recognizing coherent objects in complex visual scenes.
key_refs: Wagemans et al. 2012 / A Century of Gestalt Psychology in Visual Perception I
Rubin 1921 / Figure and ground
implication: MetroGraph must achieve clear figure-ground separation so that focal nodes/subgraphs visually pop from context (through contrast, layering, or visual hierarchy), enabling users to maintain focus on relevant parts of the graph while managing visual clutter.

definition: Empirically validated ranking of visual encoding channels by their accuracy in conveying quantitative information, established by Cleveland & McGill (1984). Hierarchy from most to least effective: position (along common scale), position (non-aligned scales), length, angle/slope, area, volume, color saturation, color hue, density/texture. Effectiveness varies by task (comparison, ranking, identification).
key_refs: Cleveland & McGill 1984 / Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application
Ware 2020 / Information Visualization: Perception for Design
implication: MetroGraph should prioritize position (2D spatial layout) and color/size (node properties) as primary encoding channels for graph structure and attributes, reserving secondary channels (texture, angle, density) for lower-priority or derived data to maintain decoding accuracy.

definition: Dimensions of visual representation (position, color, size, shape, orientation, texture, opacity, saturation, hue) used to map data to graphical form. Each channel has finite capacity, perceptual bandwidth, and effectiveness for different data types (quantitative, categorical, ordinal). Bertin's foundational framework (position, form, orientation, color, texture, value, size) was extended and validated empirically.
key_refs: Bertin 1967 / Semiology of Graphics
Ware 2020 / Information Visualization: Perception for Design
Munzner 2014 / Visualization Analysis and Design
implication: MetroGraph design must strategically allocate visual channels: spatial position for graph topology, color/size for categorical/quantitative node attributes, shape for node roles, opacity for weighted relationships. Avoid redundant or conflicting encodings that exceed perceptual bandwidth.

concept: Visual Search: Parallel Feature Search vs. Conjunction Search
definition: Two distinct visual search mechanisms: (1) parallel feature search detects a single basic feature across the visual field in ~500ms independent of display size (preattentive), while (2) conjunction search requires binding multiple features and scales linearly with display size (2-3 items/second), requiring serial focal attention. Search type determines whether a target 'pops out' or requires effortful scanning.
key_refs: Treisman & Gelade 1980 / A Feature-Integration Theory of Attention
Wolfe 2012 / The Temporal Dynamics of Visual Search
implication: MetroGraph should encode critical node properties (e.g., error states, query results) as distinct preattentive features enabling pop-out search, while complex multi-attribute queries should be supported through interactive filtering to avoid serial conjunction search overhead on large graphs.

definition: The property of a visual stimulus that causes it to stand out from surrounding elements and capture attention involuntarily. Saliency arises from bottom-up factors (sudden motion, high contrast, color distinctiveness) and top-down factors (task-driven attention, expertise). Saliency modulates preattentive processing speed and determines where focal attention is deployed first.
key_refs: Theeuwes 2010 / Stimulus Saliency Modulates Pre-Attentive Processing Speed
Wolfe 2020 / Models of Bottom-Up and Top-Down Visual Attention
implication: MetroGraph must carefully control saliency to guide user attention: highlight critical nodes/edges through color/size contrast, use motion sparingly to draw attention to changes, and suppress saliency in non-focal areas to prevent distraction and cognitive load.

concept: Perceptual Bandwidth and Working Memory Limits
definition: The limited capacity of human perception and working memory to process information simultaneously. Studies show that focal attention can track 3-4 objects, working memory holds ~4 chunks of information, and visual search becomes serial when displays exceed ~4-6 items. Change blindness and inattentional blindness demonstrate the boundaries of perceptual capacity.
key_refs: Luck & Vogel 1997 / The capacity of visual working memory
Rensink 2002 / Change blindness and visual memory
implication: MetroGraph must limit initial information density to prevent cognitive overload: show focused views of graph subsets (via zoom/pan/filtering) rather than entire graphs at once, use coordinated multiple views and progressive disclosure, and avoid animation overload by limiting concurrent motion to <4 elements.

definition: Framework distinguishing three types of cognitive load: (1) intrinsic load (inherent complexity of the task/information), (2) extraneous load (imposed by poor design/presentation), and (3) germane load (processing beneficial for learning/understanding). Effective visualization minimizes extraneous load while managing intrinsic load through progressive disclosure and layered information.
key_refs: Sweller 1988 / Cognitive Load Theory
Sweller 2011 / Visualisation and Instructional Design
implication: MetroGraph design must reduce extraneous cognitive load through clear labeling, consistent visual encoding, and uncluttered layouts. Complex queries and large graphs should use progressive disclosure (filtering, aggregation, animation) to manage intrinsic load while preserving germane load for insight discovery.

concept: Node-Link Diagram Perception and Layout Effects
definition: Graph layout significantly impacts perception of network structure, connectivity, and properties. Layout algorithms optimizing for edge crossings, node spacing, symmetry, and hierarchy enable faster comprehension of graph topology. Studies show that poor layouts increase visual search time and misreading of connections, while optimized layouts enhance pattern recognition.
key_refs: Huang & Eades 2005 / How people read graphs
Ghani et al. 2025 / Graph visualization efficiency of popular web-based libraries
implication: MetroGraph's layout algorithm must prioritize perceptual effectiveness: minimize edge crossings, use symmetry and hierarchy to organize structure, apply grouping principles to co-locate related nodes, and enable interactive layout adjustment so users can organize graphs to match mental models.

definition: Distinction between two visual processing modes: focal (what) processing via central vision identifying object properties and identity, and ambient (where) processing via peripheral vision detecting spatial location and navigation. These modes are served by distinct neural pathways (ventral vs. dorsal streams) and operate in parallel with different resolution and bandwidth.
key_refs: Ungerleider & Mishkin 1982 / Two cortical visual systems
Brogan et al. 2024 / How central and peripheral vision influence focal and ambient processing
implication: MetroGraph should support multi-scale viewing: detailed node information in focal (central) view, while maintaining graph structure context and status overview in ambient (peripheral) view via minimap, legend, or reduced visual hierarchy. This leverages both processing modes for efficient exploration.

definition: Temporal data and animated transitions in visualizations are perceived through motion perception (detecting change), temporal attention (tracking moving objects), and working memory (retaining frame-to-frame changes). Effective animation uses motion to reveal transformations, guide attention, and encode temporal relationships while avoiding cognitive overload from rapid or excessive motion.
key_refs: Chevalier et al. 2015 / Improving Engagement of Animated Visualization with Visual Foreshadowing
implication: MetroGraph should use animation sparingly and purposefully: smooth transitions to reveal layout changes and guide attention, limit concurrent animated elements to <4, use visual foreshadowing to preview changes, and ensure animation duration matches task needs (avoid both flickering and sluggishness).

definition: Color perception involves three independent channels: lightness (brightness), hue (red/green/blue/yellow), and saturation (purity). These channels have different perceptual properties: lightness is preattentive and linear, hue is categorical and limited to ~7-10 distinguishable colors, saturation is weak and nonlinear. Color effectiveness varies by task and context (e.g., categorical vs. quantitative encoding).
key_refs: Ware 2020 / Information Visualization: Perception for Design
Munzner 2014 / Visualization Analysis and Design
implication: MetroGraph should use color intentionally: lightness for quantitative node attributes (supporting preattentive comparison), distinct hue for categorical properties (node types, statuses), and reserve saturation for secondary encodings. Avoid red-green-only encoding for accessibility.

definition: Approximately 8% of males and 0.5% of females have color vision deficiency (CVD), primarily red-green confusion (protanopia, deuteranopia) or blue-yellow weakness (tritanopia). Accessible visualization design avoids red-green-only encoding, uses high-contrast color pairs testable with CVD simulators, and supplements color with secondary encodings (shape, pattern, texture, position).
key_refs: Brettel et al. 1997 / Color-blind simulator software
Deficiency-based visualization guide 2024
implication: MetroGraph must support all users: test color schemes with CVD simulators, avoid red-green-only distinctions, pair color with shape/texture/position encoding, and provide high-contrast alternatives. This ensures accessibility without sacrificing visualization effectiveness.

concept: Texture and Pattern as Composite Visual Variables
definition: Texture and pattern are complex composite visual variables combining position, orientation, scale, and spacing of repeated graphical elements. Unlike simple channels (color, size), texture perception involves grouping principles (proximity, similarity, orientation), scale-dependent processing, and working memory load. Recent work systematizes texture design for visualization, distinguishing preattentive from attentive texture discrimination.
key_refs: Kirley et al. 2025 / Reframing Pattern: A Comprehensive Approach to a Composite Visual Variable
implication: MetroGraph can use texture/pattern to encode secondary attributes (weak connection strength, deprecated nodes) or to fill large areas (clustered subgraphs) where color alone would create visual confusion. However, texture perception is weaker than position/color; reserve it for non-critical attributes or supplement with other channels.

definition: The visual system integrates fragmented contours into coherent boundaries through grouping principles (proximity, continuity, closure, good continuation) and amodal completion (filling in invisible edges behind occlusions). Contour integration operates at multiple processing levels (early visual cortex through shape perception) and is influenced by experience, attention, and task.
key_refs: Wagemans et al. 2012 / A Century of Gestalt Psychology in Visual Perception I
implication: MetroGraph's visual design should support contour completion: use consistent edge styles and colors to group related connections, leverage good continuation and closure to suggest implied relationships, and minimize visual fragmentation so edges remain perceptually coherent even when paths cross or occlude.

definition: Interactive technique coordinating multiple linked views of the same data through shared selection and filtering. Users select elements in one view and see corresponding highlights in other views, supporting multidimensional exploration by exploiting perceptual ability to track small highlighted regions across views and working memory for maintaining task context across displays.
key_refs: Buja et al. 1991 / Exploratory Visualization with Multiple Linked Views
implication: MetroGraph should support multiple linked views (e.g., detail view + overview, table + graph, temporal + structural view) where selection in one view highlights corresponding elements in others. This leverages perceptual grouping and working memory to support complex queries without overwhelming cognitive load.

definition: Visualization effectiveness is task-dependent: different chart types (bar, line, scatter, area) excel at different perceptual tasks (comparison, ranking, identification, trend detection). Empirical studies measure accuracy and response time across tasks and visualization types to guide chart selection. General principle: match visual encoding to perceptual task demands.
key_refs: Talbot et al. 2013 / Task-Based Effectiveness of Basic Visualizations
Quadri & Rosen 2021 / A Survey of Perception-Based Visualization Studies by Task
implication: MetroGraph should support task-aware visualization: provide multiple views optimized for different analysis tasks (topology inspection via hierarchical layout, similarity detection via clustering, anomaly detection via color contrast), and allow users to switch views dynamically as tasks evolve.

definition: Use of metaphorical visual structures (e.g., tree metaphors for hierarchies, metro map metaphors for networks) to leverage users' prior knowledge and domain expertise, reducing cognitive load by mapping abstract structures to familiar spatial or physical domains. Metaphor effectiveness depends on alignment between abstract structure and metaphorical domain.
key_refs: Lakoff & Johnson 1980 / Conceptual metaphor theory
Ribeiro et al. 2020 / On the role of metaphor in information visualization
implication: MetroGraph leverages the metro-map metaphor naturally: users already understand metro maps as simplified, stylized networks with spatial relationships preserved. This metaphor reduces cognitive load by aligning database graph visualization with familiar spatial reasoning, enabling rapid insight discovery.

definition: Icons are visual signs functioning as iconic (resemblance-based), indexical (causally linked), or symbolic (conventional) representations. Icon effectiveness depends on visual clarity, distinctiveness, learnability, and alignment with user mental models. Semiotic analysis guides icon selection: iconic signs are fastest for novices, symbolic signs efficient for experts.
key_refs: Peirce 1931 / Semiotics
Liu et al. 2016 / Design semiotics based icon design
implication: MetroGraph should use iconic node shapes and edge styles aligned with user domain knowledge: iconic representations of database objects, arrows for directional relationships, consistent symbology for node types. This reduces learning curve and supports rapid recognition.

concept: Affordances and Signifiers in Interface Design
definition: Affordances are action possibilities offered by an object (what can be done); signifiers are perceptual cues (visual, auditory, tactile) that communicate affordances to users. Good design aligns visual properties with actual interaction possibilities, reducing cognitive load by making actions obvious without explanation. Poor signification leads to mode errors and confusion.
key_refs: Norman 2015 / The Design of Everyday Things
implication: MetroGraph UI must signal affordances clearly: hoverable nodes should change color/scale; clickable edges should highlight; draggable elements should show grab cursors. This reduces mode errors and supports users in building correct mental models of graph interaction.

concept: Eye Tracking and Gaze-Based Saliency Metrics
definition: Eye-tracking studies measure gaze fixation patterns and saccades to assess where users look in visualizations. Gaze metrics (time to first fixation, fixation duration, fixation count) reveal which elements attract attention and demand cognitive resources. Saliency maps computed from gaze data or computational models predict attention distribution and identify design issues.
key_refs: Cai et al. 2019 / Saliency-Based Gaze Visualization for Eye Movement Analysis
implication: MetroGraph should be validated with eye-tracking studies to measure gaze distribution during common tasks (finding nodes, tracing paths, identifying clusters). Results should inform layout, color, and animation design to ensure critical elements receive appropriate attention.

definition: Visual analytics combines interactive visualization with automated analysis and statistical computation to support insight discovery and decision-making. The paradigm leverages humans' superior pattern recognition and perceptual abilities with algorithms' computational power, operating in tight feedback loops where visualization guides analysis and analysis informs visualization updates.
key_refs: PNNL / Visual Analytics for Exploring and Understanding Data
implication: MetroGraph can adopt visual analytics approach: integrate graph layout optimization, automated clustering/anomaly detection, and query suggestion alongside interactive visualization, creating tight feedback loops where user exploration (filtering, zooming) refines automated analysis and vice versa.

definition: Systematic framework mapping data variables to visual properties through a layered grammar: data (variables) to geometric objects (marks: points, lines, bars) to aesthetic mappings (position, color, size, shape) to statistical transformations to coordinate systems to faceting. This grammar enables compositional visualization design and is implemented in tools like ggplot2, Vega, and modern visualization libraries.
key_refs: Wilkinson 1999 / The Grammar of Graphics
implication: MetroGraph's design philosophy can leverage grammar-of-graphics principles: define explicit mappings from graph properties (node attributes, edge weights, relationships) to visual marks and aesthetics, enabling systematic exploration of visualization alternatives and principled composition of views.

definition: Foundational principles for effective visualization derived from perception and cognition: show the data clearly, reduce cognitive load through visual hierarchy and simplification, use visual encoding to amplify perception (leverage preattentive channels), support interaction for exploration and refinement. These principles guide selection of chart types, color schemes, layouts, and interactive features.
key_refs: Ware 2020 / Information Visualization: Perception for Design
Munzner 2014 / Visualization Analysis and Design
Tufte 1983 / The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
implication: MetroGraph design must apply these core principles: clearly encode graph structure and properties, minimize visual clutter and cognitive load through progressive disclosure and color restraint, use metro-map simplification to amplify salient relationships, and support interactive exploration to maintain engagement.

definition: Visual persistence of manipulated objects throughout interaction: users see the data/object on screen at all times, enabling perception of dynamic state changes and immediate assessment of action outcomes. Contrasts with command-line paradigm where typed commands vanish from focus.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction
Shneiderman 1981 / Direct Manipulation Techniques (first principle: continuous visible representation)
Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation
Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation: A Step Beyond Programming Languages
Tufte 1983 / The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
Tufte 1989 / Visual Design of the User Interface
implication: Graph nodes/edges must remain visible and semantically clear during all query/transform operations; hiding intermediate states or requiring modal dialogs breaks the continuous representation principle, forcing users to rely on memory rather than perception.

definition: Interaction design principle: user actions (drag, drop, delete, modify) must be undoable without penalty or loss of state. Reversibility reduces psychological friction by enabling safe exploration and error recovery, core to novice learnability and intermittent-user retention.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation: A Step Beyond Programming Languages
Nielsen 1995 / 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
implication: Every graph operation (node creation, edge deletion, property edit) must have immediate undo/redo; irreversible destructive actions require explicit multi-step confirmation, not automatic AI action.

definition: Visual and temporal response to user action: interface state updates synchronously (< 100ms perceptual latency) and visibly reflects the semantic meaning of the action. Includes animation, highlighting, state updates, and confirmation cues that maintain user's mental model of object state.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation: A Step Beyond Programming Languages
Ni et al. 1994 / Animating Direct Manipulation Interfaces
Thomas et al. 2000 / Applying Cartoon Animation Techniques to Graphical User Interfaces
implication: Graph UI must visually animate transitions (node appearing/disappearing, edge routing changes, property updates) with smooth motion to bridge semantic gaps; delayed or silent updates create perception of broken causality.

definition: Gap between user's intention and the interface meaning representing that intention. Low semantic distance: interface objects directly embody the conceptual domain (dragging a node 'feels' like moving it in logical space). Measured as cognitive steps required to translate intention into interface semantics.
key_refs: Hutchins Hollan Norman 1985 / Direct Manipulation Interfaces
Norman 1988 / The Design of Everyday Things
implication: Graph query operations must map naturally to user intent: e.g., 'show nodes where X=Y' should not require LLM translation to parameterized query syntax; direct visual filtering/highlighting reduces semantic distance.

definition: Gap between intention's semantic representation and physical/gestural form required to express it. Low articulatory distance: physical action (drag, click, gesture) closely matches the semantics of the operation. Example: dragging a node to move it has low articulatory distance; typing SQL has high articulatory distance for the same intent.
key_refs: Hutchins Hollan Norman 1985 / Direct Manipulation Interfaces
implication: Graph interactions should privilege drag, drop, and click gestures over text input; constraint-based node positioning should enable direct manipulation, not menu-driven constraint editing.

definition: Quantitative principle predicting human pointing movement time as MT = a + b·log₂(D/W+1), where D=distance to target, W=target width. Fundamental law of motor control governing direct-manipulation interface efficiency: larger buttons, closer targets, and wider interaction zones reduce movement time and error rates.
key_refs: Fitts 1954 / The Information Capacity of the Human Motor System in Controlling the Amplitude of Movement
Keim 2025 / A Systematic Review of Fitts' Law in 3D Extended Reality
implication: Graph node and edge interaction zones must be sized and spaced to minimize pointing movement; small nodes, dense layouts, or tiny drag-handle zones create high motor cost; layout should respect Fitts law via appropriately-sized interactive targets.

definition: Interface learning curve for first-time users: directness correlates strongly with rapid learnability. Direct manipulation interfaces show shallow learning curves because physical gestures map to real-world affordances (dragging feels like moving); command-syntax interfaces require memorization and show steep curves. Measured by time-to-first-task and error rates for new users.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation: A Step Beyond Programming Languages
implication: Graph visualization and interaction should be learnable within minutes for users unfamiliar with database tools; dragging to explore, clicking to inspect, visual filtering must feel natural without training manuals or LLM guidance.

definition: Efficiency advantage for experienced users: direct-manipulation interfaces enable expert users to work faster via fluent gesture mastery, keyboard shortcuts, and predictable state feedback. Contrast with command-line where expert speed requires syntax memorization and complex command composition.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation: A Step Beyond Programming Languages
implication: MetroGraph should support expert gesture fluency: hotkeys for common operations, drag-and-drop primitives, visual shortcuts that scale from novice (click-based) to expert (multi-action gestures) workflows.

definition: Interface usability for infrequent users who return after gaps: direct manipulation supports retention because physical gestures are recognizable even after memory decay; expert syntax-heavy interfaces exhibit high forgetting and require relearning.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation: A Step Beyond Programming Languages
implication: Graph interface must support intermittent usage: users returning monthly/quarterly should require no re-onboarding; UI gestures should be discoverable via visual inspection (affordances).

definition: Persistent interaction history enabling users to reverse prior actions and re-apply them. Undo-redo is essential implementation of reversibility principle; enables safe exploration, error recovery, and experimentation. Nielsen heuristic #3 emphasizes undo/redo as key to user control.
key_refs: Nielsen 1995 / 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
Prabaker 2024 / Utilizing Provenance as an Attribute for Visual Data Analysis
implication: MetroGraph's undo-redo stack must be unbounded and visible (optional history panel); users must trust that any destructive operation is recoverable within reasonable history depth (100+ steps minimum).

definition: System design minimizing errors and enabling rapid recovery: direct manipulation reduces error rate via visual clarity and reversibility; when errors occur, system should diagnose root cause, explain it in plain language (not programmer jargon), and suggest specific recovery steps. Contrasts with command-driven systems that produce cryptic syntax errors.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation: A Step Beyond Programming Languages
Nielsen 1995 / 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
implication: Graph queries that fail should provide visual highlighting of problematic nodes/edges and natural-language error messages ('Node X has no outgoing edges', not 'SQL parse error at line 3').

definition: User actions mapped to real-world physics metaphors: dragging mimics object movement, pinching mimics scaling, swiping mimics paging. Natural gesture semantics reduce cognitive load by leveraging implicit motor knowledge and real-world expectations. Contrast with abstract menu selections or arbitrary keyboard chords.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1982 / The Future of Interactive Systems and the Emergence of Direct Manipulation
Wigdor et al. 2009 / Designing User Interfaces for Multi-Touch and Gesture Devices
implication: Graph manipulation should privilege gestures: dragging nodes to reposition, dragging canvas to pan, swiping to navigate graph layers; avoid arbitrary menu commands like 'Move Node Forward' that require menu search.

definition: Principle: interface must show current state clearly and provide immediate, visible feedback to all user actions. Lack of visibility creates uncertainty; users cannot assess if actions had intended effect. Direct manipulation requires high visibility: all objects/state visible, all changes animated, all results immediately rendered.
key_refs: Norman 1988 / The Design of Everyday Things
implication: MetroGraph must avoid hidden state: all nodes/edges visible (with panning/zooming if needed, not hiding), all property changes immediately rendered, all query results immediately graphed (not delayed or paginated).

definition: Combination of constraint-based reasoning with direct manipulation: system enforces semantic rules (e.g., node layout constraints, edge connectivity rules) while permitting fluent object manipulation. Advanced DM that enables constrained interaction without requiring explicit constraint editing via menus.
key_refs: Borning & Duisberg 1986 / Constraint-Based Tools for Building User Interfaces
Zeidler 2013 / Evaluating Direct Manipulation Operations for Constraint-Based Layout
implication: MetroGraph graph operations should enforce schema constraints silently: e.g., if node type X cannot connect to type Y, dragging to create such edges should fail gracefully with visual feedback (red highlight), not open a constraint-editing dialog.

definition: Beaudouin-Lafon's generalization of direct manipulation: user manipulates domain objects (e.g., graph nodes) via interaction instruments (e.g., drag handle, selection lasso). Instrument selection is often implicit (e.g., cursor entering a node automatically enables dragging). Extends DM to multi-handed, tangible, and post-WIMP contexts.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 / Instrumental Interaction: An Interaction Model for Designing Post-WIMP User Interfaces
Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction: An Interaction Model for Designing Post-WIMP User Interfaces
Beaudouin-Lafon 2022 TOCHI / Generative Theories of Interaction
implication: MetroGraph interaction should use implicit instruments: hovering over a node reveals drag handles; selecting an edge implicitly enables bend-point editing; no need for mode-switching (e.g., 'Enter Edit Mode').

definition: Post-WIMP design framework: interaction grounded in real-world physical and spatial metaphors (touch, gesture, tangible, embodied). Four dimensions: naive physics (e.g., gravity, inertia), body awareness (proprioception), environmental awareness (spatial reasoning), social interaction (collaborative). Direct manipulation is foundation; RBI extends it beyond desktop WIMP.
key_refs: Dourish et al. 2008 / Reality-Based Interaction: A Framework for Post-WIMP Interfaces
Jacob et al. 2008 / Reality-Based Interaction: A Framework for Post-WIMP Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph should support multi-touch, gesture, and tablet interaction via RBI: pinch-to-zoom respects inertia; dragging nodes respects momentum; swiping feels weight-appropriate; environmental awareness enables spatial clustering.

definition: Evolution beyond classic Windows-Icons-Menus-Pointer (WIMP) interface: includes multitouch, gesture, speech, tangible, VR/AR, embodied interaction. Post-WIMP does not abandon DM principles; rather, extends them to new input modalities (touch, hand gesture) and output modalities (3D, immersive).
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 / Instrumental Interaction: An Interaction Model for Designing Post-WIMP User Interfaces
Dourish et al. 2008 / Reality-Based Interaction: A Framework for Post-WIMP Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph should not be confined to mouse-and-keyboard; design should extend to tablet touch, gesture, and future modalities while preserving DM core: continuous representation, reversibility, immediate feedback.

definition: Direct manipulation using physical objects as interface elements: tangible UIs bridge digital and physical (e.g., RFID-tagged blocks controlling digital processes); embodied interaction leverages body movement and proprioception (e.g., gesture-based control). Both extend DM principle of physical action to real-world tangibility.
key_refs: Hornecker 2005 / A Design Theme for Tangible Interaction: Embodied Facilitation
O'Brien 2008 / The Role of Physicality in Tangible and Embodied Interactions
implication: Future MetroGraph could leverage tangible input (e.g., physical tokens representing nodes) or embodied gesture (AR hand tracking); current design should prepare for such extensions while maintaining desktop DM foundations.

definition: Extension of DM to 3D immersive environments: Fitts's Law applies to 3D pointing; grab metaphors extend dragging to 6DOF manipulation; dual-hand interaction enables two-handed DM. VR/AR amplifies DM power via natural spatial reasoning and haptic feedback.
key_refs: Keim 2025 / A Systematic Review of Fitts' Law in 3D Extended Reality
User-Elicited 2018 / User-Elicited Dual-Hand Interactions for Manipulating 3D Objects in Virtual Reality Environments
Lin 2024 / Can I Touch This?: Survey of Virtual Reality Interactions via Haptic Solutions
implication: Future MetroGraph 3D graph visualization should support VR-grade DM: hand-tracked grab-to-manipulate, dual-hand rotation, spatial clustering that respects proprioceptive learning; haptic feedback for edge snap points.

definition: Theory of how users navigate information spaces: users follow 'information scent' (cues suggesting relevant information). Direct-manipulation visualization enhances foraging: visual prominence, color, highlighting, and interactive feedback serve as scent cues; immediate result visualization (not delayed query execution) enables rapid scent assessment.
key_refs: Pirolli & Card 1999 / Information Foraging Theory: Adaptive Interaction with Information
implication: MetroGraph query results must provide strong visual scent: filtered nodes should be highlighted distinctly (color, size, saturation), edge patterns should emerge from visualization (not require reading text results), enabling users to rapidly decide next exploration steps.

definition: Principles for mapping data to visual properties (color, size, position, shape) such that perception matches data semantics. Tufte's graphical integrity: avoid lie factor (ratio of effect size in graphic to actual data); use data-ink ratio (proportion of display showing data vs decoration). Effective visual encoding enables DM: users perceive query results immediately without decoding step.
key_refs: Tufte 1983 / The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
Munzner 2014 / Visualization Analysis and Design
implication: MetroGraph graph layout and node/edge visual encoding must follow graphical integrity: node position encodes graph structure (via layout algorithm); color should encode meaningful property (not decoration); size/shape should match data semantics; avoid visual lie factors.

definition: Laws of perceptual organization (proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, figure-ground): users automatically group visual elements based on these principles. DM UI design leverages Gestalt to signal interaction targets: related nodes grouped by proximity; interactive elements differentiated by color/shape; figure-ground contrast makes interactive elements salient.
key_refs: IxDF / Gestalt Principles: How the Brain Organizes Visual Information
Figma Resource Library / Gestalt Principles in Design
implication: MetroGraph node clustering should respect Gestalt proximity; related nodes grouped spatially; interactive elements (drag handles, context menus) should stand out via similarity/contrast; reduce visual noise to clarify figure-ground relationships.

definition: Query specification via direct manipulation of visual examples rather than text syntax: users click/drag to specify query constraints on example data. QBE is a DM paradigm for database queries: users see data, directly indicate desired subset (e.g., highlight rows), system infers query.
key_refs: Fisher et al. 2016 / Expressive Query Construction through Direct Manipulation of Nested Relational Results
IFQ / IFQ: A Visual Query Interface and Query Generator for Object-Based Media Retrieval
implication: MetroGraph query builder should support QBE: users directly highlight example nodes/edges matching criteria, system translates to query; avoids SQL syntax, reduces semantic/articulatory distance.

definition: Interactive data transformation using direct-manipulation UIs: users see data tables/views, directly manipulate (reorder columns, filter rows, split cells), system infers transformation pipeline. Wrangler and similar tools show DM effectiveness for data cleaning: visual preview + undo/redo enables rapid iterative transformation.
key_refs: Kandel 2013 / Interactive Systems for Data Transformation and Assessment
Toledo 2024 / Towards Scalable Visual Data Wrangling via Direct Manipulation
implication: MetroGraph graph transformation (schema evolution, edge rerouting, node property updates) should support direct manipulation like data wrangling: visual preview of result, undo-redo for safe iteration, inference of transformation rules.

concept: DirectGPT: Direct Manipulation for LLM Interaction
definition: Contemporary reapplication of Shneiderman's DM principles to LLM interfaces: users manipulate prompt elements visually (drag-reorder, drop-combine), see continuous preview of model output, undo-redo prior states. Empirical study shows 50% faster task completion, 72% shorter prompts vs ChatGPT chat interface.
key_refs: Masson & Casiez 2024 / DirectGPT: A Direct Manipulation Interface to Interact with Large Language Models
implication: MetroGraph graph-query/agent workflows should adopt DirectGPT lesson: enable direct manipulation of node operations (drag-to-connect tasks, visual parameter editing), not chat-based task specification; empirical advantage: faster, more user-controlled interactions.

definition: Combining multiple input modalities (direct manipulation, natural language, gesture) in single interface: DM provides precision/control, NL provides expressiveness. Contemporary systems (Liger, InterChat) show multimodal integration: users can drag to position elements, speak to filter, gestures to refine.
key_refs: Sinha 2024 / Liger: Combining Interaction Paradigms for Visual Analysis
InterChat 2024 / InterChat: Enhancing Generative Visual Analytics using Multimodal Interactions
implication: MetroGraph should support multimodal queries: drag nodes to filter, type regex patterns for text properties, speak to refine; DM as primary interaction layer, NL as secondary expressiveness mechanism; best-of-both vs AI-chat-only.

definition: Interface design principle: minimize modes (e.g., 'edit mode' vs 'view mode') requiring explicit activation; instead, provide consistent interaction semantics across contexts. Raskin's humane interface emphasizes modelessness. Direct manipulation naturally supports modelessness: users directly act on objects without mode-switching.
key_refs: Raskin 2000 / The Humane Interface: New Directions for Designing Interactive Systems
implication: MetroGraph should avoid modes: nodes are always draggable, properties always editable inline, queries always incrementally refinable; no 'lock/unlock graph', 'enter query mode', etc. Consistent gesture semantics reduce cognitive load.

definition: The cognitive gap between the conceptual model a user holds (their intention) and the representation/language the system requires to execute actions. High semantic distance means users must translate their goals into unfamiliar concepts.
key_refs: Hutchins-Hollan-Norman 1986 / Direct Manipulation Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph should allow users to express queries and graph operations in task-domain language (e.g. 'show relationships between these entities') rather than low-level graph algebra or SQL—reducing translation overhead that currently plagues RAG/agent-builder UIs.

definition: The physical and mechanical effort required to articulate an action to the system once intention is clear. It concerns input complexity, syntax requirements, and number of steps needed to invoke an action.
key_refs: Hutchins-Hollan-Norman 1986 / Direct Manipulation Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph's drag-and-drop graph metaphor (metro-map style) reduces articulatory distance vs. text-based queries—users directly manipulate edges/nodes rather than parsing command syntax.

definition: A relationship between an object's properties and an organism's capabilities that enables a particular action. In design, affordances are the action possibilities that an object offers to a perceiver, dependent on both object properties and perceiver abilities.
key_refs: Gibson 1977 / The Theory of Affordances
Gibson 1979 / The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception
Norman 1988 / The Design of Everyday Things
implication: MetroGraph nodes/edges must afford intuitive interaction: edges should afford dragging to create relationships, nodes should afford selection/deletion/property editing. Affordances must match users' existing mental models from other graph tools or geographic maps.

definition: A perceptual mark or indicator that communicates the existence and location of an affordance. Signifiers make affordances discoverable and interpretable; without them, even real affordances remain hidden from users.
key_refs: Norman 2013 / The Design of Everyday Things: Revised and Expanded
implication: MetroGraph must explicitly signal affordances: hover states on edges indicating drag-to-create, visual highlights for selectable nodes, icons/labels showing available actions. Without signifiers, users won't discover graph manipulation capabilities (major UX failure of current agent-builder tools).

definition: The capacity of a design element to afford cognitive actions (such as comparing, inferring, extracting) rather than just physical actions. Cognitive affordances describe how a visualization's design invites mental operations like pattern recognition or hypothesis formation.
key_refs: Fygenson et al. 2025 / Cognitive Affordances in Visualization
Padilla 2023 / Cognitive affordances in visualization (various)
implication: MetroGraph's visual encoding (node size, color, position, connection patterns) should afford cognitive actions: comparing node importance, detecting clusters, inferring entity relationships—reducing cognitive load and supporting exploratory analysis.

definition: Cognition is not bounded by individual minds but distributed across people, artifacts, and environment. Knowledge is encoded in tools, documents, and social structures; cognitive processes emerge from coordination between internal and external representations.
key_refs: Hutchins 1995 / Distributed Cognition (seminal work)
Hutchins 1999 / Distributed Cognition: The Organization of Cognitive Systems
implication: MetroGraph as a cognitive artifact must encode domain knowledge visually (graph structure itself becomes external memory) and support coordination between user intention and system capabilities—the graph is a 'thinking tool' that distributes the cognitive load of query construction.

definition: The user's internal, simplified representation of how a system works. Mismatches between user mental model and actual system model are a primary source of interaction failures and high gulf values.
key_refs: Norman 1983 / Some Observations on Mental Models
Norman 1988 / The Design of Everyday Things
Norman Affordances and Design
implication: MetroGraph should align with users' mental models from familiar domains (geographic maps, flowcharts, SQL joins visualized)—not introduce novel graph abstractions. The metro-map metaphor leverages existing mental models of public transportation network topology.

definition: Design elements that limit the set of possible user actions to only valid ones. Constraints reduce the gulf of execution by preventing errors at the interaction level (e.g., you cannot connect incompatible types, cannot drag to invalid targets).
key_refs: Norman 1988 / The Design of Everyday Things
Norman 2013 / The Design of Everyday Things: Revised and Expanded
implication: MetroGraph constraints: only allow edge creation between compatible nodes (entity→relation, relation→entity), only allow certain table joins based on schema—visual constraints (grayed-out invalid targets) reduce execution errors and guide correct interaction.

definition: Information returned to the user about the result of an action. Immediate, clear feedback closes the gulf of evaluation by showing whether actions achieved intended effects.
key_refs: Limerick et al. 2014
Norman 1988 / The Design of Everyday Things
Norman 2013 / The Design of Everyday Things: Revised and Expanded
Shneiderman 1983
Vig et al. 2022 / Sense of Agency and User Experience
implication: MetroGraph must provide immediate visual feedback: edge highlights on drag, query preview before execution, real-time result counts, status indicators for data loading. Absence of feedback forces users to use 'slow AI chat' as feedback mechanism.

definition: Predictive information about the likely consequences of an action before it is executed. Feedforward allows users to anticipate outcomes and adjust actions proactively, reducing the gulf of execution.
key_refs: Hollan et al. 2002 / Distributed cognition and human-computer interaction
Shneiderman et al. CHI papers on preview interactions
implication: MetroGraph preview panels showing query results as user drags/configures edges implement feedforward—users see what query will return before committing, reducing execution errors and the trial-and-error loop common in RAG/agent-builder UIs.

definition: Norman's model of human action: Goal Formation → Intention Formation → Action Specification → Execution → Perception → Interpretation → Evaluation. Gulfs of execution and evaluation map to the transition from intention to execution and from perception to interpretation.
key_refs: Norman 1986 / User Centered System Design
Norman 1988 / The Design of Everyday Things
implication: MetroGraph interaction flow aligns with stages: users form goal (analyze entity relationships), specify action (drag edge), execute (release), perceive state (visual feedback), evaluate (matches goal?). The model guides where UX failures occur.

definition: The degree to which the current state and available actions are perceptually obvious to users. High visibility closes the gulf of evaluation; poor visibility forces users to maintain complex internal models.
key_refs: Norman 1988 / The Design of Everyday Things
Norman 2013 / The Design of Everyday Things
Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation
implication: MetroGraph's metro-map view makes graph state immediately visible—users see all entities, relationships, and filters at a glance, vs. conversational UI which hides state in message history.

definition: How easily users can learn about available system features, actions, and affordances without external documentation. Poor discoverability creates execution gulf because users don't know what's possible.
key_refs: Nielsen 2020s articles on discoverability
ixdf.org Discoverability entry
implication: MetroGraph node/edge contextual menus, hover tooltips, and visual affordances make actions discoverable—users learn that clicking nodes filters, dragging creates joins, right-click shows options. Current agent-builder tools fail here.

definition: The ability to read and interpret data visualizations, including understanding visual encodings, recognizing patterns, and extracting insights. Interactive visualization literacy extends this to interaction competence.
key_refs: Lam et al. 2012 / Narrative Visualization
Lee & Kwon 2016 / VLAT: Development of a Visualization Literacy Assessment Test
León et al. 2026 / A Multiliteracy Model for Interactive Visualization Literacy
Pandey & Ottley 2023 / Mini-VLAT: A Short and Effective Measure of Visualization Literacy
implication: MetroGraph design must consider visualization literacy gaps: users unfamiliar with graph layouts, node-link encodings, or filter mechanics need visual scaffolding—the metro-map metaphor leverages existing literacy from transportation networks.

definition: The effort (cognitive, physical, time) required for a user to perform an action. High interaction cost discourages exploratory behavior and invites workarounds (like switching to chat interfaces).
key_refs: Lam et al. 2012 / Narrative Visualization
León et al. 2026 / A Multiliteracy Model for Interactive Visualization Literacy
implication: MetroGraph drag-and-drop reduces interaction cost vs. SQL/JSON config—enables rapid exploratory querying. High interaction cost in current tools is a key driver of 'flight to AI chat'.

definition: In visualization contexts, the gap between what users want to understand about data and the visualization tasks/operations available to them. Extends Norman's framework to knowledge work (León et al. 2026).
key_refs: León et al. 2026 / A Multiliteracy Model for Interactive Visualization Literacy
implication: MetroGraph users often have vague goals ('show me related entities') that don't map to standard query operations. Guided query builders, templates, or natural-language bridging must close this gulf.

definition: Distinction between interfaces designed for human cognitive interaction (emphasizing perceptibility, affordance clarity) and interfaces designed for machine invocation (emphasizing determinism, explicit semantics). Current RAG/agent tools blur this boundary problematically.
key_refs: Wang et al. 2026 / From Human Interfaces to Agent Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph is fundamentally a human interface (UI) for graph composition—not an agent interface. This is correct: humans form goals and specify operations; agents should invoke capabilities, not design interactions. Conflating these creates the 'best-of-worst' chatbot UIs.

definition: Research finding that user expectations of conversational agent capabilities dramatically exceed actual system capabilities, creating large gulfs of execution (what I can ask) and evaluation (whether the agent understood).
key_refs: Luger & Sellen 2016 / Like having a really bad PA: The gulf between user expectation and experience of conversational agents
implication: MetroGraph avoids conversational agent UIs precisely because of this gap—visual graph metaphor makes capabilities explicit and bounds expectations. Users know exactly what operations are available (connect two entities, filter by property) vs. vague chat expectations.

definition: The iterative process of exploring data through visualization, forming hypotheses, testing them interactively, and building understanding. Sensemaking depends on tight coupling between exploration, feedback, and interpretation.
key_refs: Heider et al. 2019 / On Sense Making and the Generation of Knowledge in Visual Analytics
Pirolli & Card / The Sensemaking Process in Intelligence Analysis
Zhang 2019 (various papers on sensemaking)
implication: MetroGraph's interactive query composition supports sensemaking: iteratively refine graph filters, see results immediately, form new hypotheses based on patterns—much more effective than chat-based exploration where feedback lags and causality is obscured.

definition: Recent framework (2024) reconsidering Norman's 'simplicity at all costs' principle. Some systems benefit from exposing inherent complexity visually rather than hiding it; the goal is 'appropriate' complexity, not minimal complexity.
key_refs: Hoey et al. 2024 / Complexity as Design Material
implication: MetroGraph graph structure complexity is appropriate to expose visually—users benefit from seeing schema relationships directly rather than having them abstracted away. The wedge against 'flight to chat' is showing appropriate complexity at scale, not over-simplifying.

definition: Shneiderman's three defining characteristics: (1) continuous representation of objects of interest, (2) physical actions or button presses instead of syntax, (3) rapid incremental reversible operations with immediate visible effect.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation: A Step Beyond Programming Languages
implication: MetroGraph embodies all three: graph entities continuously visible, drag edges instead of join syntax, undo/redo with instant visual updates—this is why the approach is more discoverable and low-error than SQL/chat alternatives.

definition: Approach for AI-generated UIs: instead of generating visual code, provide semantic annotations that guide layout (what information is primary vs. secondary, what actions are core vs. advanced)—reduces gulf between intent and output.
key_refs: Yuan et al. 2025 / Bridging Gulfs in UI Generation through Semantic Guidance
implication: If MetroGraph components are auto-generated by AI (e.g. query builders for custom schemas), semantic guidance ensures generated affordances match user expectations—the graph metaphor itself is semantic guidance.

definition: Paradigm where text (rather than visual shapes/widgets) becomes the primary interaction material—users manipulate text directly as a medium for creating, composing, and understanding operations.
key_refs: Yi et al. 2024-2026 / Texterial: A Text-as-Material Interaction Paradigm for LLM-Mediated Writing
implication: MetroGraph could hybridize: visual graph + text-based refinement (users type constraints or labels inline)—combining direct manipulation's spatial clarity with text's expressiveness.

definition: Principles for designing systems where users don't have a fixed search goal but iteratively refine understanding through exploration—requires strong feedback, visual scaffolding, and low interaction cost.
key_refs: SIGIR 2025 / Design Principles for Exploratory Search Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph is fundamentally an exploratory search tool for complex data/graphs. It must support iterative hypothesis formation (filter entity types) → observation (see results) → refinement (adjust filters)—this is exactly where conversational UI fails.

definition: Recent reconceptualization of affordances through computational lens: affordances as computational functions that a system makes available to an agent (human or machine) given agent capabilities and system state.
key_refs: Xu et al. 2025 / Redefining Affordance via Computational Rationality
implication: For MetroGraph: affordances = set of valid graph operations given schema and current state. Computational view clarifies why visual affordances matter: users must be able to infer the operation set from visual state.

definition: Gibson's philosophical framework: perception is direct pickup of information from the environment; organisms and environments co-evolve such that perceptual systems are attuned to invariant properties (affordances) that matter for survival and action.
key_refs: Gibson 1979 / The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception
Turvey 1992 / Affordances and Prospective Control
implication: MetroGraph visual design should attune users' perception to graph properties (entity clustering, relationship directionality, cardinality) directly, not mediated through abstract queries—leverages ecological psychology's insight about perception-action coupling.

definition: The process of transforming abstract concepts or commands into first-class interactive objects that can be directly manipulated, visualized, and reused within an interface.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon & Mackay 2000 AVI / Reification, Polymorphism and Reuse: Three Principles for Designing Visual Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph should reify abstract query concepts, transformation rules, and workflow steps as visible first-class objects users can edit and manipulate directly, not bury them in dialogs.

definition: The property enabling a single command to be applicable to objects of different types, maintaining a small command vocabulary while increasing interface power as reification adds object types.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon & Mackay 2000 AVI / Reification, Polymorphism and Reuse: Three Principles for Designing Visual Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph should support polymorphic operations (e.g., delete, copy, group) across heterogeneous node and edge types to prevent explosion of specialized commands.

definition: Making previously-provided user input or system output accessible for later use, enabling both input reuse (repeating action sequences) and output reuse (manipulating prior results).
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon & Mackay 2000 AVI / Reification, Polymorphism and Reuse: Three Principles for Designing Visual Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph should enable users to capture and replay interaction sequences, clone subgraphs, and save/parametrize common workflows as reusable patterns.

definition: Interaction paradigms that extend or replace WIMP (Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointing) conventions by leveraging new interaction techniques such as gesture, tangible objects, embodied interaction, and direct manipulation.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction
Jacob et al. 2008 / Reality-Based Interaction: A Framework for Post-WIMP Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph should move beyond traditional menu-driven design, supporting touch gestures, pen input, multi-touch, and node-graph-native affordances.

definition: The objects of primary interest within an application domain that users actively manipulate to achieve tasks, as opposed to interface chrome elements.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction
implication: MetroGraph's domain objects are nodes, edges, subgraphs, and queries; UI must prioritize these over menus, dialogs, and decorative elements.

definition: Tools or interface affordances that mediate user actions on domain objects, similar to physical tools (pens, hammers) that extend human capabilities in the real world.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction
implication: MetroGraph should expose interaction instruments as reifiable objects: selection tools, layout tools, query builders, and filter instruments that are discoverable and composable.

definition: Extension of instrumental interaction principles to AI-augmented systems where prompts are embodied as reifiable interface objects supporting reflection (multiple interpretations) and grounding (instantiation from examples).
key_refs: Riche & Offenwanger 2025 CHI / AI-Instruments: Embodying Prompts as Instruments to Abstract & Reflect Graphical Interface Commands as General-Purpose Tools
implication: MetroGraph can leverage AI to generate query instruments from natural language prompts, with visual reflection showing multiple interpretations and grounding allowing users to refine from examples.
