definition: In AI-augmented systems, the process of capturing ambiguous user intent as a reusable, directly-manipulable interaction instrument that can be edited and refined iteratively.
key_refs: Riche & Offenwanger 2025 CHI / AI-Instruments
implication: MetroGraph should allow users to capture intent (e.g., 'show high-degree nodes') as reifiable query instruments, editable and composable without returning to text prompts.

definition: In AI-augmented interaction, the design principle of presenting multiple interpretations of ambiguous user intent and multiple AI-model responses, enabling users to understand system behavior and refine intent.
key_refs: Riche & Offenwanger 2025 CHI / AI-Instruments
implication: MetroGraph should show multiple query interpretations or layout options generated by AI, allowing users to pick, compare, and blend results rather than accepting a single output.

definition: In AI-augmented systems, the principle of instantiating an AI-generated instrument from concrete examples, results, or extrapolations directly from the user's work context.
key_refs: Riche & Offenwanger 2025 CHI / AI-Instruments
implication: MetroGraph should allow users to create query instruments by selecting example nodes/edges, dragging result patterns, or modifying existing queries rather than writing syntax.

definition: Framework combining text-based instructions (prompts) with direct GUI interactions (brushing, clicking, dragging) to reduce ambiguity and improve precision in human-AI communication.
key_refs: Shen et al. 2025 / Interaction-Augmented Instruction: Modeling the Synergy of Prompts and Interactions in Human-GenAI Collaboration
implication: MetroGraph should accept both text descriptions and visual interactions (node selections, drag paths) together to ground user intent, addressing the ambiguity of text-only RAG/agent systems.

definition: Interaction paradigm where users communicate intent via natural language text prompts to AI systems, trading explicitness for intuitiveness but introducing ambiguity.
key_refs: Shen et al. 2025 / Interaction-Augmented Instruction
implication: While MetroGraph's strength is visual interaction, prompt-based queries should be an alternative channel for users familiar with text-driven workflows, augmented with visual feedback.

definition: Property of interaction where operations can be undone or reverted without permanent consequences, reducing user anxiety and encouraging exploration.
key_refs: Bitterli et al. 2023 CHI / Point of no Undo: Irreversible Interactions as a Design Strategy
DeWitt & Kurata 2014 / Delegate the Undoable, Guard the Irreversible
Shneiderman 1981 / Direct Manipulation Techniques (third principle: rapid, incremental, reversible operations)
Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation
implication: MetroGraph must support full undo/redo for all manipulation actions, with clear visual history; destructive operations should be reversible until explicitly committed.

definition: Theory that cognitive processes are grounded in the body's interactions with the world, suggesting that physical/spatial interactions in interfaces engage cognition more effectively than abstract operations.
key_refs: Embodied Interaction Design literature
Goldin-Meadow 2011 TOCHI / Embodied Cognition and the Magical Future of Interaction Design
Merleau-Ponty embodied perception
Wilson 2002 embodied cognition
implication: MetroGraph should leverage spatial layout and physical metaphors (dragging, proximity, containment) rather than menu hierarchies, since graph exploration is inherently spatial.

definition: Formal framework for grounding HCI theories in natural/social science principles and translating them into actionable design principles; moves beyond descriptive theories to prescriptive guidance.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2022 TOCHI / Generative Theories of Interaction
implication: MetroGraph design should be grounded in cognitive load theory, information foraging theory, and graph cognition research, not just UI conventions.

definition: Theory of how users seek and navigate information in systems, modeled on animal foraging behavior; users make decisions based on scent cues and effort predictions.
key_refs: Chi & Pirolli (2007) / Rational Analyses of Information Foraging
Pirolli & Card (1999) / Information Foraging in Information Access Environments
Pirolli & Card 1999 / Information Foraging Theory
Pirolli 2007 / Information Foraging Theory: Adaptive Interaction with Information
implication: MetroGraph should provide strong information scent (visual cues indicating navigation paths) and minimize effort to discover nodes/relationships, reducing cognitive foraging costs.

definition: Post-WIMP interaction paradigm using meaningful hand or body movements (swipes, pinches, rotations) to communicate intent, leveraging embodied cognition and reducing reliance on menus.
key_refs: Buxton 1990 / Gesture-Based Interaction
Buxton Gesture Based Interaction
Speech-gesture complementarity
Wobbrock & Myers 2006 TEI / Tangible Meets Gestural
implication: MetroGraph should support multi-touch gestures (pinch-to-zoom, two-finger pan, rotation) and pen gestures for annotation, not rely solely on mouse+keyboard.

definition: Design strategies for reducing or managing inherent ambiguity in user intent, especially in natural language or gesture-based systems, through clarification, feedback, and multimodal confirmation.
key_refs: Shen et al. 2025 / Interaction-Augmented Instruction
implication: MetroGraph should resolve ambiguity in user queries through visual feedback, multiple interpretations, and reflection principles, not require users to rephrase until the system guesses correctly.

definition: In interaction design, the principle of partially applying functions/commands with some arguments preset, allowing subsequent arguments to be provided in context or interactively.
key_refs: Beaudouin-Lafon 2000 CHI / Instrumental Interaction
implication: MetroGraph query builders could support curried commands where users select nodes first, then apply filters/transformations, rather than specifying all parameters upfront.

definition: A collaborative paradigm where control and initiative dynamically alternate between human and AI based on competencies, task context, and expected utility. The system proactively assists but respects user authority; the user can always override or take direct control.
key_refs: Horvitz & Paek 2007 / Mixed-initiative interaction (CHI)
Horvitz / Uncertainty, Action, and Interaction: In Pursuit of Mixed-Initiative Computing
Horvitz 1999 / Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces
Horvitz 2007 / People, Agents, and Interaction: Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces
How Users Perceive Mixed-Initiative AI (Huang et al., ACM IUI 2025, 2602.01481)
Mixed-initiative interaction (Allen, 1999)
Zuboff & Hendricks 2020 / Age of Surveillance Capitalism (control dynamics)
implication: MetroGraph must enable dynamic shifts in control: visual manipulation (direct mode) ↔ AI-suggested actions (AI mode). Users need clear affordances for taking/ceding control without friction.

definition: A decision-theoretic model for determining when the system should take action: the system acts when expected utility of proactive intervention exceeds utility of waiting for user initiative, accounting for uncertainty and user cost of manual action.
key_refs: Horvitz 1999 / Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph should only surface AI suggestions (like auto-layouts, query recommendations, visual refinements) when system confidence is high and user effort is substantial; avoid low-value interruptions that reduce engagement.

definition: The dynamic process of exchanging control and responsibility between human and AI during collaborative work; characterized by explicit or implicit negotiation of who drives the current task, with fluid transitions based on need.
key_refs: Large-scale mixed-initiative in information-seeking dialogues
Nargund 2025 / Understanding Mode Switching in Human-AI Collaboration
implication: MetroGraph must signal which entity (user or system) currently 'owns' an action; transitions should be visible and predictable (e.g., shifting from user-drawn nodes to system-suggested connections with one-click acceptance).

definition: The ability of users to dynamically switch between interaction modes (e.g., direct manipulation ↔ AI-guided assistance) based on task state, confidence, or preference. Both predictable switching rules and user-initiated mode changes.
key_refs: Nargund 2025 / Understanding Mode Switching in Human-AI Collaboration: Behavioral Insights and Predictive Modeling
implication: MetroGraph must provide explicit UI controls to switch modes (e.g., 'Let AI layout this graph' → 'Show me step-by-step') and auto-detect when a user naturally needs a different modality, triggering predictive switches without disruption.

concept: Interface Agents vs. Direct Control Debate
definition: The historical HCI tension between delegating work to autonomous agents (Maes) versus preserving user directness (Shneiderman); resolved by mixed-initiative: agents assist but don't override, users remain in control.
key_refs: Shneiderman & Maes 1997 / Direct Manipulation vs. Interface Agents: The Debate
implication: MetroGraph must NOT be a pure agent (auto-generating graphs without user input). Instead: agent proposes layouts/connections → user accepts/rejects/modifies → agent learns. This preserves the best of both paradigms.

definition: Autonomous software entities that observe user behavior, learn preferences, and proactively perform tasks on behalf of users. Characterized by personalization, proactivity, and delegation-based architecture.
key_refs: Maes / Interface Agents: A Review of the Field
implication: MetroGraph's AI components (suggesting node clusters, auto-grouping related data) should act as 'soft agents': observing user patterns, learning what graph structures the user prefers, and suggesting similar structures without taking control.

definition: A formal spectrum ranging from full human control (LOA-1) to full system autonomy (LOA-10), with intermediate levels capturing degrees of automation, advice, recommendation, and override capability. Defines decision authority at each level.
key_refs: Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents (2506 working paper)
Knight First Amendment Institute / Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents
Cloud Security Alliance 2026 / Autonomy Levels for Agentic AI
implication: MetroGraph should support users selecting an LOA for each feature: low LOA for critical graph structures (users decide), high LOA for aesthetic suggestions (system decides); expose the LOA choice in settings and per-action.

definition: The dynamic adjustment of system autonomy during task execution based on context, workload, user expertise, and task phase. System autonomy increases when safe/beneficial, decreases when high-stakes or uncertain.
key_refs: Chiou 2019 / Mixed-Initiative Variable Autonomy for Remotely Operated Mobile Robots
Hierarchical Variable Autonomy Mixed-Initiative Framework for Human-Robot Teaming (2211)
implication: MetroGraph should reduce autonomy when: user is actively editing (high control), task is critical (tight tolerances), system confidence is low. Increase autonomy when: user is reviewing/validating, task is routine, system confidence is high.

definition: A blended autonomy model where human and system simultaneously influence the same action or output. Neither party has unilateral control; both contribute continuously, with smooth arbitration of conflicting commands.
key_refs: General Arbitration Model for Robust Human-Robot Shared Control (2003)
AI-enhanced Shared Control for Assistive Robotic Arm (2306)
Shared control for autonomous robotic navigation: A review (2026)
implication: MetroGraph could enable shared control for layout refinement: user drags nodes, system applies physics-based attraction/repulsion simultaneously, yielding co-authored layouts. Neither user nor system fully determines result.

definition: The formal problem of deciding which decisions/actions belong to humans vs. AI in a collaborative system. Factors include task criticality, system capability, user expertise, time pressure, and safety requirements.
key_refs: Allocation of Decision Authority to Human and Artificial Intelligence (Stanford SIEPR 2020)
AI-Augmented Decision Rights: Redesigning Authority in Human-Machine Organizations
implication: MetroGraph must explicitly allocate decisions: Human owns (node semantics, graph semantics), AI recommends (layout, visual encoding), User+AI co-decide (performance vs. clarity tradeoffs). Make allocation visible in UX.

definition: Systems that take unsolicited initiative to offer help, suggestions, or actions before users explicitly request them. Characterized by anticipation, context-awareness, and expected-utility-based triggering.
key_refs: Horvitz / Uncertainty, Action, and Interaction
Proactive AI Adoption can be Threatening (2509)
Knowing Isn't Understanding (2602)
implication: MetroGraph should proactively suggest: missing relationships based on inferred domain semantics, cluster refinements, query optimizations. But timing is critical: suggest during review phases, not during active editing.

definition: The problem of determining when to interrupt a user with proactive help: too early disrupts flow, too late misses opportunity. Depends on task state, user cognitive load, confidence level, and interruption cost.
key_refs: Assistance or Disruption? (2502)
YETI: Proactive Interventions by Multimodal AI Agents (2501)
Precision Proactivity: Measuring Cognitive Load (2505)
implication: MetroGraph must detect cognitive load (eye tracking, interaction velocity, pause patterns) and suppress proactive help when user is in flow; trigger help during natural pause points or on-demand.

definition: The subjective belief that an AI system will perform its intended function reliably and transparently. Distinct from compliance (following AI recommendations) and reliance (depending on AI). Built through predictability, consistency, and demonstrated competence.
key_refs: Bach et al. 2023 / User Trust in AI: HCI Systematic Review
Developing trustworthy AI: insights from research on interpersonal, human-automation, and human-AI trust (2024)
Lipton 2016 / The Mythos of Model Interpretability
Trust, distrust, and appropriate reliance in (X)AI (2312)
implication: MetroGraph users must trust that suggestions are based on valid reasoning, not random. Show the basis for suggestions (data patterns, user history), acknowledge limitations, maintain consistency so behavior becomes predictable.

definition: The correct calibration of dependence on AI: users over-rely on high-confidence AI recommendations (automation bias) or under-rely due to low trust. Appropriate reliance matches user dependence to actual system capability.
key_refs: Adjust for Trust: Mitigating Trust-Induced Inappropriate Reliance (2502)
Appropriate Reliance on AI-Based Decision Support Systems (2025)
Fine-Grained Appropriate Reliance with Multi-Step Transparent Decision Workflow (2501.10909)
Over-Relying on Reliance: Towards Realistic Evaluations (2504)
Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance (Lee & See, 2004, Human Factors 46.1)
implication: MetroGraph must calibrate reliance: show confidence scores, explain when AI might be wrong, provide human validation mechanisms (edge review before applying bulk suggestions). Users should neither ignore good suggestions nor blindly accept bad ones.

definition: Users' internal, often inaccurate beliefs about how an AI system works, what it can do, and when it will fail. Gaps between users' models and actual system behavior lead to misuse, over-reliance, and frustration.
key_refs: Understanding Uncertainty: How Lay Decision-makers Perceive Uncertainty in Human-AI Decision Making (IUI 2023)
implication: MetroGraph should help users build accurate mental models: explain what the layout engine sees (entity counts, relationship types), when it struggles (sparse graphs, cycles), and how user actions influence its suggestions.

definition: The degree to which a system's behavior, reasoning, and limitations are made visible and understandable to users. Includes system state, decision factors, confidence, and failure modes.
key_refs: Establishing Appropriate Trust in AI through Transparency and Explainability (CHI 2024)
Improving Human-AI Collaboration With Descriptions of AI Behavior (2301)
Lipton 2016 / The Mythos of Model Interpretability
Saeed & Omlin 2021 / Explainable AI Meta-Survey
implication: MetroGraph should expose: which rules determined a suggestion, why a node was grouped with others, what data the layout algorithm is using, what assumptions it made. Use visual affordances (color, annotation) to signal confidence, derivation, and constraints.

definition: Methods for making AI decisions and reasoning interpretable to humans. Ranges from feature importance explanations to contrastive explanations (why this vs. that) to causal reasoning about system recommendations.
key_refs: From Explainable to Interactive AI: A Literature Review (2405)
Interpretability and Explainability: A Machine Learning Zoo Mini-tour (2012)
implication: MetroGraph should provide contrastive explanations for suggestions: 'This node is grouped here because [patterns] similar to [past user decisions]. Alternative: [other possibility with reasons].' Not just 'trust the algorithm.'

definition: Methods for representing, computing, and communicating the confidence/uncertainty of AI predictions. Enables humans to calibrate trust and decide when to verify or override AI suggestions.
key_refs: Using AI Uncertainty Quantification to Improve Human Decision-Making (2309)
Beyond Quantification: Navigating Uncertainty in Professional AI Systems (2509)
'The AI is uncertain, so am I': Navigating Shortcomings of Uncertainty Representations (2023)
implication: MetroGraph should show confidence on every suggestion: layout alternatives ranked by confidence, relationship proposals with probability scores, node positions with uncertainty ellipses. Let users see where the system is confident vs. guessing.

definition: The system's internal representation of user characteristics (expertise, preferences, goals, behavior patterns). Used to personalize interactions, predict needs, and adapt autonomy levels.
key_refs: User Modeling in Human-Computer Interaction (2000)
Creating General User Models from Computer Use (2505)
implication: MetroGraph should learn user patterns: Do they prefer hierarchical or network-style layouts? Do they validate suggestions before applying? Build implicit user models (interaction logs) and explicit (preference settings) to improve suggestions.

definition: The dynamic customization of system behavior (UI, suggestions, autonomy levels) to match individual user characteristics, preferences, and context. Balances model accuracy with perceived relevance.
key_refs: The Personalization Paradox (2103)
Learning User Preferences via Reinforcement Learning (1902)
implication: MetroGraph should personalize incrementally: after 2-3 user corrections to suggestions, reweight the suggestion model. Let users explicitly set preferences (layout style, suggestion aggressiveness). But avoid over-personalizing; some users want consistency.

definition: The system's ability to perceive and reason about contextual information (user location, task state, time, available resources, social setting) and adapt its behavior accordingly.
key_refs: Context-Awareness in Ambient Intelligence (2010)
Mixed-Initiative Context: Structuring and Managing Context for Human-AI Collaboration (2604)
implication: MetroGraph should track context: Is this a new graph or familiar data? Is user in edit mode or review mode? Are they at a decision point or mid-action? Use context to decide what type of help to offer and when.

definition: A paradigm where users iteratively teach ML models through feedback (corrections, labels, examples), and the system improves with each interaction. Tight human-AI feedback loops enable incremental learning.
key_refs: Leveraging Explanations in Interactive Machine Learning (2023)
Soliciting Human-in-the-Loop User Feedback for IML (2008)
implication: MetroGraph could implement active learning: 'Is this relationship important?' feedback trains the ranking model. Each correction refines suggestions. Show the learning progress (accuracy improvements) to users to build trust.

definition: An ML/AI system design where humans iteratively validate, correct, or refine system outputs; human feedback is used to improve model quality. Combines human judgment with algorithmic scalability.
key_refs: Human-in-the-Loop Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review (2025)
Toward Neurodivergent-Aware Productivity: HITL Framework (2507)
implication: MetroGraph should embed HITL: batch AI suggestions (e.g., 10 layout alternatives) → user reviews & picks best → system learns from pick → refines future suggestions. Combine human judgment with algorithmic breadth.

definition: Channels by which users communicate preferences, corrections, and judgments back to the system (explicit: rated feedback; implicit: behavior logs). Critical for closing human-in-the-loop learning loops.
key_refs: Interactive Machine Learning Explanations (2023)
Design Considerations for Human Oversight of AI (2510)
implication: MetroGraph should support low-friction feedback: thumbs up/down on suggestions, drag-to-correct (implicit feedback), bulk accept/reject. Make it clear that feedback trains the system, building user investment.

definition: A psychological trait reflecting whether users believe outcomes result from their own actions (internal) or external forces (external). In AI contexts: users with high internal locus prefer direct control; external locus more comfortable delegating.
key_refs: Application of Experiential Locus of Control to User Judgment (2015)
Dix et al. 2003 / Human-Computer Interaction (3rd ed.) / agency and control
Rotter 1966 / Generalized expectancies for internal versus external control of reinforcement
Rotter 1966 / Locus of Control Theory In Psychology
Trust, Shared Understanding and Locus of Control in Mixed-Initiative Robotic Systems (2107)
implication: MetroGraph's UI should respect locus-of-control differences: offer 'full control' profiles (direct drag, minimal AI) and 'trust the system' profiles (AI-driven with spot corrections). Don't assume all users want the same autonomy level.

definition: The degree to which users perceive themselves as able to influence outcomes and make meaningful choices in a system. High agency when users feel control is effective and choices matter.
key_refs: What's So Human about Human-AI Collaboration (2503)
Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence: Foundations and Approaches (2601)
implication: MetroGraph must preserve user agency: every suggestion is a proposal, never an override. Undo/redo at all levels. Show that user edits influence future suggestions (reinforcement loop). Users should feel they drive the outcome.

definition: The legal/ethical requirement that humans retain meaningful control over consequential AI decisions. Not just nominal authority, but substantive understanding, ability to override, and responsibility for outcomes.
key_refs: Human-controllable AI: Meaningful Human Control (2512)
Meaningful human control: actionable properties for AI system development
Rahwan 2025 / Human-controllable AI: Meaningful Human Control
implication: MetroGraph's graph structures often represent organizational/data models; users must meaningfully control them. Cannot auto-apply suggestions; must require explicit approval for structural changes. Maintain audit trail of who approved what.

definition: Interactive systems where humans and AI collaborate to explore, analyze, and communicate insights from data. Combines automated data processing with human visual perception and domain reasoning.
key_refs: Human-Computer Collaboration for Visual Analytics (2304)
Automating the Path: HCAI and Visualization (2504)
implication: MetroGraph is itself a visual analytics tool. Apply collaborative visualization principles: AI suggests hypotheses (potential clusters), users validate via visual inspection, system refines based on inspection patterns.

definition: Design principles for representing abstract data visually (e.g., Munzner's abstraction-based framework, Tufte's data-ink ratio, grammar of graphics). Ensures information is comprehensible and actionable.
key_refs: Munzner / Visualization Analysis and Design
Tufte / The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
implication: MetroGraph's visual encoding (node size, color, position, edge thickness) must follow vis principles: no chartjunk, maximize data-ink ratio, use color perceptually. AI-driven suggestions must respect these principles.

definition: Empirical findings on when human-AI teams outperform human-only or AI-only: varies by task type (decision vs. creative), domain, team composition, and quality of collaboration mechanisms.
key_refs: Vaccaro 2024 / When combinations of humans and AI are useful: meta-analysis of 106 studies, 370 effect sizes
implication: MetroGraph's effectiveness depends on matching task and collaboration mode: decision tasks (Is this relationship real?) → AI proposes, human verifies. Creative tasks (What graph structure best represents this?) → human leads, AI assists.

concept: Decision Task vs. Creative Task in Collaboration
definition: Meta-analytic finding that human-AI teams excel at judgment/decision tasks (validating, filtering) but may underperform at open-ended creative tasks without careful collaboration design.
key_refs: Vaccaro 2024 / When combinations of humans and AI are useful
implication: MetroGraph should detect task type: decision task (Does this relationship exist? Is this node important?) → trust AI scores. Creative task (How should this data be grouped?) → let user lead, AI suggests alternatives.

definition: Empirical taxonomy of how humans and AI exchange control during collaborative creation: sequential (human then AI), parallel (simultaneous), nested (one within the other), and dynamic switching.
key_refs: Exploring Collaboration Patterns in Human-AI Co-creation (CHI/PACM 2024)
Prototypical Human-AI Collaboration Behaviors in LLM-Assisted Writing (2505)
implication: MetroGraph should support multiple patterns: sequential (user sketches layout → AI refines), parallel (user colors while AI repositions), nested (AI processes bulk relationships; user refines specific ones). Expose patterns in tutorial/help.

definition: A design methodology prioritizing human autonomy, values, and control in AI systems. Iterative process: define human values, allocate decision authority, design feedback loops, evaluate for human outcomes.
key_refs: HCAI Methodological Framework (2311)
Human-Centered Human-AI Collaboration (HCHAC) Framework (2505)
UX 3.0 Paradigm Framework for Human-Centered AI (2506)
implication: MetroGraph's design must be grounded in HCAI: explicitly define which decisions users control (graph semantics), which AI recommends (layout), which are shared (performance tradeoffs). Iterate on human values, not just system performance.

definition: A newer paradigm where AI systems are framed as semi-autonomous agents that take initiative, learn from context, and engage in multi-turn interactions. Contrasts with tool-like or conversational-only interfaces.
key_refs: Contemporary Agent Technology (2509)
Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents (2506)
Agentic Web: Weaving the Next Web with AI Agents (2507)
implication: MetroGraph's AI layer should be agentic: proposes multi-step actions (cluster nodes, infer relationships, adjust layout), monitors outcomes, refines. But always reversible and transparent to preserve user control.

concept: Design Principles for Generative AI Applications
definition: Contemporary best practices for UI/UX with generative AI: artifact optimization (refining outputs), possibility exploration (showing alternatives), integration with workflows, transparency, and human oversight.
key_refs: Amershi et al. 2024 / Design Principles for Generative AI Applications
Chiang et al. 2023 / Toward General Design Principles for Generative AI
Design Principles for Generative AI Applications (CHI 2024)
implication: MetroGraph should follow generative AI principles: show multiple layout options (possibility exploration), let users refine suggestions (artifact optimization), integrate suggestions into workflow (not separate), surface confidence and reasoning.

definition: The human tendency to seek/favor information confirming existing beliefs. In AI oversight: users may uncritically accept suggestions that fit their prior assumptions, missing errors. Scalable oversight challenges.
key_refs: Confirmation bias: A challenge for scalable oversight (2507)
implication: MetroGraph must combat confirmation bias: deliberately surface alternative graph structures, ask for justifications before accepting bulk suggestions, log accepted-then-reverted suggestions to detect bias patterns.

definition: Using natural language dialogue as the primary control interface for systems; agent understands user intent, asks clarifying questions, and takes actions. Blurs line between chat and graphical manipulation.
key_refs: Conversational Information Seeking (2201)
DiscussLLM: Teaching Large Language Models When to Speak (2508)
Mixed-Initiative Dialog for Human-Robot Collaborative Manipulation (2508)
implication: MetroGraph could supplement visual editing with conversational commands ('Group these three nodes,' 'Find relationships to Product?'). Dialogue and visual editing coexist; system detects mode preference and adapts.

concept: Fostering Human Learning in Human-AI Collaboration
definition: Evidence that human-AI synergy requires users to learn how to work with the AI: its strengths, weaknesses, and reasoning. Systems that teach users (transparency, examples, progressive disclosure) yield better collaboration.
key_refs: Fostering human learning is crucial for boosting human-AI synergy (2512)
implication: MetroGraph should include onboarding: show how layout algorithm thinks, explain what makes a good suggestion, provide guided tours of AI capabilities. Users who understand the system collaborate better.

definition: Software entities that perceive their environment, learn from observation, and autonomously execute tasks on behalf of users to reduce cognitive burden. Assumes agent can reliably infer user intent without explicit instruction.
key_refs: Maes 1997 / Intelligent Software Agents vs. User-Controlled Direct Manipulation
Lieberman & Selker 1997 / Agents for the User Interface
Völkel et al. 2020 / What is 'Intelligent' in Intelligent User Interfaces?
implication: MetroGraph's risk of 'chat-first' agent builder interfaces: autonomous graph editing agents create flight to conversation (worst-of-both-worlds). Solution: agents as recommendations + human approval, not autonomous action.

definition: User's subjective experience of influence and control over system behavior. Psychological sense that actions produce intended outcomes; mediated by feedback quality, predictability, and reversibility. Higher agency correlates with satisfaction and adoption.
key_refs: Schachter & Singer 1962 / Cognitive, social, and physiological determinants of emotional state
Moore & Haggard 2010 / The sense of agency in human-computer interactions (neuroscience review)
Haggard & Chambon 2012 / Sense of agency
implication: Critical failure mode: autonomous agents reduce sense of agency even when improving outcome (user feels 'sidelined'). MetroGraph must preserve agency through visible intermediate steps, clear causality (what action triggered this?), and undo/modify capability.

definition: Achieving appropriate user confidence in agent capability: high enough to use recommendations, low enough to avoid over-reliance. Overcalibration (too much trust) causes misuse; undercalibration (too little trust) prevents adoption. Dynamic process requiring feedback on agent failures.
key_refs: Bach et al. 2023 / User Trust in AI: HCI Systematic Review
Calibrating Trust, Reliance and Dependence in Variable-Reliability Automation
Lee & See 2004 / Trust in automation
Lipton 2016 / The Mythos of Model Interpretability
Muir & Moray 1996 / Trust in automation: A review
Trust in AI: progress, challenges, and future directions / Nature 2024
Wang et al. 2019 / Adaptive trust calibration for human-AI collaboration
implication: MetroGraph risk: opaque agents (LLM-based without reasoning logs) cause miscalibration—users either blind-trust or refuse to use. Solution: progressive transparency that shows agent capability boundaries, failure modes, and example outputs to calibrate expectations.

definition: Design practice of exposing agent decision-making process, goals, and confidence levels to users. Not just binary (transparent/opaque) but spectrum: what information to show, when, in what form. Fluent output can mask uncertainty; effective transparency requires deliberate design.
key_refs: Amershi et al. 2019 / Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
Wang & Müller 2021 / Explanations based on the most influential training examples
Röchert et al. 2024 / AI Transparency in the Age of LLMs: A Human-Centered Research Roadmap
implication: LLM fluency masks uncertainty (critical weakness). MetroGraph must expose: agent confidence, alternative suggestions, reasoning steps, and explicit boundaries (e.g., 'agent cannot modify schema'). Transparency mechanisms are first defense against trust miscalibration.

definition: Graduated spectrum from user-controlled (human at every decision) to fully autonomous (agent acts independently). Intermediate levels: suggestions with human review, agent-initiated with veto, agent acts then reports. Design choice, not binary.
key_refs: Sheridan & Verplank 1978 / Levels of automation
Parasuraman et al. 2000 / A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation
Degani et al. 2024 / Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents
implication: MetroGraph's 'copilot-vs-autonomous-agent' distinction: start with suggestions (Level 1), progress to agent-initiated-with-approval (Level 3) only as trust earned. Variable autonomy per task type and complexity level.

definition: Tension between natural language instruction (prompts: user writes description of intent) vs. graphical direct manipulation (user acts on visual objects). Prompts offer flexibility but ambiguity risk; direct manipulation offers clarity but limits expressiveness.
key_refs: Spector et al. 2023 / DirectGPT: A Direct Manipulation Interface to Interact with Large Language Models
Shneiderman 1997 / Direct manipulation vs. interface agents (broader principle)
implication: MetroGraph core wedge: prompts (workflow graph as natural language description) create unpredictability; direct manipulation (visual nodes/edges) provides control + feedback. Best-of-both: suggestions from LLM, approval via drag-drop actions.

definition: Design distinction: Copilot (agent as assistant making suggestions, human decides) vs. Autonomous Agent (agent executes independently, reports outcomes). Copilot preserves control perception; autonomy improves efficiency at risk of overcalibration.
key_refs: Pienso 2025 / Direct Manipulation vs. Interface Agents: Revisiting the Classic HCI Debate
Lim et al. 2024 / The agentic interface: principles and patterns for autonomous User Experiences
implication: MetroGraph's critical design choice: default to copilot (suggestions + approval) to solve HCI failure of agent-builder tools. Autonomy as earned privilege post-trust calibration, scoped to reversible operations.

definition: System's ability to provide intelligible explanations of decisions/outputs to users. Distinct from transparency (showing state) and interpretability (internal model structure). Good explanation answers 'why did the agent do X?' in user's terms.
key_refs: Bach et al. 2023 / User Trust in AI-Enabled Systems: HCI Perspective
Bussone et al. 2015 / Explainability in Human-Agent Systems
Explaining Explanations in AI (2811.01439)
Holistic Explainable AI (H-XAI) (Lakkaraju et al., 2508.05792)
Lipton 2018 / The Mythos of Model Interpretability
One Explanation Does Not Fit All (2001.09734)
Saeed & Omlin 2021 / Explainable AI Meta-Survey
Selvaraju et al. 2017 / Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-based Localization
implication: For MetroGraph LLM agents: explain 'why did agent propose this transformation?' in graph-native terms (e.g., 'reduces cycles,' 'improves query performance'). Explanations in user's domain build trust faster than technical internals.

definition: Degree to which user can influence system behavior through deliberate action. Includes: input authority (what user can ask), decision authority (user approves before execution), output authority (user can edit/reject results).
key_refs: Shneiderman 1997 / Direct manipulation vs. interface agents (central to debate)
Pienso 2025 / Design principles: 'exceptional agent without thoughtful UI is destined for POC graveyard'
implication: Shneiderman-Maes core tension: agents reduce user control → unpredictability → abandonment. MetroGraph solution: design agencies (agent actions are suggestions) rather than autonomy (agent actions are decisions).

definition: Speed and quality of system response to user action. Shneiderman principle: 100ms feedback threshold for perception of responsiveness. Poor feedback (slow, ambiguous, delayed) breaks users' sense of control and increases cognitive load.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1981 / Direct Manipulation Techniques (immediate feedback principle)
Nielsen 1993 / Usability Engineering (response time thresholds)
implication: MetroGraph graph interactions (drag nodes, add edges) must respond <100ms for direct manipulation feel. Agent operations (suggestions, transformations) must show progress indicators and intermediate states, not just final result.

definition: Agents that learn from user behavior via observation or explicit instruction (programming-by-example) rather than explicit rules. Lieberman's approach: master-apprentice relationship where agent watches and generalizes user patterns.
key_refs: Lieberman 1995 / A learning interface agent for scheduling meetings
Lieberman & Selker 1997 / Agents for the User Interface (teacher-student metaphor)
implication: Contrast to prompt-based agents: learning agents reduce need for explicit instruction but introduce trust risk (what did agent learn from my actions?). MetroGraph might support learning from past query patterns, but requires extreme transparency.

definition: System that perceives user's attention (via gaze, interaction patterns, or explicit signals) and adapts agent initiative accordingly. Horvitz concept: don't interrupt when user is focused; offer assistance when user pauses or searches.
key_refs: Horvitz 2007 / People, Agents, and Interaction (attention-sensitive interface design)
Horvitz & Paek 2007 / Mixed-initiative interaction
implication: For MetroGraph: agent suggests graph optimizations proactively when user pauses or explicitly asks ('suggest query improvements'), not while user is editing. Respects user agency and reduces cognitive load from unsolicited suggestions.

definition: System design where human retains decision authority over agent actions. Agent gathers information, makes recommendations, humans approve/modify. Contrasts with fully automated systems.
key_refs: Horvitz & Paek 2007 / Mixed-initiative interaction
Bansal et al. 2024 / ResearStudio: A Human-Intervenable Framework for Building Controllable Deep-Research Agents
implication: MetroGraph's core architecture: human-in-loop at decision points. Agent identifies graph anomalies/optimization opportunities, human approves/rejects/modifies. Preserves control perception and prevents silent failures.

definition: Designing agents with human-like characteristics (names, avatars, conversational language). Increases engagement and perceived competence but risks inflating trust beyond actual capability. Design tradeoff.
key_refs: Frontiers in Computer Science 2025 / Effect of anthropomorphism and perceived intelligence in chatbot avatars
implication: MetroGraph risk: natural language agent explanations (fluent, conversational) create false trust. Counterbalance with explicit confidence markers, bounded scope declarations, and transparent failure modes rather than humanizing language.

concept: Cognitive Load Theory Applied to Agent Systems
definition: Agent systems increase cognitive load in two ways: (1) users must audit agent decisions (extraneous load), (2) users must model agent capabilities (germane load for trust). Transparency mechanisms reduce extraneous load; progressive disclosure manages learning load.
key_refs: Sweller 1988 / Cognitive load during problem solving
Springer 2022 / Theory-based approach for assessing cognitive load during time-critical resource-managing human-computer interactions
implication: MetroGraph design principle: reduce extraneous load (visual clarity, direct manipulation) and structure germane load (progressive disclosure of agent capabilities, worked examples). Agent suggestions should feel like 'helpful sidebar,' not 'overwhelming choice.'

definition: Agent's ability to produce correct outputs consistently. But in agent design, perceived reliability (user's belief about capability) matters more than actual reliability. Transparency improves calibration; failures without explanation erode trust faster.
key_refs: Amershi et al. 2019 / Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (design for graceful failures)
ArXiv 2025 / Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability
implication: MetroGraph: for graph agents, explicitly state reliability bounds (e.g., 'agent optimizes for query latency but may miss secondary metrics'). Visible failure examples (agent misclassified schema type) build accurate mental models.

definition: Shneiderman's principle: users should feel responsible for system outcomes. Agents that act autonomously disrupt this—users either blame themselves (undeserved guilt) or blame system (eroding trust). Design must clarify causality.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1997 / Direct manipulation vs. interface agents (central principle: 'responsibility will be the central issue in this debate')
implication: MetroGraph: make causality explicit—'You asked agent to optimize query, agent proposed index addition, You approved'—each step visible. Users feel responsible when they see their approval decision, not when agent silently acts.

definition: Principles from Munzner's nested model (domain → abstraction → encoding → algorithm) applied to displaying agent reasoning: what data (domain), what task does agent solve (abstraction), how to encode decisions (visual marks/channels), what algorithm renders it (efficiency).
key_refs: Munzner 2014 / Visualization Analysis and Design (nested model)
Tufte 1989 / Visual Design of the User Interface (information before polish)
implication: MetroGraph agents as visual output: visualize graph transformations as explicit edits (highlight added nodes, changed edges), not text descriptions. Use visual channels (color, animation) to show confidence, reversibility, and alternatives.

definition: Design pattern: grant autonomy proportional to reversibility of action. Two-way doors (editable, undoable) → high autonomy. One-way doors (permanent, non-recoverable) → explicit approval. Operationalizes Shneiderman's reversibility principle.
key_refs: DeWitt & Kurata 2024 / Delegate the Undoable, Guard the Irreversible: Tiering Agent Autonomy by Reversibility
implication: MetroGraph practical principle: agent can autonomously add indexes (reversible: can drop later), but requires approval for schema changes (irreversible). Scales autonomy safely without explicit capability modeling.

definition: Agents can be manipulated by adversarial UI designs (dark patterns) more easily than humans. Implications for agent-agent interaction, delegation chains, and supply chain risks. Requires human oversight even for autonomous agents.
key_refs: ArXiv 2025 / Dark Patterns Meet GUI Agents: LLM Agent Susceptibility to Manipulative Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph multi-agent scenarios: if agent calls other agents or third-party APIs, must audit for dark patterns. Visible audit trails (what agent saw, what it decided) protect against hidden manipulation.

definition: Critical finding: transparency mechanisms designed to build trust can paradoxically increase vulnerability by creating false confidence. Users over-rely on explanations without validating them. Requires complementary accountability mechanisms.
key_refs: ArXiv 2025 / Engineering Trust, Creating Vulnerability: A Socio-Technical Analysis of AI Interface Design
implication: MetroGraph caution: transparent agent reasoning logs can create false confidence. Complement transparency with: bounded scope declarations ('agent only optimizes for latency'), visible failure examples, and explicit approval for high-stakes changes.

definition: A computing paradigm that augments the real physical world by coupling digital information to everyday physical objects and environments, making information perceptually and computationally coupled to physical representations.
key_refs: Ishii & Ullmer 1997 Tangible Bits
Ullmer & Ishii foundational TUI characteristics
implication: Provides foundational paradigm for giving 'substance' and materiality to database nodes; makes abstract graph structure perceptually coupled to physical topology.

definition: Interaction grounded in phenomenological understanding where meaning arises through pre-reflective bodily engagement with the world; perception and action are inseparable, and understanding emerges from physical doing rather than abstract representation alone.
key_refs: Dourish 2001 Where the Action Is
Heidegger Wittgenstein phenomenology
implication: Explains why spatial graph metaphors feel intuitive and learnable without explicit instruction; the body 'already knows' how to navigate through embodied spatial structures.

definition: The engagement of the user's body and the physical material world as central design dimensions; includes material properties, spatial constraints, bodily affordances, and sensorimotor feedback as features that scaffold interaction.
key_refs: Hornecker & Buur 2006
Hornecker Physicality in Tangible Interaction
implication: Physical weight, texture, and constraints of nodes become design features that guide exploration without explicit instructions; material properties communicate interaction affordances.

definition: The use of spatial properties, layout, and arrangement of physical objects as primary interaction mechanisms; physical space becomes semantically meaningful and directly navigable.
key_refs: Hornecker Grip on Tangible Interaction
Spatial cognition in embodied systems
implication: Metro-map spatial layout becomes directly explorable through physical manipulation; traversing physical space mirrors query traversal through database topology.

definition: Learning through hands-on physical manipulation of tangible objects where the body and its movements are active agents in knowledge construction; haptic interaction and kinesthetic feedback enhance knowledge transfer.
key_refs: Li et al 2022 Meta-Analysis of TEI Learning
Antle & Wise embodied learning
Embodiment effects in pedagogy
implication: Exploring database graph through physical tangibles enables deeper learning of data relationships; users retain query patterns and structural understanding better through embodied manipulation.

definition: Physical and perceptual properties of objects that communicate possible actions; how material design and form 'speak' about interaction possibilities without requiring explicit instructions or labels.
key_refs: Norman 1988/2013 Design of Everyday Things
Affordances vs Signifiers distinction
implication: Node shape, texture, and weight signal their role in graph structure; edge thickness communicates relationship strength through haptic and visual affordances.

definition: Philosophical foundation asserting that perception is embodied and pre-reflective; the body engages with the world prior to conscious thought, grounding all knowledge in sensorimotor experience.
key_refs: Merleau-Ponty Phenomenology of Perception
Embodied perception as foundation
implication: Physical interaction with graph feels intuitive because it leverages pre-reflective bodily knowledge; no learning curve for basic spatial navigation.

definition: Interaction technique enabling simultaneous multi-point contact on touch-sensitive surfaces; two-handed and multi-user manipulation enables complex spatial transformations through coordinated physical actions.
key_refs: Hinckley Multi-touch Manipulation
Surface computing interaction design
implication: Multiple database analysts can simultaneously manipulate different graph regions; natural bimanual rotation/scaling/translation of subgraphs.

definition: Computer-supported physical representations of data using tangible materials and objects; analogous to data visualization but leveraging material, spatial, and embodied properties for exploration and understanding.
key_refs: Data Physicalization Wiki
Physical visualizations emerging paradigm
implication: Database graph becomes physical network structure; nodes/edges materially represent database topology, enabling tactile exploration.

definition: Physical interfaces that dynamically alter their shape, texture, or form to represent digital state or enable different affordances; morphing materials and actuated structures create responsive physical feedback.
key_refs: Shape-Changing Interfaces Survey 2018
inFORM dynamic shape display
Morphing materials
implication: Graph nodes can dynamically reshape to show importance, state changes, or query results; height variation shows metric prominence.

definition: Theoretical framework positing that meaning emerges in human-material interaction; physical objects are active agents shaping cognition and culture rather than passive vessels of information.
key_refs: Material Engagement Theory
Objects shaping thought
implication: Choice of physical material for nodes/edges becomes cognitive and semiotic choice; material properties influence how users perceive and reason about data.

definition: Tactile and kinesthetic feedback through electrical stimulation, vibration, mechanical resistance, or temperature; engages the sense of touch as active channel in interaction, complementing vision.
key_refs: Electrical Stimulation Haptic Feedback Survey 2024
Haptic technologies ERM LRA piezoelectric
implication: Tactile feedback when manipulating nodes/edges (resistance, vibration at connection points) enriches interaction and provides confirmation of actions.

definition: Tangible interfaces designed for co-located multi-user interaction where embodied constraints and spatial layout enable collaborative problem-solving, peer learning, and negotiation without explicit communication protocols.
key_refs: Hornecker Embodied Facilitation
Reactable collaborative tangible interface
TEI collaborative studies
implication: Multiple database analysts explore graph together; shared physical interface enables peer discussion and collaborative query formulation.

definition: Design theme for tangible systems where physical embodiment and spatial constraints scaffold collaborative interaction; multiple access points and tailored representations enable natural coordination and learning.
key_refs: Hornecker 2005 Embodied Facilitation ECSCW
implication: Physical graph topology naturally facilitates coordination between analysts; no need for explicit protocols—spatial arrangement guides collaborative reasoning.

definition: Paradigm shift from screen-centric computing to environment-embedded interaction; computing fades into background, enabling seamless human-world interaction without explicit focus on technology.
key_refs: Weiser 1991 Ubiquitous Computing third paradigm
implication: Physical graph becomes integrated part of analyst workspace rather than isolated application; technology disappears into data exploration task.

definition: Tangible objects designed to be grasped and physically manipulated; physical interaction with handles/graspable surfaces directly controls digital state through intuitive embodied metaphor.
key_refs: Fitzmaurice Graspable Interfaces
Ishii & Ullmer Tangible Bits graspable category
implication: Database nodes designed as graspable objects with clear grasp points; physical position and rotation directly map to query position/properties.

definition: Digital information presented in physical form at periphery of attention; leverages embodied perception and ambient awareness to convey information without requiring conscious focus or explicit interaction.
key_refs: Ishii & Ullmer Tangible Bits ambient media
Peripheral information displays
implication: Physical graph can present aggregate data properties (connectivity, density, change magnitude) as ambient properties (height variation, color gradients) perceived without active attention.

definition: Physical surfaces augmented with digital tracking, projection, and computation; real-world objects and tokens tagged with digital information create seamless hybrid interaction spaces.
key_refs: Rekimoto 1999 Augmented Surfaces CHI
Hybrid digital-physical interaction
implication: Physical tokens on augmented surface represent graph nodes; projected connections show relationships; manipulation updates digital query state.

definition: Design of embodied interfaces that actively engage spatial reasoning abilities (mental rotation, perspective-taking, wayfinding, spatial memory); physical interaction enhances development of spatial skills.
key_refs: Antle & Wise Embodied Interaction Spatial Skills
Spatial cognition development
implication: Exploring physical graph strengthens analyst's spatial understanding of database structure; 3D spatial reasoning becomes skill developed through interaction.

definition: Embodied physical interaction reduces mental/cognitive burden by offloading abstract processing to sensorimotor and kinesthetic systems; working memory load decreases through distributed cognition across body and environment.
key_refs: Cognitive Load Theory
TEI Meta-Analysis embodiment effects
Visual vs verbal cognitive load
implication: Physical graph exploration reduces working memory load compared to screen-only analysis; analysts can focus on high-level patterns rather than low-level navigation.

definition: Meaningful correspondence between physical properties/structure and digital meaning; physical affordances and layout communicate conceptual structure and enable intuitive understanding.
key_refs: TEI Meta-Analysis metaphor meanings
Embodied metaphor theory
implication: Physical arrangement of nodes mirrors database topology; edge connections physically represent data relationships; traversal metaphor matches query/exploration patterns.

definition: Tangible/physical interaction enabling remote users to have embodied presence in shared physical space; combines telepresence with tangible manipulation for distributed collaborative embodied interaction.
key_refs: HoloBots Telepresence with Tangible Robots
Remote embodied collaboration
implication: Remote data analysts can collaborate on physical graph with embodied presence; distributed teams experience shared spatial reasoning through remotely-controlled tangible proxies.

definition: Systems that sense and adapt to environmental/user/location context; interaction behavior and information presentation adjust based on contextual signals enabling location-aware and situation-appropriate responses.
key_refs: Context-Aware Computing Encyclopedia
Sensors and location-aware interfaces
implication: Physical graph display adapts to analyst location, role, task context; different analysts see different representations based on their contextual needs.

definition: Affordances that change over time or in response to interaction; physical objects morph to present different interaction possibilities as state changes, enabling responsive and contextual guidance.
key_refs: inFORM Shape Display
Dynamic affordances in shape-changing interfaces
implication: Nodes actuate to signal importance or state; edges raise to highlight connection paths; physical affordances invite interaction with high-priority data.

definition: Paradigm where physical tangible objects serve as proxies for data elements; user manipulations of tangibles directly drive analytical queries, filtering, and transformations on underlying datasets.
key_refs: TangibleNet Network Data Visualization
MarioChart Autonomous Tangibles
Tangible data exploration systems
implication: Users grasp and manipulate physical nodes to issue queries; moving node position filters; rotating node orientation changes analysis perspective; manipulation becomes query language.

definition: Interaction combining physical tangible objects with digital augmentation in mixed/augmented reality environments; tangible objects mediate digital interaction in hybrid physical-digital space.
key_refs: Mixed Reality Interaction Survey 2021
Tangible AR/VR integration
implication: Physical tokens tracked in AR space; digital information layer shows connectivity/properties on physical topology; real and virtual seamlessly integrated.

definition: Empirical characterization of gesture performance on touch-enabled displays; systematic design and evaluation of gesture vocabulary for accuracy, speed, and learnability.
key_refs: CHI 2011 Gesture Analysis Mobile
Touch gesture performance studies
implication: Gesture vocabulary for graph navigation on touch-augmented tangible surfaces designed based on empirical performance data.

definition: Psychological and emotional attachment to physical artifacts; perception of fragility, safety, ownership, and aesthetic appeal influences interaction patterns and user commitment.
key_refs: Shape-Changing Interfaces Fragility Study 2025
Emotional design and physical objects
implication: Material choice and affordance design evoke emotional investment in graph analysis; users care more about careful manipulation when objects feel valuable.

definition: Using digital fabrication technologies (3D printing, laser cutting, CNC) to rapidly prototype and customize tangible interfaces; enables domain-specific physical designs tailored to application needs.
key_refs: BrickStARt Digital Fabrication Tangible Design
Personal fabrication for interaction
implication: Custom tangible graph nodes fabricated for specific database domains; node shape encodes schema type; edge form encodes relationship semantics.

definition: Co-design methodology involving end-users as active partners in tangible interface creation; stakeholders and domain experts shape physical interaction possibilities and representations.
key_refs: Participatory Design User-Centered Research
Co-creation in HCI
implication: Database engineers and analysts co-design physical graph representation; end-user expertise shapes node affordances and connection representations.

definition: Premier international peer-reviewed venue for tangible/embedded/embodied interaction research (since 2007); establishes empirical evidence base and community standards for tangible and embodied design.
key_refs: TEI Conference DBLP Index
Li et al Meta-Analysis of TEI
implication: MetroGraph design grounded in 15+ years of peer-reviewed TEI research community standards and empirical findings; evidence base for embodied interaction efficacy.

definition: Use of spatial position, proximity, and arrangement as primary encoding mechanism for data semantics; spatial relationships become semantically meaningful rather than arbitrary, enabling direct spatial reasoning about data.
key_refs: Information Visualization spatial encoding
Tufte design principles
implication: Database topology directly encoded in physical layout; node proximity mirrors edge connectivity; traversal path encodes query logic.

definition: Design strategy leveraging fundamental embodied understanding (spatial, kinesthetic, sensorimotor) to create intuitive mappings between physical actions and digital operations.
key_refs: Embodied metaphor theory
Physical metaphors in interface design
implication: Graph rotation in hand parallels mental rotation of structure; path tracing matches query traversal; connection pulling mirrors relationship formation.

definition: The inherent inability of natural language to fully specify meaning without contextual grounding; includes word-sense ambiguity, referential ambiguity, and scope ambiguity that conversational systems struggle to resolve without visual or structural context.
key_refs: Dealing with Semantic Underspecification in Multimodal NLP (ACL 2023)
Semantic Underspecification - Language and Linguistics Compass (2010)
Disambiguation in Conversational Question Answering in the Era of LLM (2025)
implication: MetroGraph must complement conversational querying with visual node/edge representations that ground semantic meaning; pure text cannot fully specify graph structures or query intent without spatial scaffolding.

definition: The progressive loss or unavailability of sufficient contextual information across dialogue turns, causing systems to misunderstand user intent due to missing pronoun resolution, implicit references, or unstated assumptions.
key_refs: Conversational Information Seeking (2022)
A Survey of Conversational Search (2024)
Towards Universal Dialogue State Tracking (2018)
implication: MetroGraph must make query context (selected nodes, filters, scope) visually persistent; temporal linear dialogue cannot reliably maintain structured state that users expect to persist across interaction.

concept: Intent Recognition Failure in Complex Dialogue
definition: The inability of conversational systems to accurately classify user intents from natural language utterances, especially when users express multiple simultaneous goals, have out-of-distribution phrasings, or rely on conversational implicature.
key_refs: Intent Recognition in Dialogue Systems (2024)
Multi-Intent Recognition in Dialogue Understanding (2024)
Dialogue Agents 101: Critical Ingredients for Designing Effective Conversational Systems (2023)
implication: MetroGraph must provide visual intent specification (drag nodes, set constraints, compose operators) rather than relying on NLU; explicit structural inputs are more reliable than natural language for graph manipulation.

definition: The systematic failure of conversational systems to employ human-expected repair and clarification strategies when misunderstanding occurs; systems lack the contextual models and cooperative principles that humans use to recover from dialogue breakdowns.
key_refs: An analysis of dialogue repair in virtual assistants (2024)
System and User Strategies to Repair Conversational Breakdowns (2024)
Exploring human error recovery strategies: Implications for spoken dialogue systems (2005)
Clarification in Spoken Dialogue Systems (2003)
implication: MetroGraph should provide immediate visual feedback (highlighting selections, showing query results) to surface misunderstandings before requiring verbal repair; proactive error prevention through UI feedback reduces reliance on conversational error recovery.

definition: The inability of conversational systems to infer speaker intent from conversational implicature, context-dependent meaning, and cooperative principles (Grice); systems fail to understand what is meant versus what is literally said.
key_refs: Expanding the Set of Pragmatic Considerations in Conversational AI (2023)
Implicature in Interaction: Understanding Implicature Improves Alignment in Human-LLM Interaction (2024)
Towards an Analysis of Discourse and Interactional Pragmatic Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language Models (2024)
implication: MetroGraph must use explicit structural affordances (node colors, layout, annotations) to communicate system intent instead of relying on conversational implicature; visual grammar is less ambiguous than natural language pragmatics.

definition: The core architectural limitation where systems must maintain and update a consistent belief state about dialogue context across turns; heterogeneous dialogue representations, domain-specific state schemas, and cross-domain generalization failures prevent robust state maintenance.
key_refs: Dialogue State Tracking in Task-Oriented Systems (2023)
Towards Universal Dialogue State Tracking (2018)
Evaluating LLM-based Agents for Multi-Turn Conversations: A Survey (2025)
implication: MetroGraph must make graph state visually persistent through a spatial canvas instead of maintaining hidden dialogue state; explicit visual representation of nodes/edges/filters eliminates the need for context tracking across interaction turns.

concept: Constraint Discovery Problem in Conversational Interfaces
definition: Users cannot discover system capabilities, constraints, or valid input ranges through natural conversation; conversational interfaces lack affordances for revealing what is possible, leading to abandonmentin when phrasing differs from system expectations.
key_refs: Chat Failures and Troubles: Reasons and Solutions (2023)
Convo: What does conversational programming need? An exploration of machine learning interface design (2020)
The Conversation Trap: why defaulting to chat might be the biggest interaction design mistake of the AI era (2026)
implication: MetroGraph must surface operators, filters, and valid query patterns through visual UI elements (menus, drag-drop controls, schema visualization) rather than relying on users to discover them through trial-and-error conversation.

definition: Persistent disconnect between users' mental models of what a conversational system can do and its actual capabilities; transparency features paradoxically reduce satisfaction and do not bridge the comprehension gap.
key_refs: Exploring users' mental models of conversational agents: a systematic review (2025)
Transparent Conversational Agents: The Impact of Capability Communication on User Behavior and Mental Model Alignment (2024)
Understanding Mental Models of Generative Conversational Search and The Effect of Interface Transparency (2025)
arXiv 2506.03807 / Understanding Mental Models of Generative Conversational Search and The Effect of Interface Transparency
implication: MetroGraph must use visual system metaphors (graph, schema, data structures) that align with how users conceptually think about structured data; design interface to match user mental models of the problem domain rather than trying to explain system internals.

definition: Natural language alone is insufficient for specifying complex visual or structural tasks (visualization, layout, graph operations); unimodal text-only intent is inadequately grounded in spatial or visual context.
key_refs: Towards Natural Language Interfaces for Data Visualization: A Survey (2021)
Deep Learning Approaches for Multimodal Intent Recognition: A Survey (2024)
Show, Don't Tell: Reflections on the Design of Multi-modal Conversational Interfaces (2021)
implication: MetroGraph inherently requires multimodal interaction: conversational queries must be paired with visual node selection, spatial layout, and structural constraints. Graph visualization is not optional scaffolding but essential specification mechanism.

definition: Sequential turn-taking in conversational interfaces constrains exploration and multi-path reasoning; linear chat history cannot represent parallel hypotheses, branching decision trees, or non-sequential task flows that users need for complex work.
key_refs: ChatGraPhT: A Visual Conversation Interface for Multi-Path Reflection with Agentic LLM Support (2024)
Do Conversational Interfaces Limit Creativity? Exploring Visual Graph Systems for Creative Writing (2024)
Agentic Workflows for Conversational Human-AI Interaction Design (2025)
implication: MetroGraph's graph-based interface directly addresses this by representing multiple query paths, branching logic, and parallel explorations as spatial structures; graph canvas enables non-linear, exploratory interaction that linear chat cannot support.

definition: The tendency of large language models in extended conversations to repeat prior decisions or become locked into early dialogue patterns despite receiving longer context; extended context does not monotonically improve multi-turn dialogue quality.
key_refs: Mitigating Conversational Inertia in Multi-Turn Agents (2025)
implication: MetroGraph avoids dialogue inertia by using explicit visual state representation (nodes, edges, filters) that users can directly manipulate; visual representation prevents the model from being locked into prior conversational patterns.

definition: Conversational AI systems generate plausible-sounding but factually false information (hallucinations); grounding to external data is insufficient, and architectural constraints are needed to ensure conversational truthfulness in constrained domains.
key_refs: Mitigating LLM Hallucinations Using a Multi-Agent Framework (2024)
Context Window Limits: Why Your LLM Still Hallucinates (2026)
implication: MetroGraph must enforce constraints at the interface level (valid operators, schema-constrained queries, real-time result feedback) to prevent hallucinated results; conversational query must be validated against actual graph structure before execution.

concept: Query Reformulation Failure in Conversational RAG
definition: Automatic query rewriting in conversational RAG systems fails to capture user intent from conversational context, particularly for co-reference resolution and context-dependent pronoun binding.
key_refs: Can Synthetic Query Rewrites Capture User Intent Better than Humans in Retrieval-Augmented Generation? (2024)
Beyond Pipelines: A Fundamental Study on the Rise of Generative-Retrieval Architectures in Web Research (2025)
implication: MetroGraph should allow users to explicitly specify query context through visual graph annotations (selected nodes, constraints) rather than relying on conversational query reformulation to infer intent from chat history.

definition: Dialogue systems can complete tasks accurately but still produce low user satisfaction; task completion rate and dialogue efficiency are independent of user experience quality, indicating systems miss critical UX dimensions.
key_refs: Understanding User Satisfaction with Task-oriented Dialogue Systems (2022)
Assessing Interaction Quality in Human–AI Dialogue: An Integrative Review and Multi-Layer Framework for Conversational Agents (2023)
How to Evaluate Your Dialogue Models: A Review of Approaches (2021)
implication: MetroGraph must prioritize user agency, comprehension, and feedback loops alongside task completion; visual interface transparency that shows query structure, constraints, and results helps close the satisfaction gap.

concept: Direct Manipulation Superiority for Regularly-Used Tasks
definition: Foundational HCI principle that direct manipulation interfaces outperform conversational interfaces for routine, well-understood tasks; spatial, reversible, visually-encoded actions provide superior cognitive efficiency and user control.
key_refs: Direct Manipulation Interfaces (Norman, 1983)
Designing the User Interface: Strategies for Effective Human-Computer Interaction (Shneiderman, 2016)
Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design (1987)
Conversational agent or direct manipulation in human–system interaction (2005)
implication: MetroGraph embraces direct manipulation (drag nodes, draw edges, apply filters spatially) for database graph queries because users perform these queries repeatedly; direct manipulation outperforms conversation for this task class.

definition: Human information-seeking involves iterative exploration guided by information scent (Pirolli); conversations alone cannot provide the visual cues and interactive feedback that guide exploration, requiring navigation through information landscape.
key_refs: Information Seeking Behavior - an overview (Pirolli's Information Foraging Theory, 2000s)
implication: MetroGraph's graph visualization provides visual scent (node colors, edge patterns, result previews) that guides users through query exploration; conversational interfaces lack the ambient information cues needed for foraging behavior.

definition: Conversational interfaces provide no affordances for discovering available operations, constraints, or valid parameter ranges; users must resort to trial-and-error or explicit help-seeking rather than visual hints.
key_refs: The Conversation Trap: why defaulting to chat might be the biggest interaction design mistake of the AI era (2026)
Beyond the Conversation Trap: Designing for Hybrid Human-Agent Interaction Modes (2026)
implication: MetroGraph surfaces query capabilities through UI elements (visible operators, type hints, schema visualization) rather than forcing users to discover them conversationally; visual affordances enable passive learning and rapid capability discovery.

definition: Brief, transient nature of conversational turns limits opportunities for sustained user engagement; interactions are ephemeral without persistent visualization of interaction history and context.
key_refs: Agentic Workflows for Conversational Human-AI Interaction Design (2025)
implication: MetroGraph provides persistent visual canvas where query structures, results, and refinements remain visible and replayable; spatial persistence addresses the transience problem by making interaction artifacts durable.

definition: Wide range of conversational AI capabilities combined with unlimited possible user goals creates a vast ambiguous design space; users cannot easily constrain their requests to valid system functionality.
key_refs: Agentic Workflows for Conversational Human-AI Interaction Design (2025)
implication: MetroGraph constrains the design space by providing domain-specific visual operators for graph queries (node filters, edge traversals, aggregations); explicit constraints in the UI reduce ambiguity compared to open-ended natural language.

concept: Web Interface Control Failure with Pure Language
definition: LLMs controlling web interfaces through language instructions fail for visual/spatial tasks and structural navigation requiring real-time visual feedback and iterative refinement.
key_refs: WebWISE: Web Interface Control and Sequential Exploration with Large Language Models (2023)
implication: MetroGraph must maintain visual feedback loops (showing node selections, query previews, result highlights) because pure language instructions cannot reliably specify complex structural manipulations.

definition: Coordination and complexity issues emerge when multiple conversational agents operate together; chat paradigm does not scale to multi-agent scenarios requiring orchestration and role clarity.
key_refs: One Agent Too Many: User Perspectives on Approaches to Multi-agent Conversational AI (2024)
implication: MetroGraph's node-based graph model naturally supports multi-agent scenarios through visual role differentiation (node types, coloring, annotations); graph structure makes agent roles and interactions explicit.

concept: Cognitive Load of Linear Chat for Structured Tasks
definition: Conversational interfaces impose high cognitive load for structured data tasks by forcing users to maintain mental models of invisible system state, remember prior context, and reconcile linear dialogue with non-linear task logic.
key_refs: Visualization Analysis and Design (Munzner, 2014)
Designing the User Interface: Strategies for Effective Human-Computer Interaction (Shneiderman, 2016)
Conversational User Interfaces for Blind Knowledge Workers: A Case Study (2020)
implication: MetroGraph reduces cognitive load by externalizing query structure as visual graph: nodes represent entities, edges show relationships, visual constraints are spatially encoded. External representation reduces working memory demand.

concept: NL Interface Ambiguity for Structured Tasks
definition: Natural language interfaces for structured tasks (NL2VIS, NL2SQL, NL2Query) fail due to ambiguity in visual specification, context maintenance, and lack of affordances for constraint expression.
key_refs: Towards Natural Language Interfaces for Data Visualization: A Survey (2021)
implication: MetroGraph augments NL with visual graph semantics: structured queries are specified through direct manipulation (selecting nodes, composing operators visually), reducing ambiguity compared to pure NL approaches.

definition: Transparency features and explanations alone are insufficient for helping users calibrate trust in AI systems; users need to understand system boundaries, confidence limits, and failure modes beyond capability descriptions.
key_refs: Trust Calibration in Agentic AI: Designing for Appropriate Reliance, Not Blind Trust (2026)
implication: MetroGraph must design interfaces that make query semantics and execution bounds transparent (showing exactly which nodes match, what constraints apply) rather than relying on conversational explanations of AI behavior.

concept: Semantic Grounding Failure in Multi-Agent NL Interfaces
definition: Natural language interfaces for multi-agent task assignment fail due to semantic grounding challenges when mapping NL to workflows; explicit constraints are necessary to disambiguate intent.
key_refs: Towards A Natural Language Interface for Flexible Multi-Agent Task Assignment (2023)
implication: MetroGraph's graph structure provides semantic grounding for multi-query workflows: visual node composition, edge constraints, and type annotations make assignment semantics explicit without NL ambiguity.

definition: Systems struggle to maintain coherent dialogue and generate contextually appropriate responses; automatic metrics cannot capture true interaction quality beyond task completion.
key_refs: How to Evaluate Your Dialogue Models: A Review of Approaches (2021)
Survey on Evaluation Methods for Dialogue Systems (2019)
implication: MetroGraph avoids dialogue coherence problems by using explicit visual protocol (graph state, query structure) that both user and system maintain synchronously; no hidden dialogue state to maintain.

concept: Survey Consensus on Multi-User CUI Challenges
definition: Systematic reviews document persistent design challenges in conversational interfaces: context management, turn-taking ambiguity, and architectural complexity that remain unsolved across implementations.
key_refs: A Survey on Multi-User Conversational Interfaces (2024)
implication: MetroGraph's approach of combining graph visualization with optional conversational layer acknowledges these persistent challenges by not relying on conversation alone for structured queries.

definition: Conversational systems fail to effectively communicate what capabilities they do and do not have; users struggle with invisible constraints until they encounter failures.
key_refs: Convo: What does conversational programming need? An exploration of machine learning interface design (2020)
implication: MetroGraph makes capabilities explicit through UI schema (visible operators, type constraints, available node types) rather than requiring conversational discovery of what is possible.
