implication: MetroGraph should evaluate layout quality via cluster metrics; enables algorithmic selection among candidate layouts based on community structure prominence.

concept: Chord Diagrams and Visual Design Choices
definition: Specialized circular layout (chord diagram) for bipartite/flow graphs; empirical study of design choices (arc ordering, colors, width) affecting readability; task-dependent effectiveness.
key_refs: Krzywinski et al. (2009) — Circos visualization system popularizing chord diagrams
Zong et al. (2024) — CHORDination study on design choice impacts
implication: For bipartite workflow/data-flow visualization in MetroGraph, consider chord diagrams as alternative; research on visual design choices (color, width encoding) informs implementation.

definition: A four-level hierarchical framework for characterizing and validating visualization systems: domain problem characterization, data/task abstraction, visual encoding/interaction design, and algorithm implementation. Each level's decisions cascade downward, constraining choices at lower levels.
key_refs: Munzner 2009 / A Nested Model for Visualization Design and Validation
Meyer et al. 2012 / The Four-Level Nested Model Revisited: Blocks and Guidelines
implication: MetroGraph's visual-graph interface must operate across these levels: abstracting the database query problem, mapping relational structure to graph topology, designing marks/channels for properties, and optimizing layout algorithms. Poor choices at the problem level cascade into UI bloat.

definition: A refinement of the nested model distinguishing 'blocks' (outcomes of design decisions at each level: abstractions, techniques, algorithms) from 'guidelines' (statements about relationships between blocks). Within-level guidelines compare blocks at the same level; between-level guidelines map blocks across adjacent levels.
key_refs: Meyer et al. 2012 / The Four-Level Nested Model Revisited: Blocks and Guidelines
implication: For MetroGraph, this clarifies the distinction between task-to-encoding guidelines (e.g., 'node-link for small graphs') and technique-to-algorithm choices (e.g., force-directed vs. orthogonal layout). RAG/workflow tools fail when they lack clear between-level mappings, causing AI to generate mismatched output.

definition: Shneiderman's design principle for interactive information visualization: 'Overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand.' Prescribes a sequence of user actions: gaining context via a complete overview, drilling down via filtering and zooming, accessing detailed information on demand.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1996 / The Eyes Have It: A Task by Data Type Taxonomy for Information Visualizations
Shneiderman, B. 1996. The eyes have it: a task by data type taxonomy for information visualizations. Proc. VL '96.
Shneiderman, B. 2003. Designing the User Interface: Strategies for Effective Human-Computer Interaction (4th ed.).
implication: MetroGraph should surface a complete database schema graph at startup (overview), allow interactive filtering/search (zoom), and reveal details (row data, provenance) on demand. RAG agents that jump directly to details violate this principle and create cognitive overload.

definition: Empirical ranking of 10 elementary perceptual tasks by human accuracy, from highest to lowest: position on a common scale, position on non-aligned scales, length, direction, angle, area, volume, curvature, shading, color saturation. Establishes which visual encodings most effectively convey quantitative comparisons.
key_refs: Cleveland & McGill (1984) / Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods
Cleveland & McGill 1984 / Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods
implication: For MetroGraph graph labels and edge weights, position on a common axis (e.g., horizontal position for node rank) is more effective than color saturation or area. This directly constrains the choice of visual channels for database properties.

definition: Design principle that visual encodings vary in effectiveness for conveying data based on the data type (categorical, ordinal, quantitative), the task (comparison, estimation, reading exact values), and perceptual laws (preattentive processing, gestalt principles). Effectiveness is both a matter of expressiveness (can the encoding represent the data?) and accuracy (how accurately can users extract values?).
key_refs: Mackinlay 1986 / Automating the Design of Graphical Presentations of Relational Information
Card et al. 1999 / Readings in Information Visualization: Using Vision to Think
implication: MetroGraph must map data types to the most effective encodings: ordinal node importance to node size or color hue (not color saturation), categorical node types to shape, and quantitative edge weights to position or length. Poor encoding choices hide insights from the graph.

definition: Process of characterizing the data domain in terms of meaningful types: dataset types (tables, networks, hierarchies, text), attribute types (categorical, ordinal, quantitative), and dimensionality. Precedes task abstraction and guides choices of visual encodings and interaction techniques.
key_refs: Munzner 2014 / Visualization Analysis and Design
implication: For MetroGraph's wedge, the database schema (tables, foreign keys, attribute types) must be explicitly abstracted as input to the nested model. If this step is skipped (as in naive RAG tools), the UI cannot make principled encoding choices; the AI defaults to surface-area bloat.

definition: Process of characterizing user goals in terms of abstract operations (search, browse, derive, compare, correlate) independent of domain-specific context. Bridges the domain problem to visualization design by identifying what users need to accomplish, enabling reuse of visualization patterns across domains.
key_refs: Munzner 2014 / Visualization Analysis and Design
Brehmer & Munzner 2013 / A Multi-Level Typology of Abstract Visualization Tasks
implication: MetroGraph must abstract user workflows (e.g., 'find all orders by a customer' → search + filter task) before choosing interaction techniques. AI-generated interfaces that skip task abstraction produce feature bloat because the AI doesn't understand what the user is trying to accomplish.

definition: Taxonomy of 10 primitive operations that underlie most visualization tasks: locate, identify, distinguish, categorize, cluster, distribution, rank, compare values, sort, derive values. Provides a checklist for evaluating whether a visualization system supports the tasks users need to perform.
key_refs: Amar et al. 2005 / Low-Level Components of Analytic Activity in Information Visualization
implication: MetroGraph's graph UI must support low-level tasks like 'locate node X' (search), 'rank nodes by degree' (sort + visual encoding), and 'identify outliers' (cluster + color encoding). Missing support for even one of these tasks forces users to export data or use a separate tool.

definition: Three-dimensional framework organizing visualization tasks across: why (present, discover, enjoy, produce), how (how the task is performed), and task I/O (what data goes in and what comes out). Bridges domain-specific task descriptions and domain-agnostic low-level tasks.
key_refs: Brehmer & Munzner 2013 / A Multi-Level Typology of Abstract Visualization Tasks
implication: For MetroGraph, this clarifies why a user is querying a database (discover patterns vs. produce a report) and how the system should respond. A 'discover' task warrants interactive exploration; a 'produce' task warrants stable output. RAG agents conflate these, leading to UI confusion.

definition: Foundational principles of visual perception (proximity, similarity, closure, continuation, figure-ground, symmetry) that explain how humans group visual elements into meaningful wholes. Applied to visualization design to create coherent visual structures that reduce cognitive load.
key_refs: Ware 2012 / Information Visualization: Perception for Design
Gestalt Principles of Visual Perception / IxDF
implication: MetroGraph's node-link layout should apply gestalt principles: group semantically related nodes (similarity), place related nodes close together (proximity), and use visual enclosures (closure) to separate subgraphs. Violations cause visual chaos that overwhelms the viewer.

definition: Framework identifying visual dimensions that can encode data: position, size, shape, orientation, color hue, color value, and texture. Each visual variable has expressive power (range of distinct values it can represent) and effectiveness (accuracy with which users perceive differences).
key_refs: Bertin 1967/1983 / Semiologie Graphique (Semiology of Graphics)
implication: MetroGraph's graph encoding strategy must select from Bertin's visual variables to match data types and task requirements. Using shape to encode quantitative data (ineffective) vs. position (effective) is the difference between insight and confusion.

definition: Tukey's approach to data analysis emphasizing discovery-driven exploration over confirmatory hypothesis testing. Users iterate through visualization, transformation, and re-visualization to generate and test hypotheses. Contrasts with confirmatory analysis, which tests pre-specified hypotheses.
key_refs: Tukey 1977 / Exploratory Data Analysis
implication: MetroGraph should prioritize fluid iteration (zoom, filter, re-query) over static report generation. The 'Overview first, zoom and filter, details-on-demand' principle reflects Tukey's EDA philosophy: let the visual data guide the next question.

definition: Systematic framework for conducting visualization research in collaboration with domain experts. Nine-stage process: learn, winnow, cast, discover, design, implement, deploy, reflect, write. Balances rigor (problem characterization, validation) with pragmatism (real-world constraints, iteration).
key_refs: Sedlmair et al. 2012 / Design Study Methodology: Reflections from the Trenches and the Stacks
implication: For MetroGraph's development, a design study methodology approach (interviewing domain experts, iterative refinement, on-site validation) produces more effective interfaces than purely algorithmic or AI-driven approaches that skip the 'learn' and 'discover' phases.

definition: Framework for designing interaction techniques in visualization systems, organized around interaction intents (zoom, pan, filter, select, reconfigure) and task-specific techniques. Emphasizes that interaction should directly support the analysis tasks users are performing.
key_refs: Yi et al. 2007 / Toward a Deeper Understanding of the Role of Interaction in Information Visualization
Kaplunov et al. 2024 / Intents, Techniques, and Components: A Unified Analysis of Interaction Authoring Tasks in Data Visualization
implication: MetroGraph's interaction vocabulary (click, drag, zoom, search, filter) should map directly to analysis tasks. Arbitrary interactions that don't support a task (e.g., double-click to toggle a property with no visual consequence) create friction and confusion.

definition: Interaction technique enabling real-time filtering via direct manipulation (sliders, checkboxes, buttons). Database query results update within ~100 ms, creating tight feedback loop. Foundation for direct manipulation interfaces.
key_refs: Ahlberg & Shneiderman 1992 / Dynamic Queries for Information Exploration
implication: MetroGraph should support dynamic query interaction: filtering nodes/edges by property (degree, type, timestamp) via interactive controls with sub-100ms response time. Batch query models (submit → wait → results) break the exploratory feedback loop.

definition: Mackinlay's design criteria for visual encodings. Expressiveness: the encoding can represent all and only the data properties (no false mappings). Effectiveness: among expressive encodings, choose the one users can most accurately and quickly read.
key_refs: Mackinlay 1986 / Automating the Design of Graphical Presentations of Relational Information
implication: For MetroGraph, this guides the choice between candidate encodings for a given data type. All must be expressive (represent the data faithfully), but effectiveness ranking (per Cleveland-McGill) determines which is best. Using color saturation for quantity (less effective) vs. position (more effective) violates effectiveness criteria.

definition: Documented knowledge about design choices, derived from theory, empirical studies, and practice. Guidelines capture both within-level comparisons (which algorithm is faster?) and between-level mappings (which encoding suits this task?). Effective guidelines are specific enough to be actionable but general enough to transfer across domains.
key_refs: Meyer et al. 2012 / The Four-Level Nested Model Revisited: Blocks and Guidelines
Ghai et al. 2023 / Understanding the Research-Practice Gap in Visualization Design Guidelines
implication: MetroGraph's development should be grounded in explicit design guidelines (e.g., 'use node-link for graphs < 500 nodes', 'use color hue for categorical node type'). AI-generated interfaces without guidelines tend to produce ad-hoc, inconsistent designs that violate human perception principles.

definition: Design principles for color encoding: perceptual uniformity (equal steps in perceptual space should appear equal), colorblind accessibility (avoid red-green distinctions), and task fit (sequential for ordered data, diverging for data with meaningful midpoint, categorical for unordered). Scientific colormaps address rainbow colormap artifacts.
key_refs: Crameri / Scientific Colour Maps
Colorblind Accessibility in Data Visualization / deficiencyview
implication: If MetroGraph uses color to encode node properties, it must choose perceptually uniform, colorblind-friendly palettes. Default rainbow colormaps create false visual discontinuities and exclude 8% of viewers with color vision deficiency.

definition: Visual and interactive properties of chart types that suggest particular uses and task performance. Affordances (e.g., bars enable position comparison; pie charts suggest part-to-whole relationship) guide user expectations. Violating affordances creates confusion and errors.
key_refs: Pandey et al. 2024 / From Perception to Decision: Assessing the Role of Chart Types Affordances in High-Level Decision Tasks
Pandey & Manivannan 2024 / Are Pie Charts Evil? An Assessment of Pie and Donut Charts Compared to Bar Charts
implication: For MetroGraph, the node-link graph representation carries affordances: it suggests topology visualization, supports comparison of node degrees, and implies traversal. Encoding quantitative data purely in node position (breaking the 'topology' affordance) confuses users about what the graph represents.

definition: Four-level validation approach aligned with the nested model: domain validation (do we understand the problem?), abstraction validation (are the abstractions correct?), technique validation (do users perceive the encodings correctly?), algorithm validation (does it scale?). Different validation methods suit each level.
key_refs: Munzner 2009 / A Nested Model for Visualization Design and Validation
Munzner 2014 / Visualization Analysis and Design
implication: MetroGraph development should apply validation at all four levels: domain experts validate the schema model, user studies validate encoding choices, perception experiments validate preattentive feature efficacy, and benchmarks validate layout performance. Skipping validation at any level risks undetected failures.

definition: Formal framework applying semiotic theory to visualization: sign systems, representational morphisms, and structure preservation. A visualization is a sign system where data structures map to visual structures through morphisms that preserve significant relationships (e.g., graph homomorphism for network visualization).
key_refs: Goguen / Information Visualization and Semiotic Morphisms
implication: MetroGraph's graph layout is a semiotic mapping: database relationships (foreign keys, join constraints) must map to visual relationships (edges, proximity, containment). A layout that breaks this mapping (e.g., hiding edges, placing related nodes far apart) violates the semiotic principle and confuses users.

definition: The use of computer-supported, interactive visual representations of abstract data to amplify cognition. Emphasizes that InfoVis is about extending human perception and reasoning through visual encoding, not merely displaying data. Contrasts with scientific visualization (spatial data) and general graphics.
key_refs: Card et al. 1999 / Readings in Information Visualization: Using Vision to Think
implication: MetroGraph's purpose is not to pretty-print a database; it is to amplify understanding of relational structure through visual encoding and interaction. If a graph visualization doesn't enable insights that text queries cannot, it has failed its purpose.

definition: Using the visual and conceptual language of public transit/metro systems (lines, stations, interchanges) as an abstract representation for networks, data structures, or knowledge domains where geographic distance is deemphasized in favor of topological connectivity.
key_refs: Beck, H. 1933. London Underground map design
Nöllenburg, M. 2005. A survey on automated metro map layout methods
Gibson et al. 2013. A survey of two-dimensional graph layout techniques
implication: MetroGraph's core design pattern: applying metro map structure to abstract workflows/DBs surfaces topology-first thinking, addressing the RAG/workflow-graph UI bloat by adopting a proven, familiar spatial mental model from daily transit use. Users already understand metro maps cognitively.

definition: Representing a network by preserving connectivity relationships (which nodes are connected) while discarding or distorting geographic/Euclidean distance, allowing schematic layouts where node positions convey structure rather than spatial proximity.
key_refs: Fáry, I. 1948. On straight-line representation of planar graphs
Beck, H. 1933. London Underground design: topological vs geographic abstraction
Nöllenburg & Wolff 2010. Automated metro map layout
implication: Critical for MetroGraph: by discarding pseudo-geographic positioning of workflows/data, topological abstraction reduces visual clutter and cognitive overhead; focus shifts from where things are in a 2D space to how they connect—directly addressing the flight-to-chat problem where users abandon graph UIs for chat because spatial coordinates feel arbitrary.

definition: A geometric restriction requiring that edges in a schematic diagram follow only eight orientations (0°, 45°, 90°, 135°, 180°, 225°, 270°, 315°), creating a grid-like aesthetic similar to London Underground and Manhattan street grids; reduces visual clutter vs. arbitrary angles.
key_refs: Nöllenburg, M. & Wolff, A. 2010. A mixed-integer-program for drawing metro maps
Nöllenburg et al. 2022. A Survey on Computing Schematic Network Maps
Nickel & Nöllenburg 2020. Towards Data-Driven Multilinear Metro Maps
implication: MetroGraph constraint: enforcing octilinearity reduces cognitive load by providing predictable, regular line paths; users can scan edges intuitively without distraction from arbitrary curves. Foundational to metro map readability and aesthetic appeal.

definition: A specialized NP-hard variant of edge crossing minimization where a set of simple paths (metro lines) are drawn on an embedded graph, and the problem is to order lines on each edge to minimize crossings between paths; proven NP-hard with approximation algorithms available.
key_refs: Fink et al. 2013. Metro-Line Crossing Minimization: Hardness, Approximations, and Tractable Cases. Proceedings of the 24th Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms.
implication: MetroGraph's algorithmic complexity class: if workflows/data are modeled as metro lines on a base graph, MLCM NP-hardness means instant optimal layout is infeasible at scale. Trade-off between pre-computed optimal (slow, good) vs. force-directed approximations (fast, serviceable); informs MetroGraph's hybrid layout strategy.

definition: Theoretical result establishing that the metro-line crossing minimization problem (and related metro map layout variants) belong to NP-hard complexity class, meaning no known polynomial-time algorithm exists; solutions may require exponential time or approximation heuristics.
key_refs: Fink, M., et al. 2013. Metro-Line Crossing Minimization: Hardness, Approximations, and Tractable Cases. SODA '13.
Nöllenburg & Wolff 2010. A mixed-integer program for drawing metro maps
implication: Critical constraint for MetroGraph's interactive design: true optimal layout requires exponential time at scale; MetroGraph must embrace incremental, interactive layout updates over a computational strategy seeking global optimum. Informs the choice of force-directed or constraint-based approximation methods.

definition: Optimization technique that formulates graph layout as a linear program with integer constraints (e.g., coordinate positions as integers, edge segment counts); used to compute globally optimal or near-optimal metro map layouts offline, trading time for layout quality.
key_refs: Nöllenburg, M. & Wolff, A. 2010. A mixed-integer program for drawing metro maps. Journal of Graph Algorithms and Applications 14(2).
Nöllenburg et al. 2022. A Survey on Computing Schematic Network Maps.
Nickel & Nöllenburg 2020. Towards Data-Driven Multilinear Metro Maps. Diagrams 2020.
implication: MetroGraph's offline layout engine: MILP is the gold standard for precomputed, high-quality metro map layouts; use for initial/save states but impractical for real-time interaction. Suggests two-tier layout: MILP for background/export, heuristic for interactive exploration.

definition: Family of iterative algorithms that compute graph layouts by treating nodes as particles with repulsive forces and edges as attractive springs, minimizing energy to produce aesthetically pleasing, crossing-reduced layouts; favors symmetry and structure visibility without domain-specific knowledge.
key_refs: Tutte, W.T. 1963. How to draw a graph. Proc. London Math. Soc. 13(3):743–767.
Kobourov, S.G. 2012. Spring Embedders and Force Directed Graph Drawing Algorithms. arXiv:1201.3011.
Gibson et al. 2013. A survey of two-dimensional graph layout techniques for information visualisation.
implication: MetroGraph's interactive layout backbone: force-directed methods excel at real-time, responsive interaction and are computationally tractable for dynamic graphs. Can be augmented with octilinear/magnetic forces (Nickel et al.) to enforce metro aesthetics while maintaining interactivity.

definition: Graph layout style where edges are drawn using only horizontal and vertical segments (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°), forming an orthogonal/rectilinear grid; reduces visual clutter and aligns with UI conventions in software/hardware design diagrams.
key_refs: Tamassia, R. 1987. On embedding a graph in the grid with the minimum number of bends. SIAM J. Computing 16(3):421–444.
Battista, G.D., et al. 1999. Graph Drawing: Algorithms for the Visualization of Graphs. Prentice Hall.
Nöllenburg et al. 2017. Towards a Topology-Shape-Metrics Framework for Ortho-Radial Drawings. SoCG 2017.
implication: MetroGraph's geometric foundation: orthogonal (and octilinear as a superset) routing provides the clean, scannable aesthetic of metro maps. Aligns with software UI conventions and reduces cognitive load vs. arbitrary curved edges. Connects to TSM (Topology-Shape-Metrics) paradigm for constraint-based layout.

definition: Optimization objective in orthogonal/rectilinear graph drawing to reduce the number of angles or 'bends' where edges change direction; fewer bends improve visual simplicity and readability, though may require more total edge length.
key_refs: Tamassia, R. 1987. On embedding a graph in the grid with the minimum number of bends. SIAM J. Computing 16(3):421–444.
Nöllenburg et al. 2017. Towards a Topology-Shape-Metrics Framework for Ortho-Radial Drawings. SoCG 2017.
Eades & Wormald 1994. Edge crossings in drawings of bipartite graphs.
implication: MetroGraph aesthetic target: minimizing bends on metro lines maintains visual simplicity, especially for long workflows or hierarchical data. Trade-off with crossing minimization and layout stability; MILP-based methods can balance both.

definition: A simplified, topology-preserving diagram of a network (transit system, data structure, process flow) that abstracts away geographic distance and true scale in favor of emphasizing connectivity and conceptual structure; exemplified by metro systems like London Underground, but applicable to any graph-like domain.
key_refs: Nöllenburg et al. 2022. A Survey on Computing Schematic Network Maps: The Challenge to Interactivity. arXiv:2208.07301.
Gibson et al. 2013. A survey of two-dimensional graph layout techniques for information visualisation.
Smajda et al. 2017. A Taxonomy and Survey of Dynamic Graph Visualization. Computer Graphics Forum 17(3).
implication: MetroGraph's formal category: positioning it as a schematic network map tool grounds design in a well-studied, applied domain with clear algorithmic and aesthetic principles. Separates schematic (topology-focused) from geographic (coordinate-based) visualization paradigms.

definition: Tufte's ethical principle that graphics should accurately represent data through honest scaling, avoiding chartjunk (non-data-ink), and using high data-ink ratios; extends to ensuring visual design choices don't mislead or obscure quantitative relationships.
key_refs: Tufte, E.R. 1983. The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. Graphics Press.
Tufte, E.R. 1990. Envisioning Information. Graphics Press.
Tufte's Six Principles of Graphical Integrity (secondary source)
implication: MetroGraph's design ethics: when representing workflows, APIs, or data schemas as metro maps, visual distortion of topological distance (e.g., making unrelated nodes appear close) violates graphical integrity. Ensures users trust the schematic diagram as an honest model of structure, not a misleading simplification.

definition: Formal process of simplifying complex visual information by selectively omitting or aggregating details while preserving essential structure for comprehension; characterized by purpose, perceptual/cognitive effectiveness, and controlled trade-offs between fidelity and clarity.
key_refs: Viola, I., et al. 2020. Visual Abstraction. arXiv:1910.03310. (Comprehensive framework paper)
Munzner, T. 2014. Visualization Analysis and Design. AK Peters/CRC Press.
implication: MetroGraph's theoretical foundation for design decisions: abstraction is not failure but intentional design. By condensing workflows into metro lines and stations, MetroGraph abstracts detail to communicate structure; the framework clarifies which details to omit vs. preserve based on user tasks (navigation, overview, detail). Legitimizes schematic simplification.

concept: MetroSets: Visualizing Sets as Metro Maps
definition: Specific application of metro map metaphor to set visualization: models a set system as a hypergraph where hyperedges become metro lines, vertices become stations, and set membership is shown via station appearance on lines; includes set relationships (intersections, subsets) as line interchanges.
key_refs: Nöllenburg, M., et al. 2021. MetroSets: Visualizing Sets as Metro Maps. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics 27(2):1257–1267.
Eades et al. 2012. On the readability of abstract set visualizations.
implication: Direct precursor to MetroGraph's application: MetroSets proves metro map abstraction scales to set systems (e.g., API parameter sets, data structure memberships, feature dependencies). Evaluated readability metrics superior to Euler/Venn-based alternatives. Demonstrates metro metaphor's generality beyond transit.

definition: Measure of mental effort required to comprehend a graph visualization; influenced by edge crossings, node density, color/shape consistency, and layout stability; excessive cognitive load reduces task performance and increases error rates.
key_refs: Swink & Keele 1987. Processing of visual feedback in a manual control task.
Schlag et al. 2008. Scalability of Network Visualization from a Cognitive Load Perspective. IEEE InfoVis.
Hollan et al. 1986. Cognitive load and representation grain size. Proc. CHI '86.
implication: MetroGraph's optimization target: metro map design (octilinearity, crossing minimization, color coding) all directly reduce cognitive load. Research correlates lower load with faster task completion; MetroGraph's schematic approach should measure and report load reduction vs. traditional node-link diagrams.

definition: Empirical measure of user efficiency in tracing paths or finding connections in a graph; metro map studies show significant improvements in task completion time and accuracy vs. other graph layouts, with color-coding and linear edges further improving performance.
key_refs: Epstein et al. 2017. User performance and reading strategies for metro maps: An eye tracking study. Spatial Cognition & Computation 16(4):279–300.
Civeyici et al. 2019. Metro Map Colour-Coding Effect on Usability in Route Tracing. Spatial Cognition & Computation.
implication: MetroGraph's key performance metric: if workflows/data are modeled as metro routes, users should demonstrate faster path-tracing and better error rates with a metro map vs. traditional graph diagrams. Eye-tracking studies suggest octilinear lines reduce visual search; color-coded lines improve complex route identification.

concept: Color Coding Effectiveness in Metro Maps
definition: Empirical finding that assigning distinct colors to metro lines significantly reduces cognitive load and improves route-tracing task performance, particularly for complex networks; color becomes a salient feature for grouping and distinguishing lines.
key_refs: Civeyici et al. 2019. Metro Map Colour-Coding Effect on Usability in Route Tracing. In: Proceedings of CHI '19.
Epstein et al. 2017. User performance and reading strategies for metro maps: An eye tracking study. Spatial Cognition & Computation 16(4):279–300.
implication: MetroGraph's visual encoding recommendation: assigning colors to workflow lines/data clusters leverages this principle; color becomes a primary grouping mechanism independent of spatial proximity. Reduces burden on octilinearity alone to convey structure.

definition: Application of metro map aesthetics and layout algorithms to biological network diagrams (metabolic pathways); Metabopolis specifically uses grid-like, schematic layouts inspired by urban maps to simplify large biochemical networks while preserving connectivity.
key_refs: Karp et al. 2021. Pathway Tools Visualization of Organism-Scale Metabolic Networks. PLOS Biology.
Zaug et al. 2020. Metabopolis: scalable network layout for biological pathway diagrams in urban map style. BMC Bioinformatics 20:444.
implication: Proof-of-concept for MetroGraph's domain generality: if metro metaphor works for biological pathways (100s of reactions, complex feedback), it should work equally well for software workflows, API chains, and data pipelines. Demonstrates metaphor's transferability across domains.

definition: Use of graph layout techniques (including metro-inspired schematic diagrams) to represent software systems: modules as nodes, dependencies as edges, organized into hierarchical layers or feature-based groupings; improves comprehension of codebase structure.
key_refs: Koike et al. 2018. The City Metaphor in Software Visualization. In: Proc. 3rd International Workshop on Software Visualization.
Anwar et al. 2019. SArF Map: Visualizing Software Architecture from Feature and Layer Viewpoints. arXiv:1306.0958.
implication: MetroGraph's primary use case: applying metro schematic design to software/API architecture diagrams leverages established principles from this domain. Features could be modeled as metro lines, modules as stations; enables interactive architecture exploration.

definition: Tamassia's hierarchical approach to graph drawing: separate topology (planarity), shape (routing style: orthogonal, polyline, etc.), and metrics (coordinates, edge lengths) into independent optimization phases; enables modular, constraint-based layout design.
key_refs: Tamassia, R. 1987. On embedding a graph in the grid with the minimum number of bends. SIAM J. Computing 16(3):421–444.
Battista et al. 1999. Graph Drawing: Algorithms for the Visualization of Graphs. Prentice Hall.
Nöllenburg et al. 2017. Towards a Topology-Shape-Metrics Framework for Ortho-Radial Drawings. SoCG 2017.
implication: MetroGraph's modular layout architecture: TSM separates concerns—preserve planarity (topology), enforce octilinearity (shape), then optimize coordinates. Allows independent tuning of each phase and supports constraint-based extensions (e.g., spatial clusters, hierarchy levels).

definition: Cartography principle of simplifying maps by selectively removing, aggregating, or smoothing features while preserving essential structure; includes simplification (fewer nodes), smoothing (reduce jitter), grouping (cluster nearby elements), and classification (categorize elements).
key_refs: McMaster & Shea 1992. Generalization in Digital Cartography. Association of American Geographers.
Cartographic Generalization - Making Effective Maps (Colorado Pressbooks).
implication: MetroGraph's abstraction strategy: principles like aggregating low-degree nodes, grouping related workflows, and smoothing layouts apply directly. Suggests multi-scale design: detailed view shows all connections, zoomed-out view generalizes clusters into single 'super-stations'.

concept: Mental Model Stability in Dynamic Visualization
definition: Principle that layout updates in response to data changes should minimize spatial disruption to existing elements, preserving the user's internalized mental model of structure; reduces cognitive disorientation and improves task efficiency during iterative exploration.
key_refs: Nickel, S., et al. 2018. Octilinear Force-Directed Layout with Mental Map Preservation for Schematic Diagrams. In: Proc. GD 2018. Springer LNCS 10692:404–417.
Eades et al. 1991. A heuristic for graph drawing. Congressus Numerantium 42:149–160.
implication: MetroGraph's key usability feature: as workflows evolve (new steps added, dependencies change), the layout should update minimally. Nickel et al. report 50% faster task completion with mental-map preservation. Critical for iterative AI agents/workflows where the graph changes incrementally.

definition: Empirical observation that graph visualizations degrade in readability as node/edge count increases; cognitive load compounds exponentially; metro maps and hierarchical techniques partially mitigate by abstracting at scale, but fundamental limits exist (e.g., effective metro map size ~500+ stations).
key_refs: Nöllenburg et al. 2022. A Survey on Computing Schematic Network Maps.
Schlag et al. 2008. Scalability of Network Visualization from a Cognitive Load Perspective.
Smajda et al. 2017. A Taxonomy and Survey of Dynamic Graph Visualization.
implication: MetroGraph's design constraint: metro maps are not infinitely scalable; beyond ~500–1000 nodes, hierarchical/temporal decomposition becomes necessary (e.g., Treebar Maps). MetroGraph should surface scalability limits and recommend multi-scale/nested views for very large workflows.

concept: Treebar Maps: Schematic Representation at Scale
definition: Recent technique (2023) for visualizing large metro-style networks via hierarchical bar chart representation, allowing simultaneous view of multiple hierarchy levels without overload; bridges metro map aesthetics with tree visualization scalability.
key_refs: Hofmann, K., et al. 2023. Treebar Maps: Schematic Representation of Networks at Scale. arXiv:2307.12393.
implication: MetroGraph's solution for large-scale workflows: when a workflow graph exceeds single-screen metro-map capacity, Treebar-style hierarchical decomposition maintains schematic clarity. Enables MetroGraph to scale from small designs (~50 nodes) to enterprise workflows (1000+ nodes) via hierarchical drill-down.

definition: Graph-theoretic extension where nodes can be members of multiple hyperedges (subsets); naturally models set membership and intersection relations; MetroSets applies this to metro layout, with hyperedges as lines and memberships as station appearances.
key_refs: Nöllenburg, M., et al. 2021. MetroSets: Visualizing Sets as Metro Maps. IEEE TVCG 27(2):1257–1267.
implication: MetroGraph's data model generalization: if workflows have overlapping concerns/tags (e.g., a step belongs to both 'data-processing' and 'monitoring' lines), hypergraph model captures this naturally. Extends metro metaphor beyond simple graphs to richer, multi-membership structures.

concept: Wayfinding and Navigation in Schematic Maps
definition: Principles for designing maps/diagrams to support user navigation and route-finding: landmark visibility, consistent line styles, color differentiation, hierarchical structure, and interaction affordances (zoom, pan, highlight) that guide user attention and reduce search effort.
key_refs: Darken & Sibert 1996. Navigating Large Virtual Spaces. SIGGRAPH '96.
Arthur & Passini 1992. Wayfinding: People, Signs, and Architecture.
Schöttler et al. 2024. Designing complex network visualisations using the wayfinding map metaphor. Information Visualization 23(3).
implication: MetroGraph's interaction design: principles like clear landmarks (key workflow steps), consistent line styles (workflow types), color differentiation (teams/domains), and pan/zoom hierarchy support intuitive navigation of complex workflows. Directly addresses the chat-vs-graph cognition problem by making the graph directly navigable.

definition: Foundational conceptual model for representing entities, attributes, and relationships in databases. Entities are objects/things of interest; attributes describe their properties; relationships describe associations between entities with specified cardinality (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many).
key_refs: Chen 1976 / The Entity-Relationship Model—Toward a Unified View of Data
implication: MetroGraph must ground schema representation in ER semantics. The wedge solves HCI failure by making ER structure the navigable graph substrate—entities as nodes, relationships as edges, cardinality constraints as visual affordances. This unifies AI chat (natural entity/relationship talk) with structured graph exploration (click-to-filter by entity type, follow relationship chains).

definition: Extension of the ER model that adds support for specialization/generalization hierarchies, category (union) relationships, and inheritance. Allows representation of entity supertypes/subtypes and IS-A relationships.
key_refs: Elmasri & Navathe / The Enhanced Entity-Relationship Model
implication: MetroGraph must support visual representation of hierarchical entity structures. EER extension enables more expressive schema diagrams, reducing the cognitive burden of understanding inheritance and specialization—critical for complex enterprise schemas. Visualizing supertypes/subtypes as collapsible hierarchies supports progressive disclosure and reduces surface-area bloat.

definition: Task-by-data-type taxonomy providing a systematic framework for information visualization design. Core pattern: Overview → Zoom → Filter → Details-on-Demand. Classifies visualization tasks by data structure (1D, 2D, 3D, temporal, high-dimensional, networks, text) and interaction types.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1996 / The Eyes Have It: A Task by Data Type Taxonomy for Information Visualizations
implication: MetroGraph must implement the Overview-Zoom-Filter-Details pattern explicitly. For large schemas, start with abstracted overview (entity clusters), allow zoom into entities and their relationships, filter by relationship type/cardinality, and expose details (constraints, attributes) on demand. This pattern directly counters the RAG-chat failure mode (chat = abstract, no exploration; UI = drowns in details).

definition: Principled framework for visualization design with four levels: domain (problem characterization), data abstraction (transform domain data into abstract data types), task abstraction (characterize user tasks), and design idioms (choose appropriate encodings/interactions). Emphasizes separating data/task abstraction from visual encoding choices.
key_refs: Munzner 2014 / Visualization Analysis & Design
Munzner & Shimrat / Nested Model for Visualization Design and Validation
implication: MetroGraph must apply Munzner's nested model systematically: (1) Domain = schema visualization for RAG/agent-builder tools; (2) Data abstraction = table/relationship graph structures; (3) Task abstraction = entity discovery, relationship tracing, constraint understanding, schema comparison; (4) Design idioms = node-link diagrams with force-directed layout, color encoding by entity type. This grounds wedge in rigorous visualization science.

definition: Interaction pattern for managing large information spaces. Users first view overview (high-level abstraction), interactively zoom into areas of interest, filter by attributes/constraints, and access fine-grained details on demand. Reduces cognitive load by progressively revealing complexity.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1996 / The Eyes Have It
implication: MetroGraph's core interaction model. For a 500-table schema, show initial overview (10-15 key entity clusters), allow semantic zoom (click cluster to expand), filter by business domain (finance, customers, inventory), reveal constraints/cardinality/attributes in side panel. Addresses bloat failure: overview limits initial cognitive load; progressive disclosure prevents drowning in details.

definition: Class of graph drawing algorithms (spring-embedder methods) that simulate physical forces between nodes (repulsion) and edges (attraction). Iteratively adjusts positions until equilibrium, producing layouts that tend to minimize edge crossings, spread nodes evenly, and make node clusters visible.
key_refs: Fruchterman & Reingold 1991 / Graph Drawing by Force-directed Placement
Jacomy et al. 2014 / ForceAtlas2: A Graph Layout Algorithm for Handy Network Visualization
implication: MetroGraph must implement force-directed layout for large schema graphs. Provides intuitive, discoverable layouts that surface clusters (related entities) without manual arrangement. Critical for scalability: force-directed layout can handle 100s of entities with acceptable readability. Allows incremental refinement (add new entities, layout adapts).

definition: Empirical principles for readable graph diagrams. Key metrics: edge crossing minimization (strongest readability predictor), bend minimization, edge length uniformity, angular resolution, aspect ratio, and symmetry preservation. Readability correlates strongly with task completion time and error rates.
key_refs: Purchase et al. 1996 / Aesthetics and Automated Graph Layout
Purchase 2002 / Establishing Aesthetics based on Human Graph Reading Behavior
Dunne & Shneiderman 2013 / The State of the Art in Empirical User Evaluation of Graph Visualizations
implication: MetroGraph's rendering engine must optimize for readability metrics. Prioritize edge crossing minimization for entity-relationship graphs (ER diagrams are inherently high-crossing for large schemas). Use curve routing to reduce visual clutter. Test layouts empirically with users on complex schemas. Improved readability means better schema comprehension—key for RAG/agent builders to reason about data access patterns.

definition: Quantitative measures of schema structural complexity. Includes node count, edge count, density (ratio of actual to maximum edges), clustering coefficient, average degree, diameter, and specialized metrics (branching factor, inheritance depth, constraint count). Used to predict visualization difficulty and scalability requirements.
key_refs: Petrounias et al. 2012 / Database Complexity Metrics
Mota & Oliveira 2015 / Complexity Metric for XML Schema Document
Carelli & Falkenthal 2015 / Analysing complexity of XML Schemas in geospatial web services
implication: MetroGraph must compute and expose schema complexity metrics. High complexity requires stronger abstraction (clustering, hierarchies, filtering). Metrics allow automatic suggestions: 'This schema has 450 entities and 1200 relationships (density=0.12); recommend grouping by 5-8 business domains for clarity.' Complexity assessment informs interaction design (simple schemas: full view; complex: mandatory overview-zoom).

definition: Techniques for reducing graph complexity through clustering, node merging, and hierarchical abstraction. Summarizes graphs into smaller, semantically meaningful representations while preserving key structural properties. Includes community detection, supernodes (entity groups), and multi-level hierarchies.
key_refs: Navlakha et al. 2008 / Graph Summarization with Quality Guarantees
Le et al. 2018 / Summarizing Static and Dynamic Big Graphs
Xu et al. 2024 / Utility-Based Graph Summarization: New and Improved
implication: MetroGraph must use summarization for large schemas. Group related entities (e.g., customer tables, orders, products) into semantic clusters. Show cluster boundaries with visual hierarchy. Allow expansion of clusters on demand. This directly solves bloat failure: instead of 500 flat entities, show 8-12 clusters initially, each expandable. Critical for navigability and cognitive load management.

definition: Design pattern that shows essential information initially and reveals additional details through interaction (clicks, hover, expansion). Reduces cognitive load by hiding low-priority information. Key principle: show enough context to navigate, but hide complexity until needed.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1996 / The Eyes Have It
Nielsen 2006 / Prioritizing Web Usability
implication: MetroGraph's fundamental interaction strategy. Initial view: entity names only, no attributes. Hover: show cardinality, entity count. Click: expand attributes, constraints, indexes, foreign keys. This prevents overwhelming users with 500-entity, 2000-column raw schema. Aligns with agent-builder use case: agents construct queries incrementally (entity → attributes → filters → joins), matching progressive disclosure.

definition: Theory that working memory has limited capacity (~7±2 items). Extraneous cognitive load (from poorly designed UI) reduces capacity for productive tasks. Intrinsic load (task difficulty) and germane load (learning) must be optimized; extraneous load minimized through clear design, chunking, and progressive information revelation.
key_refs: Sweller 1988 / Cognitive Load During Problem Solving: Effects on Learning
Mayer 2009 / Multimedia Learning (Cognitive Load Theory)
implication: MetroGraph must actively manage cognitive load. Large ER diagrams are extraneous-load disasters: hundreds of entities, lines crossing everywhere, no clear narrative. MetroGraph reduces extraneous load through visual hierarchy (size by importance), semantic color (entity type), grouping (business domains), and labels (table purpose). Allows productive intrinsic load (understanding schema design intent) and germane load (learning data model).

definition: Psychological principles of visual perception: proximity (near items grouped), similarity (same color/shape grouped), continuity (lines followed smoothly), closure (incomplete shapes perceived as complete), figure-ground (foreground/background separation). Applied to design, these principles guide visual grouping and hierarchy.
key_refs: Wertheimer 1923 / Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt
Smashing Magazine 2014 / Design Principles: Visual Perception and the Principles of Gestalt
implication: MetroGraph applies Gestalt principles to schema diagrams. Proximity: group related entities spatially. Similarity: use consistent color for entity types, edge styles for relationship types. Continuity: route edges smoothly to avoid visual breaks. Closure: use implicit grouping (light backgrounds) for entity clusters without explicit containers. Figure-ground: highlight query path (figure) against schema (ground) for exploration tasks.

definition: Visual notation for representing relationship cardinality constraints in ER diagrams. Three major notations: Chen (1:1, 1:N, M:N symbols), Crow's Foot (crow's foot symbols for one/many), UML (multiplicity labels like 0..1, 1..*, *). Each notation makes different constraints visually salient.
key_refs: Chen 1976 / The Entity-Relationship Model
Barker 1989 / CASE*Method: Entity/Relationship Modelling (Crow's Foot notation)
OMG 2015 / Unified Modeling Language (UML) Specification
implication: MetroGraph must support multiple cardinality notations (at minimum Chen and Crow's Foot). Cardinality is critical for query construction: agents need to know if relationship is 1:1 (lookup) or 1:N (joined scan). Visual clarity of cardinality reduces errors in data model reasoning. Crow's Foot is more intuitive for practitioners; Chen is more formal. Allow users to toggle between notations.

definition: Mapping of data attributes to visual properties. Effectiveness depends on visual channel properties: position is most accurate, followed by length/size, then color/angle. Different channels suit different data types: categorical data uses color/shape; ordered data uses size/brightness; nominal uses color. Redundant encoding (multiple channels for same attribute) improves accessibility.
key_refs: Mackinlay 1986 / Automating the Design of Graphical Presentations
Cleveland & McGill 1984 / Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods
Bostock et al. 2024 / A Survey of Perception-Based Visualization Studies by Task
implication: MetroGraph must encode schema semantics systematically. Position: use force-directed layout (nodes positioned by relationships). Size: entity importance (by row count or query frequency). Color: entity type/domain (red=transactions, blue=customers, green=inventory). Shape: relationship type (solid=foreign key, dashed=many-to-many). Redundant encoding (color + icon for entity type) improves accessibility for color-blind users and offline readability.

definition: Visualization approach where schemas and data are displayed with respect to a query context. Highlights tables/columns accessed by a query, shows data flow, and enables interactive query refinement. Bridges schema visualization and query execution by making both visible and linked.
key_refs: Gatterbauer et al. 2023 / A Tutorial on Visual Representations of Relational Queries
Li et al. 2015 / Zenvisage: Effortless Data Exploration with Visual Analytics
implication: MetroGraph's query-driven mode. When building a query, highlight the entities/columns involved. Show data lineage: which tables feed which joins. Allow users to click relationships to add joins, attributes to add to SELECT clause. This directly supports agent builders and RAG workflows: agents construct queries incrementally (start with one table, add filters, add joins), and MetroGraph visualizes the query context live, reducing need for separate query editor.

definition: Information visualization pattern using multiple coordinated views of the same data. Interaction in one view (e.g., selection) updates others. Linked brushing allows cross-view filtering and highlighting. Enables complementary representations (schema overview + attribute details, entity list + relationship graph).
key_refs: Roberts 2007 / Multiple and Coordinated Views in Information Visualization
Baudel & Brodbeck 1992 / Interaction in Ilvs: Through Constrained Optimization
implication: MetroGraph uses multi-view coordination. Left panel: entity list with search/filtering. Center: graph visualization of schema with force-directed layout. Right panel: selected entity's attributes/constraints. Selecting an entity highlights it in graph and shows details. Typing a relationship type filters graph to show only those relationships. This coordination prevents the RAG-chat failure (chat = can't see data; UI = can't reason about it): see entire schema + can focus on entity of interest.

definition: Visualization techniques for semi-structured/flexible schemas in document-oriented (MongoDB), column-oriented (Cassandra), and key-value stores. Challenges: no fixed schema, nested structures, variable attributes. Solutions: aggregate models (show common schema patterns), nested visualization (treemaps, sunburst), schema inference (extract from sample documents).
key_refs: Wang et al. 2018 / Exploring the Visualization of Schemas for Aggregate-Oriented NoSQL Databases
implication: MetroGraph must support NoSQL visualization (increasingly common in modern stacks). For MongoDB collections, show common document structure, highlight variants, allow drilling into nested objects (embedded documents). Use color to show frequency (common attributes vs. rare). For hierarchical NoSQL (JSON documents), use treemap/sunburst layouts. This extends MetroGraph's applicability beyond relational databases, supporting more modern data architectures.

definition: Visualization of property graph and RDF schema structures. Property graphs have labeled nodes/edges with properties. RDF has triples (subject-predicate-object). Schema visualization shows: node types and their properties, edge types and their semantics, type hierarchies (rdfs:subClassOf), and cardinality constraints. Unique challenge: schema can be implicit (inferred from instances).
key_refs: Bonifati et al. 2023 / DiscoPG: Property Graph Schema Discovery and Exploration
Glimm et al. / RDF Knowledge Graph Visualization From a Knowledge Extraction System
Kraemer et al. 2022 / The World of Graph Databases from An Industry Perspective
implication: MetroGraph must support graph database visualization (Neo4j, RDF, knowledge graphs). Property graphs are natural for entity-relationship visualization: nodes=entities, edges=relationships. RDF requires semantic rendering of predicates and type hierarchies. Schema discovery (inferring schema from data) is critical for schemaless graphs. This extends MetroGraph into AI/knowledge-graph tools, supporting LLM embeddings and reasoning.

definition: Techniques for automatically inferring schema from data when no explicit schema exists (schemaless databases, legacy systems, data lakes). Methods: sampling documents/rows, statistical analysis, constraint discovery, type inference, clustering similar records. Results: inferred schema, confidence metrics, variant patterns.
key_refs: Golab et al. 2024 / Introducing Schema Inference as a Scalable SQL Function
Souibgui et al. 2024 / DBAutoDoc: Automated Discovery and Documentation of Undocumented Database Schemas via Statistical Analysis and Iterative LLM Refinement
Zhou et al. 2025 / ScheMatiQ: From Research Question to Structured Data through Interactive Schema Discovery
implication: MetroGraph must integrate schema discovery for legacy/undocumented databases and schemaless data. When user uploads a CSV, JSON, or Parquet file, MetroGraph infers schema (detect types, cardinalities, relationships) and displays it. For property graphs without explicit schema, MetroGraph samples instances and visualizes inferred schema. This supports RAG's critical use case: indexing heterogeneous data sources with unknown structure. Agents can then reason about inferred schema.

definition: Visualization techniques for nested/hierarchical data. Treemaps: partition rectangular area into smaller rectangles proportional to data values, preserving parent-child hierarchy. Sunburst: concentric rings with center = root, inner rings = children. Both show structure and size simultaneously in compact space.
key_refs: Johnson & Shneiderman 1991 / Tree-Maps: A Space-Filling Approach to the Visualization of Hierarchical Information
Stasko & Zhang 2000 / Focus+Context Display and Navigation Techniques for Enhancing Radial, Space-Filling Hierarchies
implication: MetroGraph uses hierarchical visualization for nested/hierarchical schemas. JSON schema with nested objects → sunburst. EER with entity specialization hierarchies → treemap. Shows both structure and cardinality (rectangle size = row count). Allows drill-down (click to zoom into hierarchy level). This supports complex domain models and semi-structured data, expanding MetroGraph's applicability.

definition: Principle from Edward Tufte: maximize the proportion of visualization devoted to representing data (data-ink) versus non-data elements (chartjunk). Remove decorative elements, redundant labels, and visual noise. Higher data-ink ratio improves clarity and efficiency.
key_refs: Tufte 1983 / The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
Tufte 1997 / Visual Explanations
implication: MetroGraph applies Tufte's principles rigorously. No gratuitous 3D effects, gradients, or decorations. Every pixel should represent schema structure: node position, edge routing, color for entity type, size for cardinality. Labels must be concise (table names, not full documentation). This clarity is critical for understanding large schemas and reduces cognitive load—especially important for agent-builder UIs where clarity enables reasoning.

definition: Visualization of schema evolution and temporal changes. Shows schema versions over time, highlights additions/deletions/modifications. Techniques: timeline view (schema state at each version), diff visualization (changes highlighted), animation (schema evolution animated over time).
key_refs: Braun et al. 2018 / DBChEx: Interactive Exploration of Data and Schema Change
Lin et al. 2023 / Multiscale Snapshots: Visual Analysis of Temporal Summaries in Dynamic Graphs
implication: MetroGraph supports schema versioning and evolution tracking. For RAG systems indexing production databases, agents need to understand schema changes (new tables, dropped columns, renamed fields). MetroGraph visualizes schema diff (before/after), animated transitions, and version history. This enables robust agent reasoning: agents can detect schema mismatches, handle migrations, and validate data access patterns against schema versions.

definition: Visual representation of database constraints: primary keys (PKs), foreign keys (FKs), unique constraints, check constraints, not-null constraints, default values. Techniques: color highlighting (PK in bold), icons (FK as arrow), labels (constraint type), visual separation (constraints in sidebar).
key_refs: Chen 1976 / The Entity-Relationship Model
Elmasri & Navathe 2010 / Fundamentals of Database Systems
implication: MetroGraph makes constraints explicit and visually salient. Primary keys: bold entity names or PK icon. Foreign keys: edge type (solid red line). Unique/check constraints: attribute-level icons. This is critical for query construction: agents must know which fields are unique (can be join keys), which are non-null (safe filters), which have defaults. Visual constraint representation enables agents to reason about query validity.

definition: User interfaces for constructing database queries without SQL. Users select tables/columns from schema, specify conditions visually, and system generates query. QBE (Zloof, 1977) pioneered tabular approach; modern variants use graph-based builders (connect tables visually) or form-based builders (fill in fields).
key_refs: Zloof 1977 / Query-by-Example: A Data Base Language
Halpin 2005 / Visual Formal Methods for Conceptual Modelling
implication: MetroGraph's query-by-example mode: users click entities to add to query, click relationships to add joins, right-click attributes to add filters. Schema graph provides the visual query builder substrate. This is powerful for RAG and agent builders: agents construct queries incrementally by navigating the schema graph (click this entity → see its relationships → choose join path → refine). Reduces need for complex query syntax.

concept: Semantic Web and RDF Schema Visualization
definition: Visualization of RDF (Resource Description Framework) and OWL (Web Ontology Language) schemas. RDF/OWL represent knowledge as triples (subject-predicate-object). Visualization challenges: triple-based representation is abstract; type hierarchies and logical constraints are implicit. Techniques: graph layout (entities as nodes, predicates as edges), node/edge filtering (show only important classes/properties), constraint visualization.
key_refs: Catarci et al. 2005 / Ontology-Based Information Visualization: Toward Semantic Web Applications
Vargas-Vera & Lytras 2006 / Visualising Ontologies
implication: MetroGraph supports RDF and knowledge graph visualization. For AI/LLM agents, semantic web schema visualization is critical: enables reasoning over structured knowledge. MetroGraph shows RDF classes (as entities), properties (as relationships), and type hierarchies. Pattern-based visualization highlights common structural patterns (e.g., person → knows → person). This extends MetroGraph to knowledge graphs and semantic AI.

definition: Formal framework (2025) for principled database visualization. Defines: data abstraction (table/relation structure), task abstraction (exploration, query, analysis), and decomposition patterns (how tables map to visualization types—table to bar chart, scatter plot, etc.). Provides theoretical foundation for tool design.
key_refs: Sharma et al. 2025 / A Formalism and Library for Database Visualization
implication: MetroGraph is grounded in this formal framework. Database (relational schema) → abstract as graph of entities/relationships → choose visualization (for overview use node-link; for attributes use tabular; for cardinality use size/color). Framework enables systematic visualization design and justifies MetroGraph's choices. This provides theoretical rigor and enables replicability.

definition: Interactive systems for exploring unfamiliar schemas (schema discovery). Users navigate by clicking/searching entities, and system provides guidance (popular tables, related entities, query suggestions). Systems combine schema visualization with interactive recommendation and search to help users understand and navigate complex data.
key_refs: Bonifati et al. 2023 / DiscoPG: Property Graph Schema Discovery and Exploration
Nakamura & Ito 2018 / FreebaseViz: Interactive Exploration of Freebase Schema Using Query-Driven Visualisation
implication: MetroGraph's core strength: schema exploration. When agents or users encounter an unknown schema, MetroGraph helps them explore: search by table name, visualize relationships, see popular join paths, highlight query-relevant entities. For RAG, this enables agents to discover data sources automatically (what tables are related to 'customer'?). Combines visualization with search/recommendation for efficient discovery.

definition: Vocabulary of 14+ design dimensions (abstraction, closeness of mapping, consistency, diffuseness, error-proneness, hidden dependencies, premature commitment, secondary notation, visibility, viscosity) for evaluating notational system usability. Each dimension describes design tradeoffs: improving one dimension often degrades another.
key_refs: Green 1989 Cognitive Dimensions of Notations at HCI
Green & Petre 1996 Usability Analysis of Visual Programming Environments
implication: MetroGraph design must explicitly balance cognitive dimensions: expressiveness vs. learnability, abstraction vs. viscosity, visibility vs. clutter. Visual programming achieves high closure-of-mapping at cost of increased diffuseness and viscosity in complex programs.

definition: Interaction principle enabling users to directly act on visible objects (not modal commands) with immediate, reversible feedback. Reduces mode complexity, memory load, and semantic distance between user intent and system action.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1982 Direct Manipulation Interfaces and Design Principles
Shneiderman 1983 Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design
implication: MetroGraph succeeds when node manipulation (drag, connect, edit) directly affects query/visualization without modal dialogs. Spatial layout itself becomes direct representation of data relationships, minimizing abstraction distance between intent and representation.

definition: Cognitive scalability ceiling: humans can reliably distinguish approximately 50 distinct visual primitives before confusion, disorientation, and comprehension failure occurs. Attributed to L. Peter Deutsch; explains why visual programming languages face inherent complexity limits vs. textual code.
key_refs: Deutsch, L.P. (attributed) The Deutsch Limit
implication: MetroGraph cannot scale by adding more node types, connector styles, or visual dimensions. Must use abstraction hierarchies, folding/unfolding, and semantic clustering to stay within 50-primitive budget per viewport. Directly addresses user complaint about node-canvas builders: surface-area bloat and cognitive overload.

definition: Computation model treating programs as networks of black-box processes with predefined connections passing information packets. Processes run asynchronously and independently; computation emerges from message-passing topology rather than sequential control flow.
key_refs: Morrison 1994 Flow-Based Programming
Morrison 2010 Flow-Based Programming: A New Approach
implication: MetroGraph aligns naturally with FBP semantics: nodes as transformers, edges as data channels, layout encodes dependency graph. This visual-semantic alignment (high closure of mapping) is why dataflow UIs are intuitive but hit complexity limits at approximately 50 nodes.

definition: Empirical evidence that visual dataflow representations (LabVIEW, Pure Data) enable faster tracing of execution paths and parallelism detection than textual equivalents, especially for novices. Advantage persists only for small-to-medium programs (under approximately 50 nodes); breaks down in large programs where layout becomes unmanageable.
key_refs: Green & Petre 2005 Evidence in favor of visual representation for the dataflow paradigm: LabVIEW
Burnett et al. 2001 Visual Programming in the Wild: Survey of 227 LabVIEW Programmers
implication: MetroGraph visual advantage strongest for DB schema visualization, filter composition, and execution planning. Empirically confirmed scalability wall: users abandon visual tools at approximately 50-100 node complexity, switching to text-based query languages or scripting.

definition: Scratch-style block-based syntax reduces extraneous cognitive load by eliminating syntax errors and visual parsing overhead; drag-drop assembly replaces text typing and parsing. Reduces intrinsic load by chunking related operations into semantic blocks.
key_refs: Weintrop & Wilensky 2015 Using Computational Thinking in Learning
Alt et al. 2016 Exploring perceived cognitive load in Scratch
implication: MetroGraph should adopt block/card-based chunking for complex operations: bundle related node properties into collapsible panels, use predefined filter templates as blocks. Reduces decision overhead vs. generic node-editor where every property is equally visible.

definition: Clutter defined as degradation of visual search efficiency from excess graphical elements. Feature congestion metric: higher ratio of pixels to semantic elements (node density, edge density, label density) directly impairs visual attention, comprehension, and decision speed.
key_refs: Rosenholtz et al. 2005 Measuring Visual Clutter, Journal of Vision
implication: MetroGraph metro-map inspiration directly addresses clutter: simplified topology, large spacing, high stroke contrast reduce feature congestion. At Deutsch limit boundary, aesthetic simplification (removing visual details) becomes functionally necessary for cognition, not just style.

definition: Body of guidelines (from graph drawing literature) for optimizing comprehension of node-link diagrams: crossing reduction, edge bundling, hierarchical layout, node size proportional to importance, color/shape coding for categories, spacing for visual separation, consistency in arrow direction.
key_refs: Kobourov et al. 2024 GuidelineExplorer: Navigating through actionable guidelines on node-link visualization
implication: MetroGraph metro-map inspiration embodies these principles: hierarchical regions minimize crossings, consistent arrow directions, large node spacing, categorical coloring. Foundational to achieving Deutsch-limit-compliant layouts for 50 plus node graphs.

definition: Empirical research (eye-tracking, fMRI) shows program comprehension requires sequential topological search of code structure, building spatial mental models. Programmers scan code in patterns matching data-dependency graphs, not linear text order.
key_refs: Pennington 1987 Stimulus Structures and Mental Representations
Walz et al. 1993 Visualizing the Program
implication: MetroGraph aligns with natural comprehension strategy: spatial layout directly encodes logical dependency structure. Text-based queries force reconstruction of spatial topology from sequential symbols; visual layout offloads this reconstruction cost.

definition: Cognitive dimension describing resistance to change: high viscosity means small modifications require disproportionate effort (e.g., moving nodes in canvas requires retying all edges). Low-viscosity systems allow rapid iterative refinement.
key_refs: Green 1989 Cognitive Dimensions
Green & Petre 1996 Cognitive Dimensions Framework
implication: Node-canvas builders typically have high viscosity: moving node breaks all connections, requiring manual edge re-routing. MetroGraph must minimize viscosity via smart re-layout on edits, auto-routing, or constraint-based positioning.

definition: Strategy for managing visual complexity by enabling users to collapse complex subgraphs into single abstract nodes (folding), revealing detail only on demand. Reduces displayed node count below Deutsch limit by pushing complexity into collapsed subtrees.
key_refs: Card & Mackinlay 1999 Readings in Information Visualization
implication: MetroGraph folding/composite-node feature essential scalability mechanism: users work with hierarchical abstractions (database schemas as single nodes, query subcompositions as collapsible blocks) without exceeding 50-primitive visual budget per viewport.

definition: Domain of making programming accessible to non-expert users via visual, example-based, or DSL approaches. Core challenge: balancing expressiveness (covering real-world use cases) against learnability and cognitive load for non-professionals.
key_refs: Nardi 1993 A Small Matter of Programming
Lieberman & Liu 2006 Programming by Example
implication: MetroGraph target audience is technically unsophisticated database analysts. Visual-programming principles apply: avoid syntax, use semantic chunking (templates, presets), provide progressive scaffolding from simple filters to complex subqueries.

definition: Perceptual organizing principles: proximity (items close together appear grouped), similarity (same color/shape appear related), continuity (smooth curves grouped before sharp breaks), closure (incomplete shapes completed mentally). Govern automatic visual parsing before conscious attention.
key_refs: Gestalt Psychology Foundation early 20th century
Norman 2013 Design of Everyday Things
implication: MetroGraph leverages Gestalt: proximity groups related parameters, similarity (color/icon) identifies semantic categories, continuity guides edge following. Violating Gestalt principles increases cognitive load independent of information quantity.

concept: Visual versus Textual Programming: Empirical Comparison
definition: Systematic review of educational outcomes comparing block-based, visual-dataflow, and text-based programming instruction. Meta-analysis shows visual approaches accelerate initial learning and reduce syntax errors; effect size diminishes above intermediate complexity. Text-based systems preferred for advanced tasks.
key_refs: Robins et al. 2010 Learning and teaching programming: A review
Siraj et al. 2017 Visual and Textual Programming Languages: A Systematic Review
implication: MetroGraph visual advantage proven for novices and intermediate complexity (10-50 nodes). Must plan graceful degradation: visual-textual hybrid (show generated SQL alongside canvas), or text-box nodes for experts authoring complex filters.

definition: Visual languages designed for specific domains (SQL, workflow automation, data transformation) with limited but domain-optimized node vocabularies. Trade generality for expressiveness within narrow scope; achieves higher usability by reducing semantic load.
key_refs: Mernik et al. 2005 When and how to develop domain-specific languages
Andova et al. 2015 Ontology-Based Evaluation and Design of DSVLs
implication: MetroGraph inherently DSVL for database/workflow domain. Constraint vocabulary to 20-30 filter types plus 10-15 data source connectors stays well below Deutsch limit. Generality is liability; domain specialization is strength.

definition: Graphical systems enabling non-technical users to author database queries via visual composition (query-by-example, visual joins, drag-drop filters) instead of SQL text. Success requires balancing query expressiveness with comprehensibility.
key_refs: Catarci et al. 2000 Visual Query Systems
Duarte & Gras 2023 Visual Query Languages: Systematic Review
implication: MetroGraph is instance of visual query language. Empirical lesson: users accept reduced expressiveness if interface is intuitive. Opportunity to defer complexity (custom SQL nodes for power users) rather than surfacing all complexity visually.

definition: Automated generation of executable code from visual sketches, block diagrams, or example-based specifications. Shifts programming burden from syntax authoring to intent specification; system infers implementation details.
key_refs: Gulwani et al. 2015 Program Synthesis
Chandra et al. 2023 Program Synthesis from Visual Specification
implication: MetroGraph could leverage program synthesis: visual specification of filter logic (drag columns, specify conditions) auto-generates optimized SQL. Addresses scalability: visual complexity stays low because system fills in procedural details. Emerging hybrid approach overcomes pure-visual limits.

definition: Fundamental tension in language/system design: maximizing expressiveness (what programs can be written) typically requires larger vocabulary, complex semantics, and steeper learning curves. Visual systems sacrifice expressiveness to achieve learnability.
key_refs: Green & Petre 1996 Cognitive Dimensions Framework
Norman 1988 Psychology of Everyday Things
implication: MetroGraph must consciously accept reduced SQL expressiveness (no window functions, no CTEs, no complex subqueries) to maintain visual learnability. Design: 80 percent of use cases with visual interface plus text-box nodes for remaining 20 percent of complex queries.

concept: Spatial Mental Models in Code Comprehension
definition: Empirical evidence that programmers build mental representations of code structure as spatial/topological maps, not sequential text. Eye-tracking shows non-linear scan patterns following logical/data-flow topology. Visuospatial working memory dominates comprehension.
key_refs: Zhao et al. 2023 Developers Visuo-spatial Mental Model
Walz et al. 1987 Visualizing the Program
implication: MetroGraph directly leverages spatial cognition: literal spatial layout mirrors mental topology. Users spend no cognitive effort reconstructing spatial structure from sequential text; layout IS the structure. Explains intuitive appeal vs. SQL for novices.

definition: Action possibilities suggested by object properties (e.g., button shape affords pressing, slider affords dragging). Well-designed affordances enable discovery without instruction; poor affordances cause failed interactions and learned helplessness.
key_refs: Norman 1988 Design of Everyday Things (revised 2013)
implication: MetroGraph nodes must have clear affordances: draggable handles on edges invite connection, resize handles invite resizing, parameter boxes invite clicking. Visual metaphors (database icon for source, filter icon for where-clause) enable intuitive discovery.

definition: Perceived likelihood that following a path (clicking a node, expanding a section) will lead to desired information, based on visual cues. Strong scent (clear labels, relevant icons, spatial proximity) encourages exploration; weak scent causes abandonment.
key_refs: Pirolli & Card 1999 Information Foraging Theory
Chi et al. 2000 Towards Effective Information Foraging
implication: MetroGraph nodes must have strong information scent: descriptive labels, domain-relevant icons (database, filter, join symbols), spatial grouping by function. Weak scent causes users to miss relevant operations or data sources.

definition: Challenge of making visual/canvas-based programming accessible to blind and low-vision users. Requires alternative modalities (sonification, haptic feedback, screen reader optimization) that preserve semantic structure without visual layout.
key_refs: Jadud et al. 2023 Extension-Based Accessibility Framework for Blockly
implication: MetroGraph canvas-centric paradigm presents accessibility barriers. Must support: keyboard-only navigation (arrow keys to traverse graph, tab to cycle through nodes), semantic HTML export (generated query readout), screen reader optimization.

definition: Degree to which the form of the representation matches the concept represented (isomorphism). High closure means intuitive mapping between visual form and semantic meaning (e.g., spatial proximity in diagram matches logical dependency in code). Low closure requires translation effort.
key_refs: Green 1989 Cognitive Dimensions
Green & Petre 1996 Cognitive Dimensions Framework
implication: MetroGraph achieves high closure of mapping: connected nodes represent connected queries, visual hierarchy matches logical hierarchy, data flow direction matches left-to-right scan direction. This is primary cognitive advantage over text-based SQL.

definition: Industry analysis of visual/low-code platforms reveals consistent scalability ceiling around 50-100 nodes; beyond that, custom code nodes required or platform abandoned for traditional development. Root cause: complexity overhead of visual composition exceeds text-based development.
key_refs: Codebridge 2024 Low-Code and No-Code Development: Limitations
Forrester Research analyses
implication: MetroGraph must acknowledge this boundary: visual composition scales to approximately 50 filter/join nodes; beyond that, accept limitations or provide text-code escape hatch (custom SQL nodes, subquery templates). Optimize for 20-40 node workflows.

concept: Natural Language to Code and Hybrid Approaches
definition: Emerging hybrid paradigm combining natural language specification (written intent, DSL annotations) with visual composition and code generation. Addresses visual scalability ceiling by offloading complex logic to NL description or auto-generated subexpressions.
key_refs: Li et al. 2023 Natural Language to Code: A Structured Survey
Raychev et al. 2014 Code Completion with Neural Attention
