implication: MetroGraph could integrate NL annotations on nodes (e.g., get orders from last 7 days) that auto-expand to SQL WHERE clauses. Or combine visual schema with textual query refinement (show SQL alongside canvas, allow in-place editing). Overcomes pure-visual cognitive ceiling.

definition: Tufte principle: proportion of ink (pixels) devoted to representing data vs. decorative/redundant elements. Higher data-ink ratio equals clearer communication. Chartjunk reduces efficiency; minimalist design maximizes clarity per unit visual area.
key_refs: Tufte 1983 The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
implication: MetroGraph must ruthlessly eliminate decorative elements: no gradient fills, no drop shadows, no rounded corners unless semantically meaningful. Every pixel should represent either node function or connection relationship. Metro-map aesthetic optimizes data-ink ratio.

definition: A visual design pattern that provides simultaneous access to both detailed view of a selected region (focus) and surrounding information (context) within a single display, reducing cognitive load during exploration of large graphs.
key_refs: Munzner (2000) / Interactive Visualization of Large Graphs and Networks
Furnas (1986) / Generalized Fisheye Views
implication: MetroGraph's metro-map interaction should use focus+context (e.g., highlighted stations/neighborhoods + surrounding context) to let users zoom deeply into subgraphs without losing spatial orientation or overview context.

definition: Interaction paradigm enabling users to directly interact with visual objects (drag, resize, filter) rather than typing commands, reducing abstraction layers and improving perceived control and feedback.
key_refs: Shneiderman (1992) / Tree Visualization with Tree-Maps: 2-D Space-Filling Approach
Norman (2013) / The Design of Everyday Things
implication: MetroGraph must prioritize drag-and-drop node repositioning, click-to-filter edges, and gestural pan/zoom over command-line queries; avoids the 'flight to chat' anti-pattern by keeping control in the user's hands via visual affordances.

definition: Non-linear magnification technique applying smooth scaling gradients from a focal point, compressing peripheral areas while magnifying focus region to show both detail and context in continuous space without jarring discontinuities.
key_refs: Furnas (1986) / Generalized Fisheye Views
Sarkar & Brown (1994) / Graphical Fisheye Views
implication: MetroGraph could employ fisheye lensing on dense graph regions to prevent node/edge clutter while allowing users to see local neighborhoods without multiple zoom levels; smooths the interaction cost vs. visual clarity trade-off.

definition: Formal framework (Furnas) computing importance scores for graph nodes based on distance from user's focus, structural properties, and user-specified weights; enables principled selective rendering and progressive disclosure.
key_refs: Furnas (1986) / Generalized Fisheye Views
Perer (2009) / Search, Show Context, Expand on Demand: Supporting Large Graph Exploration with Degree-of-Interest
implication: MetroGraph can formalize node/edge visibility decisions using DOI: nodes close to selected subway stations show full detail, distant regions collapse to abstract clusters; prevents visual overload while maintaining navigability.

definition: Non-Euclidean space embedding using 3D hyperbolic geometry to achieve exponential space expansion, enabling efficient visualization of tree-like graphs with 100K+ nodes via radial focus+context projection while maintaining graph topology.
key_refs: Munzner & Burchard (1995) / H3: Laying Out Large Directed Graphs in 3D Hyperbolic Space
implication: While hyperbolic geometry is specialized, its principle applies to MetroGraph: use layout algorithms (force-directed, hierarchical) that allocate exponentially more space to focused regions, allowing massive graphs to scale without extreme zoom factors.

definition: Seven fundamental visual dimensions (position, size, value, texture, color, orientation, shape) used to encode data attributes; provides principled basis for assigning data dimensions to visual properties according to data type and task requirements.
key_refs: Bertin (1967) / Semiology of Graphics
implication: MetroGraph's design should assign graph attributes to visual variables systematically: node position encodes spatial proximity/layout, color encodes data type/category, size encodes importance/degree, ensuring consistent and perceptually effective encoding.

definition: Design principles for node-link layouts including edge crossing minimization, uniform edge lengths, symmetry preservation, and clustering; empirically shown to improve user comprehension and task performance (Purchase et al.).
key_refs: Purchase (1997) / Cognitive Measurements of Graph Aesthetics
Purchase et al. (2001) / Empirical Evaluation of Graph Drawing Aesthetics
implication: MetroGraph's layout algorithms must minimize edge crossings, maintain symmetry, and balance edge lengths to improve visual clarity; use automated readability metrics (edge crossing counts, node occlusion) during layout generation.

definition: Technique reducing visual clutter in dense graphs by routing similar/nearby edges along common paths, revealing aggregate flow patterns and high-level connectivity structure while suppressing low-level edge details.
key_refs: Holten (2006) / Hierarchical Edge Bundling for Visualization of Large Graphs
Holten et al. (2017) / Force-Directed Edge Bundling
implication: MetroGraph could apply edge bundling to dense workflow/agent graphs, grouping edges by destination or relationship type to reveal macro-patterns; enables pattern discovery without node repositioning.

definition: Progressive disclosure technique changing visual representation at different zoom levels: at low zoom, nodes aggregate into clusters with summary statistics; at high zoom, individual nodes and attributes appear; prevents visual overload while enabling detail-on-demand.
key_refs: Perlin & Fox (1993) / Pad: An Alternative Approach to the Computer Interface
Bederson & Hollan (1994) / Pad++: A Zoomable Graphical Sketchpad
implication: MetroGraph's zoom levels should transition smoothly between abstraction levels: zoom-out shows data lineage as colored arrows between tables; zoom-in reveals individual fields, transforms, and metadata; prevents overwhelming users while allowing deep exploration.

definition: Multi-level representation strategy organizing graph nodes into nested clusters at increasing levels of abstraction, enabling navigation from high-level overview to granular details; supports summarization, filtering, and progressive refinement.
key_refs: Munzner (2000) / Interactive Visualization of Large Graphs and Networks
Balzer & Deussen (2005) / Level-of-Detail Visualization
implication: MetroGraph should organize graphs hierarchically: Databases > Tables > Fields, Workflows > Steps > Tasks, Agents > Components; users explore via expand/collapse, with aggregated view showing summary statistics (table row counts, execution times).

definition: Two complementary graph representations: node-link diagrams excel at topology/path tasks and spatial understanding; adjacency matrices excel at density/connectivity assessment and scaled to larger graphs; hybrid approaches combine strengths.
key_refs: Ghoniem et al. (2004) / Matrices or Node-Link Diagrams: Which Visual Representation is Better for Visualising Connectivity Models?
Henry & Fekete (2006) / MatrixExplorer: A Dual-Representation System for Exploring Structured Relations
implication: MetroGraph could offer dual views: node-link diagram for intuitive data lineage navigation; adjacency matrix for dense dependency analysis; linked brushing between views surfaces different insights (topology vs. connectivity patterns).

definition: Interaction technique enabling coordinated selection across multiple linked views: selection in one view (e.g., highlighting nodes) automatically highlights corresponding elements in complementary views, enabling rapid cross-view pattern discovery.
key_refs: Becker & Cleveland (1987) / Brushing Scatterplots
Roberts (2007) / State of the Art: Coordinated and Multiple Views in Exploratory Visualization
implication: MetroGraph could highlight workflow execution traces across node-link diagram and timeline view; clicking a table in the graph highlights all upstream/downstream tables and their dependencies across multiple linked views.

definition: Visual cues (e.g., mini-previews in widget controls, node color, edge labels) signaling content relevance and reducing uncertainty about navigation outcomes; strong scent improves search efficiency and reduces cognitive load.
key_refs: Chi & Pirolli (2007) / Rational Analyses of Information Foraging on the Web
Olston & Chi (2003) / ScentTrails: Integrating Browsing and Searching on the Web
implication: MetroGraph should embed scent cues: hovering over a table shows record count, column names; hovering over a workflow shows execution status, average runtime; edge labels indicate join conditions or transformation types.

definition: Iterative cognitive process (evidence → hypotheses → schemas) in which users formulate interpretations from information fragments via cycles of search (evidence foraging), synthesis, and schema building; visualization supports rapid hypothesis-evidence cycles.
key_refs: Pirolli & Card (2005) / The Sensemaking Process and Leverage Points for Analyst Technology
implication: MetroGraph's interaction must support rapid hypothesis testing: users should easily explore 'what if I remove this table?' (filter), 'where does this transform apply?' (highlight), 'how many rows flow through this step?' (aggregation) — enabling iterative schema refinement.

definition: Smooth interpolation between graph states (layout changes, filtering, highlighting) with staged animations and visual continuity; improves perception of object correspondence and enables users to track changing elements.
key_refs: Heer & Robertson (2007) / Animated Transitions in Statistical Data Graphics
Lin & Dunne (2018) / Common Fate for Animated Transitions
implication: MetroGraph's pan/zoom/filter operations should use smooth animations (200-500ms) rather than instant changes; animating both movement (edges/nodes) and appearance (opacity fades) helps users track state changes and maintain spatial orientation.

definition: Direct-manipulation interfaces enabling end-users to construct queries via visual means (dragging nodes, clicking edges, selecting attributes) rather than text syntax; improves accessibility and encourages exploratory querying.
key_refs: Catarci et al. (1997) / Visual Query Systems: A Perspective
Soutou (2017) / GraphTQL: A Visual Query System for Graph Databases
implication: MetroGraph should enable visual query construction: users drag two tables onto canvas to define a join; right-click to add filter conditions; edge labels auto-suggest join columns; avoids SQL syntax while enabling complex queries through visual composition.

definition: Visual or interactive cues (color, shape, border, cursor changes) signaling actionable properties of interface elements; strong affordances improve discoverability by making possible interactions obvious without explicit instruction.
key_refs: Norman (2013) / The Design of Everyday Things
Saffer (2009) / Designing Gestural Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph's nodes should show clear affordances: draggable nodes have cursor change on hover, clickable nodes show hand cursor, contextual menu buttons appear on selection; reduces need for documentation while guiding intuitive interaction.

definition: Design principle ensuring interactive capabilities are visible and learnable without requiring external documentation; achieved through consistent affordances, progressive disclosure, and contextual help.
key_refs: Nielsen & Norman (2000) / Information Architecture and Usability
implication: MetroGraph must avoid hidden features: interaction capabilities should be visible (drag handles on nodes, right-click menu labels), progressive disclosure reveals advanced options (on hover or submenu), enabling users to self-discover features.

definition: Graph structures with multiple levels of hierarchy (nodes contain sub-nodes) or clustering (nodes grouped into super-nodes); requires specialized visualization combining node-link diagrams at multiple abstraction levels with edge bundling across hierarchy levels.
key_refs: Eades & Feng (1997) / Compound Graph Visualization
Sander & Scholl (2005) / Orthogonal Hypergraph Layout
implication: MetroGraph's data lineage graphs are inherently hierarchical (schemas > tables > fields, workflows > stages > tasks); support expand/collapse of compound nodes, with inter-level edges showing cross-hierarchy relationships.

definition: Hardware-accelerated techniques (GPU rendering, spatial indexing, level-of-detail culling) enabling interactive pan/zoom of millions of nodes/edges; essential for maintaining 60+ FPS responsiveness on large datasets.
key_refs: Munzner (2000) / Guaranteed Frame-Rate Drawing
Li et al. (2019) / Deck.gl: Large-scale Web-based Visual Analytics Made Easy
implication: MetroGraph should use WebGL or similar GPU acceleration, spatial indexing for culling off-screen nodes, and level-of-detail rendering (simplify node shapes at small zoom) to enable smooth interaction with 100K+ node graphs.

definition: Algorithmic techniques aggregating nodes/edges into summary supergraphs while preserving macro-structure; reduces graph complexity for visualization and analysis while enabling drill-down to original granularity.
key_refs: Navlakha et al. (2008) / Graph Summarization with Bounded Error
implication: MetroGraph could summarize large data lineage graphs: multiple related tables aggregate into 'table clusters', multiple pipeline stages collapse into macro-steps; users explore via expand/collapse, revealing detail on demand.

definition: Techniques for visualizing graphs that change over time: animation (showing change via frame sequences), small multiples (side-by-side snapshots), or hybrid approaches; must preserve mental map while showing temporal evolution.
key_refs: Beck et al. (2015) / A Taxonomy and Survey of Dynamic Graph Visualization
implication: MetroGraph could visualize workflow execution evolution: animation shows task progression over time, or side-by-side snapshots (small multiples) show pipeline state at different timestamps; enables understanding of dynamic behavior.

definition: Specialized interaction techniques enabling efficient navigation of very large graphs: search/filter (reduce visible nodes), focus+context (zoom while preserving overview), aggregation (collapse similar nodes), and progressive refinement.
key_refs: Munzner (2000) / Interactive Visualization of Large Graphs and Networks
implication: MetroGraph must support scalable interaction: users should search/filter by table name, workflow status, or dependency type to reduce graph size; focus+context keeps orientation; aggregation collapses unrelated nodes; enables exploring enterprise-scale data lineage.

concept: Eighteen Design Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
definition: A set of 18 design guidelines (Amershi et al., CHI 2019) covering four design principles: give control to users, enable graceful failure, support operator with information, and encourage appropriate reliance. Validated across 20 AI products with 49 practitioners.
key_refs: Amershi et al. 2019 / Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
Amershi et al. 2021 / Assessing Human-AI Interaction Early through Factorial Surveys
implication: MetroGraph must implement these 18 principles across its interface design to ensure users maintain appropriate control, can recover from failures, have visibility into system reasoning, and develop calibrated trust.

definition: The process of bringing user trust in alignment with actual system performance (not over-trust or under-trust). Involves designing informative explanations that enable accurate mental models rather than persuasive explanations that increase reliance regardless of correctness.
key_refs: Bansal et al. 2021 / Does the Whole Exceed its Parts?
Wang & Yin 2024 / Practising Appropriate Trust
implication: MetroGraph should prioritize informative explanations that calibrate user trust accurately; explanations must help users understand both capabilities and limitations rather than simply increase reliance.

concept: Mental Models and User Understanding of AI Capabilities
definition: Users' internal representations of how AI systems work and what they can/cannot do. Misaligned mental models lead to inappropriate use, unmet expectations, and reduced team performance. Must be elicited and designed for explicitly.
key_refs: Norman 2013 / The Design of Everyday Things
Amershi & Vaughan 2024 / User Mental Models in AI Code Completion
Kaushik et al. 2024 / Exploring Mental Models of Early Adopters
implication: MetroGraph design must surface and support formation of accurate mental models of graph reasoning, agent behavior, and query execution; use progressive disclosure and examples to avoid capability mismatches.

definition: Explainability (why did the system decide X), interpretability (how does the system work internally), and transparency (what data/processes are being used) are distinct design concerns with different cognitive and trust implications. Not all are needed equally for all user types.
key_refs: Mohseni et al. 2019 / Multidisciplinary Survey and Framework
Springer et al. 2024 / Towards Human-Centered Explainable AI Survey
Mohseni & Weld 2024 / From Explainable to Interactive AI
implication: MetroGraph must carefully target which form of explanation (explainability, interpretability, or transparency) best serves each user type (domain expert vs. non-expert querying graph structure); avoid over-explaining simple operations.

concept: User Control and Agency in Human-AI Interaction
definition: The degree to which users can direct, modify, or override AI system behavior. Critical for human dignity, error recovery, and trust. Ranges from consultative (users seek AI input) to delegative (AI acts autonomously with user oversight).
key_refs: Amershi et al. 2019 / Guidelines (Principle 1: Give Control to Users)
Miller et al. 2024 / Design Considerations for Human Oversight of AI
Norman & Stappers 2015 / AI Systems as Agents
implication: MetroGraph must embed user control throughout the interaction model: users must be able to inspect queries, modify graph traversal, override suggestions, and rewind agent decisions; avoid over-automation.

definition: Designing systems to fail in predictable, recoverable ways rather than catastrophically. Users need visibility into what went wrong, why, and how to recover. Critical for trust and continued engagement.
key_refs: Amershi et al. 2019 / Guidelines (Principle 2: Explain Graceful Failures)
Google PAIR Guidebook 2024 / Errors + Graceful Failure chapter
implication: MetroGraph must implement transparent error states: show users when agents fail, why, which data/relationships caused issues, and offer clear recovery paths (retry, alternative query, manual override).

definition: How to visually and textually represent AI system uncertainty (confidence, prediction intervals, alternative answers). Raw probability is less effective than calibrated frequency or visual representations. Affects user reliance and decision quality.
key_refs: Kaur et al. 2023 / Designing for Appropriate Reliance: Uncertainty Presentation
Banerjee & Chakraborty 2023 / Understanding Uncertainty: How Lay Decision-makers Perceive Uncertainty
implication: MetroGraph should represent agent/query uncertainty through calibrated frequency bands, visual confidence indicators, or alternative suggestions rather than raw percentages; design should match user expertise and task context.

definition: Users may rely on AI too much (over-reliance, automation bias) or too little (under-reliance) based on mismatches between perceived and actual system capability. Design must actively support appropriate levels of reliance through transparency and control.
key_refs: Bansal et al. 2021 / Complementary Team Performance
Amershi & Kaur 2023 / Designing for Appropriate Reliance
implication: MetroGraph design must surface when users should and shouldn't trust agent suggestions through signals (confidence scores, failure histories, complexity warnings) to prevent both under-reliance (missing valuable suggestions) and over-reliance (accepting flawed reasoning).

definition: The set of competencies users need to interact effectively with AI systems: understanding AI capabilities/limitations, mental models of how systems work, ability to recognize failure modes, and knowing when to trust or override. Varies significantly by user background.
key_refs: Kaur et al. 2020 / What is AI Literacy? Competencies and Design Considerations
Huang et al. 2024 / AI Literacy for Community Colleges
implication: MetroGraph must provide scaffolding for users with varying AI literacy: onboarding that builds correct mental models, progressive disclosure of complexity, in-context help for recognizing agent limitations, and design that doesn't assume AI expertise.

definition: Systematic design for integrating human judgment into AI systems through feedback loops. Includes active learning, human annotation, preference learning (RLHF), and collaborative refinement. Process-oriented rather than reactive.
key_refs: Madaio et al. 2021 / Human-in-the-Loop Design Cycles
Casper et al. 2023 / RLHF Survey
Lim et al. 2021 / Guidelines for Designing Human-in-the-Loop Machine Training Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph should embed feedback mechanisms throughout: users can correct graph interpretations, validate query logic, refine agent behavior, and teach the system domain-specific patterns; feedback must flow back into model/agent training.

definition: Research on how humans and AI agents combine to outperform either alone. Depends critically on appropriate task allocation, communication patterns, and user understanding of agent capabilities. Complementarity requires both entities play to their strengths.
key_refs: Bansal et al. 2021 / Does the Whole Exceed its Parts?
Xu et al. 2025 / Collaborating with AI Agents: Field Experiments
Ahmed et al. 2023 / AI Teammate Communication Strategies
implication: MetroGraph should be designed as a team player, not a replacement: highlight where agent reasoning excels and where human oversight is essential; design communication (what agent explains, when it asks for help) to maximize complementarity.

definition: Actively shaping and maintaining user expectations about what AI can do to match actual capabilities and limitations. Poor expectation management leads to disappointment, loss of trust, and abandonment. Requires upfront communication and ongoing calibration.
key_refs: Sap et al. 2020 / Will You Accept an Imperfect AI?
Lai et al. 2024 / Expectation Management in AI Framework
implication: MetroGraph's onboarding and messaging must set realistic expectations about graph coverage, query complexity limits, reasoning depth, and error rates; use progressive difficulty and clear success criteria to calibrate expectations over time.

concept: Proactive AI and Appropriate Autonomy Levels
definition: Systems that initiate actions without explicit user request. User preferences for proactivity vary by context, task criticality, and relationship type. Over-proactivity feels intrusive; under-proactivity misses opportunities. Requires explicit design of autonomy boundaries.
key_refs: Sap et al. 2020 / Exploring User Expectations of Proactive AI Systems
implication: MetroGraph should calibrate when agents proactively suggest queries, refine traversals, or flag relationships vs. waiting for user direction; design should make autonomy level explicit and allow adjustment per user preference.

definition: Reusable solutions to recurring HCI+AI problems: feedback patterns (confidence indicators, alternatives, explanations), control patterns (override, refine, undo), error patterns (recovery, graceful degradation), and learning patterns (progressive disclosure, onboarding).
key_refs: Liu et al. 2024 / Survey of UI Design in Generative AI Applications
Bussone et al. 2024 / Taxonomy of Human-Generative-AI Interactions
Amershi et al. 2019 / Guidelines (implicit patterns)
implication: MetroGraph should adopt proven interaction patterns: confidence badges for agent suggestions, undo/redo for query refinements, in-context tooltips for complex reasoning, progressive disclosure of advanced features, and clear error recovery flows.

concept: Harmful Design Patterns and Dark Patterns in AI
definition: Design patterns that harm users: over-anthropomorphization (making AI seem more capable than it is), deceptive confidence displays, guilt-based feedback, obfuscated limitations, making override difficult, addictive engagement mechanics that replace critical thinking.
key_refs: Gray et al. 2024 / Characterizing and Modeling Harms from Design Patterns
implication: MetroGraph must explicitly avoid harmful patterns: don't anthropomorphize agents excessively, clearly mark limitations, make override easy, avoid guilt-based feedback for not using agent suggestions, and prevent dark patterns that exploit cognitive biases.

concept: Interaction Primitives and Design Space Decomposition
definition: Breaking down human-AI interactions into fundamental primitives (query, explain, refine, feedback, undo, override) and mapping them to a design space. Enables systematic coverage of design options and comparison across AI applications.
key_refs: Amershi et al. 2024 / Unpacking Human-AI Interactions: Primitives to Design Space
implication: MetroGraph should be designed systematically across primitives: support query (user specifies intent), explain (system reveals reasoning), refine (user adjusts parameters), feedback (user corrects mistakes), undo (revert decisions), and override (take control). Each primitive needs coherent design.

definition: Specialized HCI considerations for chatbots, dialogue systems, and conversational agents: turn-taking, clarification strategies, context management, error recovery in dialogue, multimodal integration, and conversation history.
key_refs: Moore et al. 2023 / On the Design of and Interaction with Conversational Agents
implication: If MetroGraph includes conversational query interfaces (query-by-dialog), apply dialogue design patterns: explicit confirmation of intent, clear context windows, easy clarification mechanisms, and history navigation to prevent misunderstandings.

concept: Creative Collaboration and Co-creation with AI
definition: Designing AI systems to augment human creativity through suggestion, exploration, and co-ideation rather than replacement. Requires maintaining user control, avoiding excessive constraint from AI suggestions, and enabling serendipitous discovery.
key_refs: Zhang et al. 2024 / Evaluating AI-Assisted Creative Ideation
Xu et al. 2025 / Exploring Creativity in Human-AI Co-creation
implication: If MetroGraph serves exploratory/creative graph queries (discovering unexpected relationships), design for co-creation: surface multiple query paths, show why agent suggests certain traversals, allow deviation from suggestions without penalty, celebrate serendipitous findings.

concept: Recommender System Interfaces and Explanation Design
definition: Specialized HCI for AI systems that suggest items, rankings, or actions. Must build trust through transparent explanations, support user agency through filtering/overriding, and avoid filter bubbles. Distinct from other AI interfaces due to personalization.
key_refs: Taube et al. 2006 / Trust-Inspiring Explanation Interfaces for Recommender Systems
Liu et al. 2020 / How Do Users Interact with Algorithm Recommender Systems?
implication: If MetroGraph recommends graph queries or relationships, design explanations around recommendation rationale (why this path?), allow users to explore alternatives, and provide control to refine or reject suggestions.

definition: Methods for collecting human preferences and using them to fine-tune AI model behavior. Requires interface design for preference collection that is cognitive scalable, unbiased, and connected to downstream model updates. Critical for personalization and user agency.
key_refs: Ouyang et al. 2023 / A Survey of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
implication: MetroGraph could use RLHF to personalize agent behavior: collect user preferences for query styles, reasoning depth, and explanation types; ensure feedback interface is lightweight and users understand how feedback shapes future behavior.

definition: Guidelines for multi-agent systems where humans coordinate with software agents: emphasizing transparency (what is each agent doing?), communication (clear delegation and status updates), and appropriate autonomy (humans know when agents act independently).
key_refs: Zhang et al. 2024 / Design Principles for Human-Agent Interaction
implication: MetroGraph's agents must communicate openly: surface what reasoning is happening, distinguish human vs. AI decisions, enable human agents to direct AI agents, and provide clear status updates on query execution progress.

definition: Psychological and interface barriers that prevent users from providing feedback to conversational agents (effort, unclear impact, social awkwardness, lack of feedback mechanisms). Removing barriers increases user control and system improvement.
key_refs: Al-Natour et al. 2025 / Feedback by Design: User Barriers in Conversational Agents
implication: MetroGraph must lower friction for user feedback: provide lightweight feedback mechanisms (thumbs up/down, quick corrections), show how feedback was used, make feedback feel natural in dialogue (not intrusive), and explicitly request feedback when most useful.

concept: AI Agent Behavioral Science and Adaptive Interaction
definition: Understanding how AI agents behave in response to human input and how to design agents that adapt to user preferences, communication styles, and expertise levels. Agents should learn user patterns and adjust behavior accordingly.
key_refs: Amershi et al. 2025 / AI Agent Behavioral Science
implication: MetroGraph agents should adapt: learn user query patterns, adjust explanation complexity to match user expertise over time, adapt suggestion types based on user feedback history, and communicate when shifting behavior.

concept: User-First Approach to AI Ethics and Values
definition: Designing AI systems with values that reflect user preferences and cultural contexts rather than imposing designer values. Requires participatory design, testing across diverse populations, and ongoing adaptation to user needs.
key_refs: Ahmed et al. 2024 / The User-First Approach to AI Ethics
implication: MetroGraph should incorporate user values: allow users to specify what relationships matter most, expose algorithmic choices that reflect values (e.g., path-finding trade-offs), and test design with diverse user communities to avoid cultural biases.

concept: Human-AI Interaction Design Standards and Frameworks
definition: Emerging standards and systematic frameworks for human-AI interaction design: ISO-style guidelines, maturity models, design templates, and evaluation criteria. Provide structure for practitioners and consistency across products.
key_refs: Zhang et al. 2025 / Human-AI Interaction Design Standards
Sap et al. 2021 / The Future of Human-AI Collaboration: Hybrid Intelligence Taxonomy
implication: MetroGraph's design should align with emerging standards: follow documented design principles, use consistent patterns, provide design rationale documentation, and enable systematic evaluation against established criteria.

definition: Framing AI as augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities. Hybrid intelligence systems emphasize strengths division: AI excels at scale/pattern-matching, humans at judgment/context. Success requires explicit design of complementarity.
key_refs: Sap et al. 2021 / The Future of Human-AI Collaboration: Hybrid Intelligence Taxonomy
Shneiderman 2022 / Human-Centered AI
implication: MetroGraph should be designed explicitly for human-AI complementarity: graph pattern discovery (AI) + domain validation (human), exhaustive traversal (AI) + semantic judgment (human), rapid suggestions (AI) + intentional refinement (human).

concept: Information Design and Visualization for AI Outputs
definition: Applying principles from information visualization and design to present AI outputs effectively: data-ink ratio, graphical integrity, chart selection, color theory, and reducing cognitive load in high-dimensional output spaces.
key_refs: Tufte 2001 / The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
Munzner 2014 / Visualization Analysis and Design
implication: MetroGraph's visualization of graph queries and agent reasoning must follow visualization principles: minimize non-data ink, use color meaningfully (not decoratively), choose graph layouts for clarity not aesthetics, and reduce visual complexity through progressive disclosure.

concept: Design Psychology and Affordances in AI Interfaces
definition: Foundational HCI principles applied to AI: affordances (visual cues for actionability), signifiers (indicating state), mental model support (design matches how users think), and discoverability (users find features without help).
key_refs: Norman 2013 / The Design of Everyday Things
Preece et al. 2022 / Interaction Design (6th Edition)
implication: MetroGraph must apply design psychology: affordances should signal when users can refine queries, override suggestions, or undo actions; system state (executing, failed, ambiguous) should be visually obvious; interaction patterns must match user mental models of graphs.

definition: Shneiderman's foundational framework emphasizing AI as augmenting human capabilities, maintaining human control, supporting human values, and enabling human understanding. Opposes AI-only and human-only approaches.
key_refs: Shneiderman 2022 / Human-Centered AI: Ensuring Human Control While Increasing Automation
Shneiderman 2022 / Human-Centered AI: Reliable, Safe & Trustworthy
implication: MetroGraph's entire design philosophy should align with HCAI: position agents as augmenters not replacers, design for user control and understanding, expose values in design choices, and maintain human judgment as final authority on graph interpretation.

concept: Design Trajectory and Evolutionary Design for AI Systems
definition: Systematic mapping of design evolution for AI systems, particularly human-AI collaborative learning systems. Shows how designs should evolve as systems learn, users gain expertise, and interaction patterns stabilize.
key_refs: Sun et al. 2024 / A Design Trajectory Map of Human-AI Collaborative Reinforcement Learning Systems
implication: MetroGraph should be designed with evolutionary trajectory in mind: early onboarding heavy, transitioning to expert shortcuts; early suggestions conservative, becoming more bold as user trust/expertise grows; feedback mechanisms simple initially, more sophisticated later.

definition: A multidimensional construct encompassing explainability (why agent chose action), legibility (observability of state/intent), and predictability (user ability to forecast behavior); measured empirically via TOROS scale across three factors.
key_refs: TOROS Scale (2025) - Nature Scientific Reports / arXiv 2408.16865
Measuring Transparency in Intelligent Robots (2025)
implication: MetroGraph wedge must expose agent state changes, action rationales, and next-step constraints through layered disclosure (overview+details), not buried in logs. Transparency becomes a regulatory lever for governance.

definition: Immediate perceivability of an agent's current state, capabilities, and constraints; a dimension of transparency that enables users to observe (without full explanation) what an agent is doing and why in real time.
key_refs: TOROS Measurement Framework (Scheutz et al., HRI)
Measuring Transparency in Intelligent Robots (2025)
implication: MetroGraph must support real-time state visualization (e.g., which tool is active, what context is in scope, which approval gates are pending) so users can answer 'what is happening now' without cognitive effort.

definition: User's ability to accurately forecast agent behavior in novel situations; depends on algorithms being available (inspectable), compact (comprehensible), and aligned (behavior matches stated intent); enables users to form accurate mental models.
key_refs: People Can Accurately Predict Behavior of Complex Algorithms (Popowski et al., Stanford 2601.18966)
TOROS Scale (2025)
implication: MetroGraph's agent interactions must be compact (step decomposition, not opaque multi-step rollups), available (showing intermediate states), and aligned (agent action matches stated next step); users can then trust step-by-step logs as prediction anchors.

definition: User's internal representation of how an agent works; accurate mental models are formed when agent behavior is visible, consistent, and comprehensible; users with poor mental models misunderstand agent capabilities and make inappropriate reliance decisions.
key_refs: Users' Mental Models of Generative AI Chatbot Ecosystems (Huang et al., ACM IUI 2025, 2501.19211)
Building Appropriate Mental Models (Mao et al., ACM IUI)
implication: MetroGraph must surface agent architecture visibly (e.g., 'approval gates → tool invocation → result review') so users build correct models of what agent can/cannot do; reduce 'black box' perception that leads to both over-reliance and under-reliance.

definition: User's ability to halt agent execution mid-task and redirect it; requires safe interruption mechanisms (virtualization, sandbox execution, or state rollback) to prevent agent learning to disable kill switches or resist interruption.
key_refs: Enter the Matrix: Safely Interruptible Autonomous Systems via Virtualization (Riedl & Harrison, 1703.10284)
When Users Change Their Mind: Evaluating Interruptible Agents in Long-Horizon Web Navigation (arXiv 2604.00892)
implication: MetroGraph must support pause/resume patterns with clear state capture; users perceive 'interruption is safe and cheap' only if they see agent can be paused at any step, state preserved, and resumed without unexpected side effects.

definition: UI mechanisms for user to accept/reject agent actions before execution (approval before) or after review (post-execution veto); examples: step-by-step confirmation, batch approval with rollback, confidence thresholds triggering human review.
key_refs: On the Regulatory Potential of User Interfaces for AI Agent Governance (Feng et al., 2512.00742)
4 UX Design Principles for Autonomous Multi-Agent AI Systems (Dibia, 2024)
implication: MetroGraph's core interaction pattern: every high-risk agent action (data modification, tool invocation) shows a clear decision point where user can see what agent proposes, why, and approve/reject/modify before commit.

definition: Transition of initiative between human and agent; spectrum from agent-initiated proposals (user approves/rejects) to human-initiated requests (agent executes autonomously), with explicit visibility of who owns current task step.
key_refs: Mixed-initiative interaction (Allen, 1999, IEEE Intelligent Systems)
Adaptive Human-Agent Teaming (2504.10918)
Human-Centered Human-AI Collaboration (HCHAC) Framework (2505.22477)
implication: MetroGraph must visualize control flow: when user is directing (e.g., 'approve this action'), when agent is proposing (e.g., 'next step: call API'), when human review is required. Ambiguity about who owns the task creates disorientation.

definition: User interface displaying agent decomposition of a task into discrete, sequenced steps; shows current step, completion status, and intermediate results; enables user to verify agent reasoning and catch errors early.
key_refs: Fine-Grained Appropriate Reliance with Multi-Step Transparent Decision Workflow (2501.10909)
From Plan to Action: How Well Do Agents Follow the Plan? (2604.12147)
Anteater: Interactive Visualization of Program Execution (1907.02872)
implication: MetroGraph's primary UX pattern: step-by-step logs must be *interactive* (not passive), showing agent state transitions, tool outputs, and decision points; users should be able to drill into any step, see why agent chose it, and approve/reject before moving to next.

definition: Continuous communication of agent state (idle, planning, executing, waiting for approval) and task progress (steps completed, current bottleneck); prevents user disorientation and enables opportune intervention.
key_refs: Designing a Dashboard for Transparency and Control of Conversational AI (2406.07882)
Visualizing Confidence in Delivery Robots (CHI 2025, 3706599.3719695)
The effects of cues on task interruption recovery (Nature SR 2025, 2025-09358)
implication: MetroGraph should surface agent state continuously: 'thinking', 'waiting for tool response', 'blocked on approval', 'complete'; also show confidence/error rates to help users assess reliability.

definition: Persistent, queryable record of agent actions (what did it do, when, why, what were inputs/outputs); supports post-hoc verification, debugging, compliance, and user trust building.
key_refs: On the Regulatory Potential of User Interfaces for AI Agent Governance (2512.00742)
Interpreting Agentic Systems: Beyond Model Explanations to System-Level Accountability (2601.17168)
implication: MetroGraph must log agent decisions with sufficient detail for replay/audit: what data was accessed, which rules applied, what confidence was assigned; enables regulatory compliance and user debugging.

definition: User's ability to resume interrupted task efficiently; depends on interface cues that restore context (what was task state? what was I doing?), minimize working-memory load, and signal resumption-relevant information.
key_refs: Resuming a Dynamic Task Following Long Interruptions (PMC8247645)
The effects of cues on task interruption recovery in multitasking (Nature SR 2025)
Examining cognitive processes underlying resumption costs (PMC10896823)
implication: When MetroGraph user pauses an agent mid-task, UI must preserve and re-surface: prior steps completed, current state of data being modified, next pending steps; reduces cognitive load on resumption.

definition: Process of building understanding of complex agent behavior through exploratory interaction with visual representations; users query, filter, drill-down, and compare visualized agent state/decisions to form coherent mental models.
key_refs: Sensemaking with Interactive Data Visualization (ResearchGate)
On Sense Making and Knowledge Generation in Visual Analytics (MDPI 2813-2203)
Semantic Interaction for Narrative Map Sensemaking (2603.29651)
implication: MetroGraph's visualization should enable exploratory sensemaking: users can ask 'what decisions did agent make?', 'where did it get stuck?', 'what assumptions underlay step X?' through interactive, narrative-driven views, not static logs.

definition: Agent's communication of its own uncertainty (e.g., 'high confidence' vs. 'uncertain'); enables users to calibrate trust and apply scrutiny proportional to risk; reduces both complacency (ignoring agent output) and automation bias (over-trusting).
key_refs: Overcoming Algorithm Aversion with Transparency (2508.03168)
Visualizing Confidence in Delivery Robots (CHI 2025)
Consumer Autonomy in Generative AI Services (NCBI 2024)
implication: MetroGraph should show agent confidence/uncertainty alongside each decision: e.g., 'found record (high confidence)' vs. 'inferred relationship (low confidence)'; helps users decide when to inspect closely or override.

definition: User's perception that they can meaningfully influence agent behavior and outcomes; requires actual control points (not illusory), visibility of available options, and system responsiveness to user input.
key_refs: Consumer Autonomy in Generative AI Services (2024)
Human-controllable AI: Meaningful Human Control (2512.04334)
Exploring Collaboration Patterns through the Lens of Agency (2507.06000)
implication: MetroGraph must provide real decision points (not rubber-stamp approvals): users can reject agent proposals, request alternative approaches, and see their input reflected in subsequent steps; illusion of control breeds frustration.

definition: Agent's opportune intervention to offer suggestions or ask for direction; must be timed to user's cognitive state (not interrupt during focus) and accompanied by rationale; personalized to user preferences for autonomy vs. guidance.
key_refs: Sensing What Surveys Miss: Personalizing Proactive LLM Support (2602.00880)
Predicting Routine Object Usage for Proactive Robot Assistance (2309.06252)
After Personas: Learning Preference-Aligned Proactive Assistants (2602.04000)
implication: MetroGraph's proactive agent features (e.g., 'suggest next step?') should be personalized and deferential; not all users want autonomy, and interruption at wrong time creates cognitive load; observe user patterns to time interventions.

definition: User-driven explanation where user can ask 'why did agent choose X?', explore 'what if I changed this input?', and interactively test counterfactuals; shifts from static post-hoc explanations to hypothesis-driven inquiry.
key_refs: Holistic Explainable AI (H-XAI) (2508.05792)
X-SYS: Reference Architecture for Interactive Explanation Systems (2602.12748)
One Explanation Does Not Fit All (2001.09734)
implication: MetroGraph's explanation UI should be query-driven: user clicks on agent decision, sees rationale, can manipulate inputs to see how decision would change, and asks follow-up questions; reduces over-interpretation of static explanations.

definition: User tendency to over-rely on agent and disengage from monitoring; especially acute when agent is reliable; requires interface design that maintains user engagement (e.g., unpredictable alerts, periodic verification tasks, confidence signals).
key_refs: Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010, Human Factors 52.3)
Humans and Automation: Misuse, Disuse, Abuse (Parasuraman & Riley, 1997)
implication: MetroGraph should design against complacency: periodic spot-checks where user verifies agent output, confidence thresholds that trigger review, and confidence *variability* (not monotonic high confidence) to maintain alertness.

definition: User interface principle enabling users to directly modify agent outputs/state with immediate visible feedback; foundational design principle (Shneiderman) where system visibility and reversibility reduce cognitive load.
key_refs: Direct manipulation for comprehensible, predictable and controllable user interfaces (Shneiderman, ACM IUI 1997/1982)
The Design of Everyday Things (Norman, 2013)
implication: MetroGraph should enable users to directly edit agent-proposed steps, modify data before agent uses it, and see immediate consequences; avoid modeless interactions or dialog boxes that hide state.

definition: Perceptual cues signaling what actions are available (affordances) and where relevant information can be found (information scent); users navigate exploratory tasks more efficiently when affordances are visible and information scent guides them.
key_refs: Information Foraging Theory (Pirolli, 2007)
Information Foraging: How People Navigate on the Web (Pirolli & Card, UIST 1999)
implication: MetroGraph's agent UI must make affordances obvious (e.g., 'edit this step', 'inspect tool output', 'approve all remaining steps') and provide information scent guiding users to next-relevant action.

definition: The degree to which the insights provided by an explanation system can make sense to the targeted audience based on their domain knowledge and context. Interpretability is a property of individual explanations or model components, distinct from the broader action of explanation.
key_refs: Saeed & Omlin 2021 / Explainable AI Meta-Survey
Lipton 2016 / The Mythos of Model Interpretability
implication: In MetroGraph, interpretability is audience-specific: a data analyst needs different node/edge semantics than an ML engineer debugging model performance. The graph interface should adapt cognitive load and jargon level per user role, making 'interpretability' a design parameter, not an assumption.

definition: Explanations generated after a model has made a decision, rather than explanations derived from the model's internal structure. Post hoc methods (like saliency maps, counterfactuals) explain what a model did without revealing how it works internally, contrasting with transparent models that expose mechanisms.
key_refs: Lipton 2016 / The Mythos of Model Interpretability
Saeed & Omlin 2021 / Explainable AI Meta-Survey
implication: In MetroGraph, post hoc explanations (e.g., 'this answer was ranked high because the question matched keywords in source X') provide explanation without requiring interpretable-by-design models. This pragmatism is critical for LLM-based RAG where internal transparency is infeasible; instead, surface the decision context (retrieval scoring, confidence) as a post hoc lens.

definition: A canonical model-agnostic method that explains individual predictions by fitting a simple, interpretable model (typically linear) in the local neighborhood of the instance being explained. LIME works across model types and provides feature-attribution explanations showing which input features most influenced a prediction.
key_refs: Ribeiro et al. / LIME: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations
Saeed & Omlin 2021 / Explainable AI Meta-Survey
implication: For MetroGraph's agent-builder component, LIME-like local explanations can show 'why this workflow decision was made for this input' by highlighting which task features triggered which branches. This is essential UX—users need per-instance reasoning, not global model structure.

definition: A game-theoretic approach to feature attribution using Shapley values, distributing a model's output prediction fairly among input features by considering all possible feature subsets. SHAP provides consistent, theoretically grounded feature importance explanations with both local and global interpretation modes.
key_refs: Lundberg & Lee / SHAP: Shapley Additive Explanations
Christoph Molnar / Interpretable ML Book
implication: In MetroGraph's graph nodes (representing RAG retrieval or agent decisions), SHAP values on edge weights quantify 'how much did each source contribute to the final answer?' This aligns with fairness in credit assignment and helps users understand multi-source reasoning without exposing opaque weighting.

definition: A rule-based explanation method that identifies minimal, interpretable if-then rules (called 'anchors') that locally bound model behavior around a specific prediction. Anchors provide high-precision, human-readable explanations guaranteeing that if the anchor conditions hold, the prediction remains stable.
key_refs: Ribeiro et al. / Anchors: High-Precision Model-Agnostic Explanations
Saeed & Omlin 2021 / Explainable AI Meta-Survey
implication: For MetroGraph's workflow graphs, anchors could express 'if task type = X and input length > Y, then this branch is taken.' This gives non-ML users readable logic they can verify and even override, making human-in-the-loop workflow debugging feasible without ML expertise.

definition: Explanations that highlight why a decision was made by contrasting it with counterfactual alternatives ('why this, not that?'). Grounded in cognitive science, contrastive explanations are more human-comprehensible than additive explanations, as humans naturally reason comparatively.
key_refs: Miller et al. / What Makes a Good Explanation: Cognitive Dimensions
Wachter et al. / Alterfactual Explanations
implication: MetroGraph should show contrastive explanations: 'this source ranked first (score: 0.92) rather than the second source (score: 0.81) because it matched on [key phrase].' This comparison is more informative than absolute scores and aligns with how users naturally think about relevance.

definition: Explanations that specify what changes to input features would alter a model's prediction (e.g., 'if the income were 10k higher, the loan would be approved'). Counterfactuals are actionable, contrastive, and psychologically grounded, helping users understand both the decision boundary and paths to different outcomes.
key_refs: Wachter et al. / Counterfactual Explanations without Opening the Black Box
Wachter et al. / Alterfactual Explanations
implication: For RAG in MetroGraph, counterfactual UX might show: 'if you added [these keywords] to your query, source Y would rank higher.' This surfaces query-refinement strategies and empowers users to steer the system interactively, moving beyond passive answer-reading toward active exploration.

definition: The property of explanations being selective rather than exhaustive—highlighting the most important factors rather than listing all factors. Cognitive science shows humans prefer sparse, salient explanations over complete enumerations, as selectivity reduces cognitive load and improves comprehension.
key_refs: Miller et al. / What Makes a Good Explanation: Cognitive Dimensions
implication: MetroGraph's graph should highlight the most impactful nodes/edges in a reasoning chain, de-emphasizing minor contributions. This aligns with selective explanation and prevents cognitive bloat—users see the 'plot' of the answer without the subplot. Graph layout itself becomes a selection mechanism.

definition: The degree to which explanations invoke causal relationships rather than mere correlations. Humans prefer causal explanations ('X caused Y') to correlational ones ('X and Y are associated'), and causal reasoning is foundational to understanding why a decision was made and what could change the outcome.
key_refs: Miller et al. / What Makes a Good Explanation: Cognitive Dimensions
Lipton 2016 / The Mythos of Model Interpretability
implication: In MetroGraph, edge labels should convey causal language where valid ('source A retrieved because query matched keyword') rather than purely correlational ('source A and query are similar'). This supports mental model building and user agency in understanding and debugging recommendations.

definition: The mental effort required to comprehend an explanation. High cognitive load (complex jargon, too many factors, dense visual layouts) reduces explanation effectiveness. Good explanations minimize load through progressive disclosure, clear hierarchy, and audience-specific terminology.
key_refs: Miller et al. / What Makes a Good Explanation: Cognitive Dimensions
Shneiderman / The Purpose of Visualization is Insight
implication: MetroGraph must modulate cognitive load dynamically: data scientists see full reasoning chains; business users see simplified summary graphs with drill-down on demand. The same data, different cognitive entry points. This directly combats the 'bloat' wedge—not all surfaces are equally complex.

definition: The design and evaluation of interfaces that present AI explanations to users. XUI bridges XAI (explanation methods) and HCI (user interaction), focusing on how explanations are visualized, made interactive, and contextualized for different users and tasks. Effective XUI is evaluated on comprehension, trust calibration, and task performance.
key_refs: Lipton 2016 / The Mythos of Model Interpretability
Safian et al. 2024 / How Human-Centered Explainable AI Interfaces Are Designed and Evaluated
implication: MetroGraph IS an XUI: the graph itself is the explanation interface. Design decisions—node size, edge opacity, progressive disclosure, filtering by confidence—all affect how well users understand and trust the system. Every pixel is an explanation choice.

definition: The design of visual representations (charts, graphs, maps) to facilitate analytical reasoning and insight. Effective information visualization reduces cognitive load, highlights patterns, and enables exploratory analysis. Visualization quality is measured by accuracy of user perception, speed of comprehension, and actionability of insights.
key_refs: Tufte / The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
Shneiderman / The Purpose of Visualization is Insight
implication: MetroGraph is fundamentally a visualization choice: graphs over text, spatial layout over linear narrative. By making reasoning chains visual and spatial, users can pattern-match, compare alternatives, and spot anomalies faster than reading chat transcripts—reducing cognitive load while increasing trust by transparency.

definition: Standardized documentation artifacts for AI models, introduced by Gebru et al., that transparently report model specifications, performance metrics, training data characteristics, ethical considerations, and known limitations. Model cards enable stakeholders to assess model appropriateness for a use case and identify potential harms.
key_refs: Gebru et al. / Model Cards for Model Reporting
Saleh et al. / What's Documented in AI: Systematic Analysis of 32K Model Cards
implication: MetroGraph could surface model card data inline: hover a source → see training dataset size, bias disclaimers, failure modes. Or hover a ranking edge → see what performance metrics were optimized. This makes provenance and limitations visible without modal dialogs, keeping users in the 'flow' while staying informed.

definition: The process and design of displaying which retrieved documents or sources contributed to a RAG system's generated answer. Effective source attribution includes source identity, retrieval score/confidence, relevance justification, and (optionally) the extracted passages used. Attribution is foundational for trust calibration in RAG.
key_refs: Wazir et al. / Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems: A Survey
Zhang et al. / Trust Me on This: RAG User Study
implication: This is THE core of MetroGraph's RAG-UX wedge: instead of 'Here is an answer' (chat interface), show 'Here is how I assembled the answer from sources X, Y, Z with confidence scores.' Attribution makes the 'hallucination risk' tangible and actionable—users can verify, cross-check, and weight evidence themselves.

definition: The visibility and explainability of the retrieval stage in RAG systems—showing users which documents were retrieved, why they were selected (matching criteria, ranking scores), and how they contributed to the final answer. Retrieval transparency combats the perception of LLM-as-oracle by making the evidence chain visible.
key_refs: Wazir et al. / Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems: A Survey
Zhang et al. / Trust Me on This: RAG User Study
implication: MetroGraph's core feature: the retrieval stage is not hidden in an LLM's weights but visualized as a graph layer. Users see 'query → matching documents → ranked results → generation input,' making RAG's separation-of-concerns explicit. This combats both over-trust (I see sources) and under-trust (I can verify).

definition: A multidimensional concept encompassing the reliability, transparency, and appropriateness of RAG systems. Key factors include retrieval accuracy, source quality, generation fidelity (not hallucinating beyond sources), confidence calibration, and user ability to verify answers. Trustworthiness differs from mere accuracy—a low-accuracy RAG with transparent sources may be more trustworthy than a high-accuracy black-box.
key_refs: Wazir et al. / Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems: A Survey
Zhang et al. / Trust Me on This: RAG User Study
implication: MetroGraph directly addresses RAG trustworthiness by making transparency the design principle: users build trust not through a single 'trust score' but through visible reasoning. If the graph shows strong sources but weak connections, users mistrust the synthesis. If weak sources but strong connections, they reconsider. Trust becomes granular and justified.

definition: The degree to which an explanation accurately reflects the model's actual decision process. A faithful explanation represents what the model truly does (not a simplified or altered version); fidelity is measured by how well humans' interventions based on the explanation actually change model behavior as expected. Unfaithful explanations erode trust when users discover the explanation doesn't match reality.
key_refs: Ghosh et al. / A Comprehensive Study on Fidelity Metrics for XAI
implication: In MetroGraph, fidelity means the graph faithfully represents how the RAG actually ranked sources—not a post-hoc rationalization. If the user changes a query and sources re-rank, the graph updates accordingly, validating the explanation's fidelity. This prevents users from building false mental models.

definition: The assessment of explanation quality across dimensions like correctness (does it match the model?), completeness (does it cover key factors?), comprehensibility (can users understand it?), and actionability (can users act on it?). Evaluation can be computational (fidelity metrics), human-centered (comprehension tasks), or task-based (user performance improvements).
key_refs: Safian et al. / How Human-Centered XAI Interfaces Are Designed and Evaluated
Mohseni et al. / Evaluating Explainable AI: Which Explanations Help Users Predict Model Behavior?
implication: MetroGraph's graphs must be evaluated not just for visual clarity but for their impact on user task performance: Can users better verify answers with the graph? Do they catch errors faster? This shifts from 'is the explanation pretty?' to 'does it enable better decision-making?'—the real measure of effective XUI.

definition: A legal principle established by GDPR entitling users to request explanations for algorithmic decisions that significantly affect them (e.g., loan denials, medical diagnoses). The right to explanation creates regulatory demand for explainability, though the extent to which XAI methods satisfy this right remains contested.
key_refs: Brkan / European Union Regulations on Algorithmic Decision-Making and a 'Right to Explanation'
implication: For regulated domains (finance, healthcare), MetroGraph's explainability is not optional—it's compliance infrastructure. By making reasoning visible and auditable, MetroGraph helps organizations meet legal obligations while simultaneously improving user trust and decision quality.

definition: The principle that AI systems should be responsible for their decisions, with mechanisms for oversight, recourse, and correction. Accountability requires transparency (users can understand decisions), auditability (stakeholders can review decisions), and redress (users can appeal or appeal decisions). Explainability is a prerequisite for accountability.
key_refs: Brkan / European Union Regulations on Algorithmic Decision-Making
implication: MetroGraph enables accountability by creating an audit trail: the graph shows not just the answer but the reasoning path, making it auditable. If a decision is wrong, stakeholders can examine the graph, identify where the reasoning broke down (bad retrieval? weak ranking?), and correct the system—moving from black-box decisions to accountable ones.

definition: The property that AI systems make decisions without unfair discrimination based on protected characteristics (race, gender, age). Bias in AI can arise from training data, model architecture, or deployment context. Interpretability and explainability are tools for identifying and mitigating bias, enabling fair outcomes.
key_refs: Barocas et al. / A Survey on Bias and Fairness in Machine Learning
implication: In MetroGraph, if a RAG system consistently retrieves sources biased toward one demographic, the graph makes this bias visible—users see the pattern in retrieved documents. This transparency is the first step to fairness: you can't correct bias you can't see. MetroGraph doesn't solve bias but enables detection and remediation.

definition: An emerging subfield of interpretability focused on understanding and reverse-engineering the internal mechanics of deep neural networks (especially LLMs) at a granular level—identifying circuits, motifs, and causal mechanisms within learned weights. Mechanistic interpretability aims to achieve true transparency rather than post hoc explanations.
key_refs: Zou et al. / Mechanistic Interpretability for LLM Alignment
implication: While mechanistic interpretability of LLMs remains research-stage, MetroGraph can prepare for it: as mechanistic understanding improves, the graph could highlight discovered circuits ('this output relied on a fairness circuit'). For now, MetroGraph remains at the RAG/workflow level, where reasoning chains are more tractable than neural networks.

definition: The process of estimating and communicating the confidence or uncertainty in AI predictions. Uncertainty can be epistemic (reducible through more data/training) or aleatoric (irreducible, inherent to the problem). Communicating uncertainty enables users to calibrate trust—high uncertainty means skepticism warranted.
key_refs: Chen et al. / Uncertainty Quantification and Confidence Calibration in LLMs: A Survey
implication: MetroGraph should show uncertainty as edge widths, colors, or probability bands: strong retrieval match (high confidence) vs. weak match (high uncertainty). This enables users to see not just 'what the system thinks' but 'how confident is it?' Uncertainty visualization supports calibrated skepticism.

definition: The design of systems where humans and AI work together complementarily, with each compensating for the other's weaknesses. Effective teaming requires clear task allocation, appropriate trust calibration, and mechanisms for humans to validate, correct, and override AI decisions. Collaboration is more effective than pure human or pure AI.
key_refs: Amershi et al. / Toward a Science of Human-AI Teaming for Decision Making
implication: MetroGraph is fundamentally a collaboration interface: the graph shows the AI's reasoning, the human verifies and refines it. The user can see why sources ranked high, tweak the query, and see re-ranking—a human-in-the-loop cycle better than 'user asks → AI answers.' This enables true collaboration where each party's strengths shine.

definition: AI models constructed with interpretability as a design principle from the start, rather than attempting to explain black boxes post hoc. Examples include decision trees, rule-based systems, and sparse linear models. Interpretable-by-design trades off accuracy for transparency but avoids the fidelity concerns of post hoc explanations.
key_refs: Caruana et al. / Intelligible Models for Healthcare
Rudin / Interpretable ML: Fundamental Principles and 10 Grand Challenges
implication: For MetroGraph's agent-builder (workflow definition), interpretable-by-design is the goal: users write explicit rules and decision nodes, not train opaque models. This aligns with the wedge of 'best-of-both'—you get explainability by construction, not explanation by retroactive analysis. Rules are transparent by nature.

definition: The alignment between a model's confidence estimates and actual accuracy—well-calibrated models assign high confidence to correct predictions and low confidence to incorrect ones. Calibration is distinct from accuracy; a model can be accurate (right answers) but overconfident (assigns high confidence to wrong answers), eroding trust.
key_refs: Chen et al. / Uncertainty Quantification and Confidence Calibration in LLMs
implication: MetroGraph should validate that confidence scores are honest: if the system shows 95% confidence but is wrong, users quickly learn to ignore confidence. By making confidence visible and measurable, MetroGraph creates accountability for calibration—poorly calibrated models become obvious.

definition: Standardized documentation for datasets, parallel to model cards, specifying dataset composition, creation process, labeling procedures, known biases, and ethical considerations. Datasheets enable stakeholders to assess data quality and identify potential sources of bias or harm.
key_refs: Gebru et al. / Datasheets for Datasets
implication: In MetroGraph's RAG context, surfacing dataset metadata ('These 1000 sources are from 2020-2022; 60% are news, 40% are academic') gives users context for source reliability. A datasheet hover reveals potential biases in the retrieval corpus, supporting informed skepticism.

definition: The assumption that interpretable models sacrifice accuracy for transparency. Recent evidence suggests this tradeoff is not always necessary—interpretable-by-design models can achieve competitive accuracy if designed thoughtfully. The tradeoff is more about design choices than fundamental limits.
key_refs: Ghai et al. / Enforcing Interpretability and its Statistical Impacts
Caruana et al. / Intelligible Models for Healthcare
implication: For MetroGraph, this is liberating: explainability is not a price paid (accuracy loss) but a feature gained (trust, auditability). By building on explicit retrieval and ranking (not opaque neural scoring), MetroGraph can be both transparent and accurate, avoiding the false choice between 'good but black box' and 'understandable but weak.'

definition: The stability and consistency of explanations across similar inputs or slight model changes. Explanations that change dramatically for minor input variations are not robust and indicate the explanation may not faithfully reflect the model's reasoning. Robustness ensures explanations are trustworthy.
key_refs: Ghosh et al. / Fidelity Metrics for XAI
implication: In MetroGraph, robustness means the graph structure for similar queries should be similar: if two queries are nearly identical, their reasoning graphs should show similar retrieval patterns. Erratic explanations signal poor ranking stability and warrant skepticism.

concept: Overview First, Zoom and Filter, Then Details on Demand
definition: Shneiderman's foundational interaction principle for navigating large information spaces: present a high-level overview to establish context, enable filtering/zooming to focus on regions of interest, and provide detailed views for selected elements. Reduces cognitive load by progressively revealing information.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1996 / Treemaps for space-constrained visualization
implication: MetroGraph should support three-level agent workflow exploration: (1) Overview shows entire DAG with per-step latencies aggregated (2) Zoom/filter on subgraphs (e.g., by agent, by tool type, by time range) (3) Detail view shows specific step state, inputs, outputs, intermediate values when clicked. Reduces cognitive overload for complex multi-step agent traces.

definition: Pirolli and Card's theory that users navigate information spaces by following 'scent'—cues suggesting valuable information lies in a particular direction. Users make local decisions based on these cues, seeking to maximize value-per-unit-effort in finding target information.
key_refs: Pirolli & Card 1999 / Information Foraging: A Theory of How People Navigate on the Web
implication: Workflow visualization must provide clear visual scent to guide users toward understanding agent behavior: step labels with status, latency indicators (color intensity), error markers, and tool icons should all signal relevant information density. Design should help users quickly identify anomalous or critical steps (high latency, errors) without exhaustive reading.

definition: Tufte's principle that effective visualization maximizes the proportion of visual effort devoted to representing data (data-ink) versus decorative elements (chartjunk). Reduces cognitive load and improves readability.
key_refs: Tufte 1983 / The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
implication: Agent workflow visualization should strip away decorative borders, unnecessary labels, and redundant encodings. Every pixel should communicate execution data: step names, latencies, dependencies, status. Avoid 3D effects, gradients, or animations that distract from the core workflow structure and timing information.

definition: Design space for visualizing sequences of discrete events over time, balancing temporal relationships, event attributes, and occurrence patterns. Key challenge: rendering dense sequences at multiple levels of granularity (individual events, clusters, trends) without losing detail or context.
key_refs: Brehmer & Munzner 2013 / A multi-level typology of abstract visualization tasks
implication: Agent execution traces are inherently temporal event sequences (tool calls, LLM outputs, function returns). MetroGraph should adopt event sequence visualization techniques: allow users to view sequences at coarse granularity (5 steps per second) or fine granularity (per millisecond), with interactive transition between scales.

definition: A novel visual encoding combining spatial position (temporal sequence), categorical attributes (event types, agent names), and quantitative attributes (durations, parameter values) within bounded rectangular containers. Enables multivariate event analysis through coordinated marks and channels.
key_refs: Montana et al. 2025 / EventBox: A Novel Visual Encoding for Interactive Analysis of Temporal and Multivariate Attributes in Event Sequences
implication: MetroGraph's workflow step visualization could adopt EventBox encoding: represent each agent step as a box whose width encodes duration, color encodes status (running/completed/error), and internal layout shows input parameters and outputs. Enables rapid pattern recognition across many steps.

concept: Multilevel Temporal Abstraction with Hierarchical Aggregation
definition: Technique for rendering temporal sequences at multiple levels of abstraction by recursively grouping events into clusters and re-representing clusters at higher levels. Users can drill down from summary (cluster view) to detail (individual events) through interactive navigation.
key_refs: Magallanes et al. 2021 / Sequen-C: A Multilevel Overview of Temporal Event Sequences
implication: Agent workflows with hundreds of steps benefit from hierarchical abstraction: show high-level tool chains (LLM call → parser → tool invoke → result process) at top level, then drill into sub-steps and intermediate values. Align-Score-Simplify pattern from Sequen-C is directly applicable to agent workflow summarization.

concept: Workflow Provenance Visualization and Data Lineage
definition: Representation of data provenance graphs showing how data was generated and transformed through multi-step workflows. Challenges include scalability (large provenance graphs), abstraction (balancing detail with overview), and interactive exploration (navigating complex dependency structures).
key_refs: Stitz et al. 2016 / AVOCADO: Visualization of Workflow-Derived Data Provenance for Reproducible Biomedical Research
implication: Agent execution traces are provenance graphs: each step depends on prior steps' outputs. MetroGraph should visualize this lineage structure, showing how data flows through the agent workflow. AVOCADO's approach to aggregating provenance nodes at different scales applies directly to agent step visualization.

definition: Visual encoding of execution time per workflow step, enabling identification of performance bottlenecks and slowdowns. Techniques include bar charts (absolute time per step), heat maps (relative duration), and waterfall diagrams (cumulative time).
key_refs: Montana et al. 2025 / EventBox (temporal encoding of event durations)
Brehmer & Munzner 2013 / Temporal Analysis Tasks
implication: Critical for MetroGraph: users need to understand why agent workflows are slow. Per-step latency visualization (step 1: 50ms, step 2: 3200ms ← bottleneck, step 3: 150ms) enables rapid bottleneck identification. Should support both absolute durations and relative comparisons across similar workflows.

definition: Systems that combine autonomous AI agent execution with human oversight, control, and decision-making at key points. Enables humans to guide agent behavior, correct mistakes, and maintain safety/alignment without fully automating all tasks.
key_refs: Mozannar et al. 2025 / Magentic-UI: Towards Human-in-the-loop Agentic Systems
implication: MetroGraph must support human interruption and oversight: visualization should highlight decision points where human input is needed or where the agent is uncertain. Interaction mechanisms (co-planning, co-tasking, action guards from Magentic-UI) should be surfaced through clear UI affordances at the step level.

definition: Predefined locations in an agentic workflow where execution pauses to allow human review, approval, or correction before proceeding. Formal treatment views interruptions as first-class computation constructs with well-defined semantics.
key_refs: Macke et al. 2017 / Formalizing Interruptible Algorithms for Human over-the-loop Analytics
implication: MetroGraph should visualize interruption points as explicit affordances: pause icons, confirmation dialogs, or highlighted decision nodes where humans can intervene. Formal semantics (blocking vs. non-blocking, confirmation required vs. optional) should be visually encoded to clarify when human input is mandatory.

definition: Systems combining human-directed exploration with automated computational suggestions and analysis. Users remain in control (mixed) while automation handles computational heavy-lifting, creating hybrid intelligence that leverages human intuition and machine processing.
key_refs: Bach et al. 2025 / A Scoping Review of Mixed Initiative Visual Analytics in the Automation Renaissance
implication: MetroGraph is inherently mixed-initiative: the agent performs work autonomously while humans monitor and guide. Visualization should combine automated anomaly detection (highlight slow steps, error states) with human-driven exploration (filtering, drill-down, comparison). Neither humans nor automation should dominate.

definition: Design pattern where multiple linked visualizations of the same dataset are presented side-by-side, with interactions in one view automatically updating others. Enables complementary perspectives on complex data.
key_refs: Magallanes et al. 2021 / Sequen-C uses three coordinated views: summary, cluster, detail
Brehmer & Munzner 2013 / Coordination and multiplicity
implication: MetroGraph should support coordinated views: (1) Timeline view showing step execution over time, (2) DAG view showing dependencies, (3) Detail panel showing current step state. Selecting a step in timeline highlights it in DAG and updates detail panel; filtering by agent type updates all views.

definition: Algorithms for laying out directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to minimize edge crossings, maximize readability, and show hierarchical structure. Includes hierarchical layouts (Sugiyama), layered approaches, and force-directed methods adapted for DAGs.
key_refs: Sugiyama et al. 1981 / Methods for Visual Understanding of Hierarchical System Structures
implication: Agent workflow DAGs are inherently hierarchical (sequence of steps, branching on conditionals). MetroGraph should apply Sugiyama layering to position steps left-to-right (chronologically) while minimizing edge crossings. Dynamic workflows with loops need specialized handling (cycle breaking, feedback edge marking).
