definition: Visualization technique showing flow of quantities through a process, with band width proportional to flow magnitude. Commonly used for showing data distribution or energy/resource flow through transformation steps.
key_refs: D3.js Sankey / Bostock et al.
implication: Sankey overlays on agent workflows could show token flow through steps: band width represents token count at each step (narrow after filtering, wide after expansion). Useful for visualizing data cardinality changes through multi-step workflows.

definition: Techniques for adding textual and visual annotations to visualizations to provide context, explain patterns, highlight insights. Annotations can be manual or automatically generated, and should be positioned to avoid clutter while remaining visible.
key_refs: Echtler et al. 2024 / A Survey on Annotations in Information Visualization
implication: Agent workflow visualization should support annotations on critical steps: automated callouts for bottlenecks ('LLM call: 3.2s'), manual user notes ('this step sometimes fails'), explanatory labels for step purpose. Annotations should not overwhelm the view but should be accessible on demand.

definition: Cognitive load theory (Sweller) posits that working memory has limited capacity; effective visualization and interaction design must manage extraneous cognitive load (unnecessary effort), intrinsic load (task complexity), and germane load (useful effort toward understanding).
key_refs: Sweller 1988 / Cognitive load during problem solving
implication: Large agent workflows (100+ steps) rapidly exceed working memory. MetroGraph must manage cognitive load through: (1) extraneous: remove visual clutter, (2) intrinsic: use hierarchical abstraction to reduce perceived complexity, (3) germane: guide attention to critical patterns through color/size coding.

definition: Visualization techniques for data arriving continuously or in real-time, requiring incremental rendering, efficient updates, and handling of temporal locality (recent events more relevant than old ones). Challenges include memory management and responsiveness.
key_refs: Andrienko & Andrienko 2013 / Visual analytics of movement
implication: Agent workflows are inherently streaming: steps complete in real-time. MetroGraph must render new steps incrementally (append to timeline), update latencies as steps complete, and keep the view responsive. Should support both live streaming and historical replay of completed workflows.

definition: Using smooth animation to transition between different visual representations (e.g., node-link to parallel coordinates), helping users maintain mental continuity and understand the relationship between views.
key_refs: Heer & Robertson 2007 / Animated Transitions in Statistical Data Graphics
Chen et al. 2025 / Animated Transition between Node-Link and Parallel Coordinates Visualizations
implication: MetroGraph could support smooth transitions between workflow representations: DAG → timeline → Sankey flow. Animation helps users track identity of elements across views, reducing disorientation. Particularly useful when toggling between structural view (dependencies) and temporal view (execution order).

concept: LLM Agent Provenance and Observable Traces
definition: Systems and techniques for capturing, storing, and querying the complete execution trace of LLM-powered agents, including: prompts sent, LLM outputs, tool calls made, tool results received, and intermediate reasoning steps. Enables post-hoc analysis and real-time observability.
key_refs: Souza et al. 2025 / LLM Agents for Interactive Workflow Provenance
implication: MetroGraph must capture complete agent provenance: every LLM call with full prompt + output, every tool invocation with args + results, every decision point and branching. This data becomes the input to visualization; Magentic-UI and other systems show this can be queried interactively in natural language via agents themselves.

definition: Visualization of systems where multiple autonomous agents work together, showing inter-agent communication, task delegation, synchronization points, and specialization patterns. Adds complexity of showing both individual agent traces and collective workflow.
key_refs: Bansal et al. 2025 / CoDA: Agentic Systems for Collaborative Data Visualization
implication: Future agent systems will likely use multi-agent orchestration. MetroGraph should support visualization of agent pools: show which agent performed each step, highlight communication between agents (messages, data handoffs), reveal bottlenecks in agent-to-agent coordination.

definition: Interaction pattern combining visualization, interaction, and computational analysis to support open-ended exploration and hypothesis formation. User-visualization interaction loop enables iterative refinement of understanding.
key_refs: Andrienko & Andrienko 2006 / Exploratory geovisualization
implication: MetroGraph users need to explore agent behavior iteratively: filter to specific agents or tool types, sort by latency, drill into failures, compare across runs. Each interaction should update views and suggest next analytical steps. Should support saving/sharing exploration paths.

definition: Techniques for visually representing uncertainty, confidence intervals, and probabilistic outcomes in visualizations. Relevant when displaying agent confidence scores, probabilistic decision outputs, or uncertainty in predictions.
key_refs: Kay & Hullman 2025 / A General Approach to Visualizing Uncertainty in Statistical Graphics
implication: LLM agents often produce probabilistic outputs and confidence estimates. MetroGraph should support displaying agent uncertainty: show confidence bands around latency estimates, visualize probability distributions for multi-choice decision points, indicate model uncertainty with visual texture/opacity.

concept: Knowledge Graph and Reasoning Graph Visualization
definition: Visualization of knowledge graphs and reasoning chains showing entities, relationships, and inference steps. Challenges include managing scale (thousands of nodes/edges) and clarity of relationships.
key_refs: Zhu et al. 2024 / Visualization of Knowledge Graphs with Embeddings
implication: Agent reasoning often involves knowledge retrieval and chain-of-thought. MetroGraph could surface agent reasoning graphs: show which facts/documents were retrieved, how they connect to form reasoning chain, which entities are central to the decision. Graph visualization techniques directly applicable.

definition: Principles for designing interaction techniques (selection, filtering, drilling, linking) for complex information-rich systems. Should minimize cognitive load while maximizing expressiveness and responsiveness.
key_refs: Preece, Rogers & Sharp 2015 / Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction
implication: MetroGraph's interaction model must support: (1) filtering (by agent, tool type, status), (2) selection (individual step or step range), (3) navigation (overview/detail, temporal scroll, dependency follow), (4) annotation (note-taking on interesting steps). All interactions should provide immediate feedback and maintain context.

definition: The active process of constructing meaningful representations from complex, ambiguous information. Core loop of information foraging (seeking) and synthesis (organizing). Users develop mental models through iterative hypothesis formation and revision.
key_refs: Pirolli & Card / A Functional Model of Sensemaking
Pirolli / Information Foraging
implication: MetroGraph users engage in sensemaking loops when exploring agent workflows or query results. Explicit visualization of agent states and dependencies supports rapid iteration between hypothesis ("what should happen") and observation ("what did happen"). Poor sensemaking support causes users to blame UI rather than understanding actual system behavior.

concept: Mental Model Shifts in LLM Interaction
definition: Documented empirical phenomenon where users' mental models of LLM capabilities and limitations evolve through repeated interaction, often becoming more accurate but sometimes diverging from actual system behavior.
key_refs: Mental model shifts in human-LLM interactions / Journal of Intelligent Information Systems 2025
implication: MetroGraph users' mental models of multi-agent orchestration will shift as they interact. System must track and surface mental model accuracy (via explanations, feedback loops) to prevent users from settling into inaccurate stabilized models that later cause surprises or blame attribution.

definition: Users' folk-psychological tendency to attribute consciousness, emotions, reasoning, and intent to AI systems, independent of whether those systems possess such capacities. Attributions split into two dimensions: agency (reasoning) and experience (emotion/consciousness).
key_refs: The influence of mental state attributions on trust in large language models / PMC 2024
implication: Users may blame 'intentional' agent failures differently than 'accidental' ones, or trust systems more when they attribute reasoning but not consciousness. MetroGraph must avoid anthropomorphic language that invites incorrect mental state attributions; clear naming ("orchestrator agent", "subprocess") prevents users from misunderstanding autonomy levels.

definition: When AI systems fail, users attribute failures either to design (unintentional system limitation) or intent (the system chose not to do something). Stance attribution affects blame assignment and subsequent trust decisions.
key_refs: Intentional or Designed? The Impact of Stance Attribution on Cognitive Processing / Brain Sciences 2024
implication: MetroGraph users will attribute agent failures differently based on whether they perceive a deliberate choice vs. a capability limit. Transparent logging ("agent did not attempt step X because constraint Y") supports accurate stance attribution and prevents users from blaming UI when blame belongs elsewhere.

definition: Experts and novices construct qualitatively different mental models: experts organize knowledge around deep principles and constraints; novices rely on surface features and memorized patterns. Expert mental models are richer but require different interface support.
key_refs: Expert and Novice User Differences and Implications for Product Design / CHI
Dreyfus Model of Skill Acquisition
implication: MetroGraph must support both novice users (who think in terms of simple agent sequences) and expert users (who reason about dependency graphs and constraint propagation). Progressive disclosure and optional advanced visualizations address this gap without overwhelming either group.

definition: A cognitive bias where users constrain their interaction strategies with LLMs to familiar patterns from prior tools (search engines, command-line interfaces, virtual assistants), preventing exploration of the system's fuller capabilities.
key_refs: Trapped by Expectations: Functional Fixedness in LLM-Enabled Chat Search / ACM 2025
implication: MetroGraph users with database or search-engine backgrounds will try to use MetroGraph like a query interface. Functional fixedness prevents them from discovering graph visualization affordances or multi-agent orchestration features. Progressive scaffolding (tutorial, contextual hints) and explicit affordance signaling help overcome this bias.

definition: System-provided reasoning traces or decision justifications intended to help users understand AI behavior and correct their mental models. However, explanations can destabilize (polarize) existing mental models if they contradict prior expectations.
key_refs: Human-centered evaluation of explainable AI applications / PMC 2024
Explainable AI from a user perspective / ScienceDirect
Polarizing Effects of Algorithmic Transparency / arXiv 2018
implication: MetroGraph explanations of agent decisions must be calibrated to user expertise and expectations. Overly detailed traces can increase cognitive load and confusion; inadequate explanations leave users guessing. Dialogue-based explanation (user asks why, system responds) supports active mental model construction better than one-way explanations.

definition: Shift from passive explanation (system tells user) to interactive dialogue where users ask questions and systems respond. Interactive modalities support dynamic mental model construction and grounding better than static explanations.
key_refs: From Explainable to Interactive AI: A Literature Review on Current Trends / arXiv 2024
implication: MetroGraph should support users asking 'why did this agent fail?' rather than only showing pre-generated explanations. Interactive drill-down into subgoal states and agent decisions enables users to actively construct mental models of system behavior.

concept: Common Ground and Grounding in Dialogue
definition: In dialogue, participants develop shared understanding (common ground) through collaborative acknowledgment and repair. For human-AI systems, robust mental models require clear grounding that user understanding matches system semantics.
key_refs: Common ground, cooperation, and recipient design in human-computer interactions / Clark & Brennan
implication: MetroGraph requires explicit grounding mechanisms (confirm goal parsing before execution, ask clarifying questions about constraints) so users and the system align on what multi-agent orchestration entails. Misalignment is a primary source of blame attribution.

definition: When failures occur in human-AI systems, users distribute blame among human choice, AI design, and AI autonomy based on their mental models of who (human or system) had control and responsibility at each step.
key_refs: Responsibility Attribution in Human Interactions with Everyday AI Systems / CHI 2025
When AI Fails, Who Do We Blame? / IEEE ITTS
implication: If users misunderstand whether an agent autonomously made a decision or followed human guidance, they will blame the wrong party. MetroGraph must clearly surface which decisions humans made (goal setting, constraint specification) vs. which agents made (execution choices) so blame attribution is accurate.

definition: Structured taxonomy distinguishing degrees of agent autonomy from operator (human controls all) to observer (AI executes with no human input). Users require accurate mental models of which level applies to each agent or subgoal.
key_refs: Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents Working Paper / arXiv 2025
implication: MetroGraph must label each agent or subgoal with its autonomy level (human-supervised vs. independent). Without this, users will construct inconsistent mental models and be surprised by failures.

definition: Displaying intermediate reasoning steps (chain-of-thought) or planning artifacts that show how an AI system is solving a problem. Users perceive systems with visible reasoning as more intelligent and trustworthy, but reasoning traces can also trigger miscalibration if users over-interpret intermediate steps.
key_refs: Watching AI Think: User Perceptions of Visible Thinking in Chatbots / arXiv 2026
implication: MetroGraph can display agent planning and subgoal decomposition to support user mental models, but must guard against users becoming over-confident in intermediate outputs that may still fail.

definition: User mental models of multi-agent systems are qualitatively different from single-agent models: users must track inter-agent dependencies, communication, and failure propagation. Early adopters of multi-agent tools develop mental models of teams (divide-and-conquer), whereas transparency limitations block accurate models.
key_refs: Exploring Human-AI Collaboration Using Mental Models of Early Adopters of Multi-Agent Generative AI Tools / arXiv 2024
implication: MetroGraph's core problem is surfacing multi-agent interactions so users develop accurate mental models. Qualitative research shows that transparency about agent roles and task dependencies is essential; visualizing OrchVis-style hierarchical goals directly addresses this need.

concept: Hierarchical Goal Decomposition and User Mental Models
definition: When complex tasks are decomposed into hierarchical goals (abstract to concrete), users develop mental models organized around goal satisfaction rather than action sequences. Explicit goal visualization supports accurate models.
key_refs: OrchVis: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Orchestration for Human Oversight / arXiv 2025
implication: MetroGraph's hierarchical goal-agent mapping directly supports accurate user mental models. Users focus on whether goals are met (outcome) rather than micromanaging task steps. This reduces surface-area bloat and supports expert oversight.

definition: Visual representations shape how users construct mental models from data. Effective visualizations reduce the mismatch between user expectations and actual system behavior by highlighting structure, dependencies, and state changes.
key_refs: Visualization Analysis and Design / Munzner
The Visual Display of Quantitative Information / Tufte
Iceberg Sensemaking: A Process Model for Critical Data Analysis and Visualization
implication: MetroGraph's metro-map-style visualization must be designed to highlight agent roles, state flow, and dependencies. Poor visualization design (inadequate distinction between node types, unclear edge semantics) causes mental model errors.

concept: Cognitive Biases in AI-Assisted Decision Making
definition: Users' cognitive biases (confirmation bias, anchoring, representativeness heuristic) interact with AI systems to distort mental models. Users selectively weight evidence that confirms current hypotheses and resist revising beliefs even with strong contrary evidence.
key_refs: The Role of Cognitive Biases in AI-assisted Decision-making
Bias in the Loop: How Humans Evaluate AI-Generated Suggestions
implication: MetroGraph users will be prone to anchoring on first-seen goal decomposition and confirmation bias toward hypotheses that early agent outputs support. Actively eliciting alternative explanations and constraint violations helps counter these biases.

concept: Prompting Behavior and Mental Model Adaptation
definition: Users develop and refine mental models of LLM/AI systems through iterative prompting strategies. Training in LLM mechanics improves mental model accuracy and prompting effectiveness. Users adapt prompting based on observed system responses.
key_refs: Understanding Learner-LLM Chatbot Interactions and the Impact of Prompting Guidelines / arXiv 2024
How understanding large language models can inform the use of ChatGPT in physics education
implication: MetroGraph users will develop prompting/interaction strategies for the orchestration UI. Explicit guidance on how to set goals, specify constraints, and interpret results accelerates mental model development.

definition: Emerging regulations (EU AI Act Article 13, etc.) mandate that AI systems provide transparent documentation of capabilities, limitations, and decision-making to users. This is a legal requirement, not just a UX best practice.
key_refs: EU AI Act Article 13: Transparency and Provision of Information to Deployers
Transparency and explainability in AI systems: global perspectives and regulation in Australia (2025)
implication: MetroGraph's transparency features (goal parsing, agent status, failure reasons) are not optional; regulatory landscape increasingly requires them. This directly addresses the wedge: MetroGraph can't be a simple tool; it must surface transparency to meet legal obligations for user understanding.

definition: Bandura's concept of belief in one's capacity to execute actions and produce desired outcomes; foundational psychological theory underlying perceived control, agency, and motivation in technology use.
key_refs: Bandura 1997 / Self-Efficacy: The Exercise of Control
implication: MetroGraph's interaction design must enable mastery experiences through progressive complexity disclosure and clear success feedback; users should feel their learning and effort produce competence in graph querying and exploration.

definition: Optimal psychological state achieved through balance of challenge and skill, clear goals, immediate feedback, and sense of control; flow state is intrinsically motivated and characterized by loss of self-consciousness and time distortion.
key_refs: Csikszentmihalyi 1990 / Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience
implication: MetroGraph should calibrate graph complexity and task difficulty to user skill level; provide real-time feedback on queries, enable progressive disclosure of advanced features, and ensure immediate visibility of query results to sustain flow.

definition: Subjective experience of controlling one's body and external environment; comprises implicit pre-reflective feeling of agency and explicit judgement of agency; arises from integration of internal sensorimotor signals and external situational cues.
key_refs: Limerick, Coyle, Moore 2014 / The experience of agency in human-computer interactions
Limerick, Coyle, Moore 2022 / The sense of agency in emerging technologies
implication: MetroGraph must minimize latency, provide immediate system feedback to user actions (graph updates, highlights), and ensure predictability of cause-effect relationships in graph interactions to sustain sense of agency.

definition: Shneiderman's interface design rule mandating support for internal locus of control; users should feel they are in charge of the system and that systems respond to their actions, not system-mediated decisions.
key_refs: Shneiderman & Plaisant 2004 / Rules of Interface Design
Shneiderman 2022 / Human-Centered AI
implication: MetroGraph must make all graph transformations traceable to user actions; avoid silent algorithmic simplification or node collapsing without explicit user request; every graph change should be attributable to a user command.

definition: Theory that human action is fundamentally contextual and opportunistic rather than following pre-specified plans; emphasizes how agents respond to real-time environmental cues and situated constraints.
key_refs: Suchman 1987 / Plans and Situated Actions
implication: MetroGraph should support exploratory, non-linear graph navigation; avoid prescriptive query workflows; enable users to adjust exploration strategy on-the-fly based on emerging graph patterns rather than committing to pre-planned analysis.

definition: Visibility of system decision-making processes, data sources, and algorithmic criteria; enables users to evaluate AI outputs, build appropriate trust, and exercise informed control over system behavior.
key_refs: Wang et al. 2026 / Seeing to Think? How Source Transparency Design Shapes Interactive Information Seeking
Yang 2024 / From Explainable to Interactive AI
implication: MetroGraph should surface the data sources and query logic underlying graph suggestions; show why certain nodes/edges appear, what fields were filtered, enabling users to understand and critique system outputs.

definition: Human tendency to over-rely on automated systems and under-weight contradictory evidence from non-automated sources; compromises user agency through reduced critical evaluation of system outputs.
key_refs: Wickens 2015 / Human-Automation Interaction Research: Past, Present, and Future
implication: MetroGraph should avoid presenting algorithmic recommendations without qualification; always show confidence levels, alternative suggestions, and mechanisms for user challenge/override to maintain critical stance.

definition: Bidirectional influence between humans and autonomous systems; control is negotiated rather than fixed; systems influence human choices while respecting human authority and values.
key_refs: Taddeo 2024 / Negotiating the Shared Agency between Humans & AI in the Recommender System
Lim 2026 / When to Hand Off, When to Work Together
Mohseni 2024 / Complementarity in Human-AI Collaboration
implication: MetroGraph must make explicit when users are responding to system suggestions vs. acting independently; support users teaching the system about their preferences through feedback mechanisms (marking results as relevant/irrelevant).

definition: Nissenbaum's framework for privacy grounded in norms of appropriate information flow within contexts; privacy violations occur when information moves to inappropriate contexts; enables user control over data flows.
key_refs: Nissenbaum 2009 / Values in Design
Nissenbaum / Regulatory CI: Adaptively Regulating Privacy as Contextual Integrity
implication: MetroGraph should clarify data usage contexts and enable users to control what metadata (query history, exploration patterns) is retained or shared; make explicit the norms governing data access and retention.

definition: HCI methodology systematically integrating human values (autonomy, privacy, informed consent, fairness) into design through conceptual, empirical, and technical investigations; treats values as design constraints.
key_refs: Friedman & Hendry 2003 / Value Sensitive Design and Information Systems
implication: MetroGraph should be designed with explicit value commitments to user autonomy (explicit control), transparency (clear mechanics), and fairness (no hidden algorithmic manipulation); conduct empirical studies validating these values are supported.

definition: Recommendation mechanisms that preserve user agency through explicit control levers enabling users to adjust exploration strategy, filter diversity, and resist algorithmic filter bubbles.
key_refs: Kirman 2022 / User-controllable Recommendation Against Filter Bubbles
Xie 2025 / Design of a Serendipity-Incorporated Recommender System
implication: MetroGraph recommendations (e.g., suggested nodes, paths, patterns) should include user-adjustable controls: diversity slider, confidence threshold, recommendation style toggle; make serendipity an explicit option.

definition: Taxonomy of distinct collaborative modes between humans and AI ranging from simple (system-initiated, one-way recommendations) to complex (reciprocal turn-taking, multi-step dialogue); empirical review reveals dominance of simplistic patterns.
key_refs: Liu et al. 2024 / Human-AI collaboration is not very collaborative yet
implication: MetroGraph should go beyond simple recommendations to support reciprocal interaction patterns; enable users to ask follow-up questions about suggestions, critique results, and dynamically adjust query strategy in conversation-like flow.

concept: Sense of Agency & User Experience Relationship
definition: Empirical relationship between users' perceived sense of agency and overall satisfaction/UX; system feedback mechanisms and control responsiveness significantly impact both agency and user satisfaction.
key_refs: Vig et al. 2022 / Sense of Agency and User Experience: Is There a Link?
implication: MetroGraph's success depends on supporting sense of agency; every design decision about responsiveness, feedback visibility, and control transparency directly impacts user satisfaction and adoption.

definition: Shared understanding of AI system state, capabilities, and current actions enabling human operators to maintain predictability and agency; requires transparency about agent behavior and intentions.
key_refs: Goler 2023 / Agent Teaming Situation Awareness (ATSA)
Degani 2016 / Human Factors Considerations in Aviation
implication: MetroGraph should clearly display algorithmic system state (what suggestions are being computed, what data is being accessed); enable users to interrupt/pause automated processes and understand what the system is doing at any moment.

definition: Tension between automated personalization/adaptation and user autonomy; adaptive systems must provide transparency and override mechanisms to preserve user sense of control when systems adjust behavior.
key_refs: Scheuerman 2014 / User Control in Adaptive User Interfaces for Accessibility
Amershi 2025 / Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns
implication: MetroGraph should support personalization (remembering user preferences) but make personalizations visible and modifiable; users should understand why the interface adapted and be able to reset to defaults.

definition: User perception of fairness in algorithmic outcomes influenced by transparency, development procedures, and understanding; users perceive algorithms as fairer when they understand decision criteria.
key_refs: Anjomshoae 2019 / Factors Influencing Perceived Fairness in Algorithmic Decision-Making
implication: MetroGraph's graph algorithms (ranking, layout, clustering) should be explainable; show criteria and trade-offs (e.g., why certain nodes are grouped, why edges are weighted); users perceive fairer outcomes when decisions are transparent.

concept: Error Taxonomy: Slips, Mistakes, and Lapses
definition: Foundational classification distinguishing unintended execution errors (slips: right intention, wrong action), problem-solving errors (mistakes: wrong intention), and memory lapses. Errors arise from design failures, not user incompetence.
key_refs: Norman 1988 / The Design of Everyday Things (Revised 2013)
implication: MetroGraph must distinguish error types in its feedback: slips need visibility/undo, mistakes need corrected mental models, lapses need contextual reminders. One-size error recovery fails.

definition: Trust in automation (willingness to depend) and reliance behavior (actual usage) are dissociated: users can hold steady trust while adjusting reliance with reliability shifts, or maintain reliance despite declining trust. Trust is necessary but insufficient to predict dependence.
key_refs: Dzindolet et al. 2003 / The Role of Trust in Automation Reliance
Rittenberg et al. 2024 / Calibrating Trust, Reliance and Dependence in Variable-Reliability Automation
implication: MetroGraph cannot rely on trust signals alone to prevent over-reliance. Must design explicit reliance calibration: showing when to verify vs. defer. Trust displays may backfire if decoupled from actual system capability.

definition: The tension between confirmation burden (every-step verification is exhausting; confirm-at-end misses cascading failures). Optimal check frequency minimizes total task time while preventing error propagation. Users exhibit CDCR pattern: Confirm→Diagnose→Correct→Redo.
key_refs: Zhou et al. 2026 CHI / When Should Users Check? A Decision-Theoretic Model of Confirmation Frequency in Multi-Step AI Agent Tasks
implication: MetroGraph's wedge: surface confirmation points at decision-critical junctures (not every step), making error visibility before cascades. Decision-theoretic model for 'when to ask' reduces both interruption fatigue and failure costs.

concept: Before/After Visibility and Gulf of Evaluation
definition: Users detect errors by comparing perceived state against intention. Gulf of evaluation widens if system state is opaque or feedback ambiguous. Before/after consequence visibility (showing what changed, why) enables error recognition and correction urgency.
key_refs: Norman 1988 / Seven Stages of Action
Nielsen 1994 / Ten Usability Heuristics
implication: MetroGraph must show before/after for agent actions: 'what changed in the DB because of this operation?' Opaque side effects cause undetected cascading errors. Real-time state mirroring (delta visibility) is prerequisite for error detection.

concept: Reversibility and Undo/Redo as Error Recovery
definition: Reversible operations (undo/redo) enable low-cost error recovery by preserving prior states. Reduces fear of mistakes, supports exploration, and allows users to correct without cascading. Requires command pattern architecture enabling state snapshots.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1985 / Eight Golden Rules (Rule 9: Help Recover from Errors)
Interacto 2021 / User Interaction Processing Model
implication: MetroGraph should prioritize reversible operations over destructive dialogs. Multi-level undo for graph edits reduces confirmation burden and enables safe exploration. Version history visible in UI signals recoverability.

definition: Users preferentially accept automated recommendations even when evidence of unreliability is present (automation bias). Trust miscalibration persists despite explanations. Single errors can destroy trust; recovery requires consistent reliability plus transparency on uncertainty.
key_refs: Dzindolet et al. 2003 / Role of Trust in Automation Reliance
arXiv 2502.13321 / Adjust for Trust: Mitigating Trust-Induced Inappropriate Reliance
arXiv 2310.13544 / Diachronic Perspective on User Trust in AI Under Uncertainty
implication: MetroGraph must counter automation bias with uncertainty communication and cognitive forcing functions (e.g., 'explain why you disagree with this suggestion'). Showing failure modes and recovery paths restores calibrated skepticism.

definition: Transparency (showing explanations, uncertainty quantification) can increase trust even when explanations are false. Explanation quality directly affects error detection; poor explanations increase inappropriate reliance. Transparency without veracity checking amplifies misjudgment.
key_refs: arXiv 2005.02335 / Don't Explain Without Verifying Veracity
arXiv 2306.01941 / AI Transparency in the Age of LLMs: A Human-Centered Research Roadmap
implication: MetroGraph must not expose explanations without ground truth anchoring. Show confidence bounds and failure examples alongside reasoning. Transparency that obscures error ≠ transparency that enables detection.

concept: Cognitive Load in Error Correction Loops
definition: Repeated error correction (confirmation fatigue) depletes attentional resources, reducing error detection accuracy over time. Cognitive load from decision-making compounds across long tasks. Think-time affordances and periodic pauses improve detection rates.
key_refs: arXiv 2601.20683 / Polite But Boring? Trade-offs Between Engagement and Psychological Reactance to Chatbot Feedback Styles
implication: MetroGraph must minimize unnecessary confirmations and provide 'cognitive breaks': summarize corrections, highlight patterns, suggest batching. Long workflows need intermediate pauses to reset attention.

concept: Persuasion Paradox: When Corrections Trigger Reactance
definition: System-initiated corrections (especially those perceived as controlling or paternalistic) trigger psychological reactance: users reject the correction to reassert autonomy, even if it would improve outcomes. Tone, framing, and perceived agency affect acceptance.
key_refs: arXiv 2508.05238 / Driver Assistant: Persuading Drivers to Adjust Secondary Tasks Using Large Language Models
implication: MetroGraph must frame corrections as suggestions preserving user control, not system overrides. 'Consider reversing this step' ≠ 'this is wrong, fix it.' Collaborative error recovery language reduces reactance.

concept: Situation Awareness and Error Detection in Complex State
definition: Error detection requires maintaining accurate situation awareness (Endsley model): perception of current state, comprehension of patterns, projection of consequences. In multi-step workflows, loss of situational awareness enables undetected errors. Context-sensitive UI aids awareness.
key_refs: IEEE / Situation Awareness, Mental Models and Understanding
arXiv 1504.03731 / Safety Enhancement through Situation-Aware User Interfaces
implication: MetroGraph must make system state salient at decision points: show downstream impacts (what else might cascade?), highlight critical states. Situation-aware hints ('you're about to delete 5 rows...') prevent overlooked errors.

concept: User Agency and Locus of Control in Error Correction
definition: Perceived control over error recovery (ability to influence outcomes, understand why corrections occur, reverse changes) shapes user acceptance and reliance. Systems that reduce user agency over correction foster learned helplessness and over-reliance.
key_refs: CHI 2023 / How Does HCI Understand Human Agency and Autonomy?
IUI 2020 / Digging Into User Control in Algorithm-Assisted Decision-Making
implication: MetroGraph's wedge: users must understand 'why' corrections are offered and retain 'how' to reverse them. Opaque AI corrections → learned helplessness. Transparent, reversible actions → calibrated skepticism.

concept: Distributed Cognition in Human-AI Error Recovery Teams
definition: Errors arise not just from individual mistakes but from coordination failures across human-AI teams. Mental model misalignment, communication gaps, and unclear responsibility boundaries amplify error propagation. Recovery requires shared understanding of who verifies what.
key_refs: arXiv 2504.14996 / Distributed Cognition for AI-supported Remote Operations
implication: MetroGraph must surface responsibility boundaries: 'AI will handle validation; you verify consequences.' Explicit role clarity in error recovery workflows prevents diffusion of accountability.

concept: Knowledge in the World vs. Knowledge in the Head
definition: Errors occur when required knowledge exists only in user's memory (knowledge-in-the-head) rather than visible in the interface (knowledge-in-the-world). Constraints, affordances, and signifiers externalize knowledge, reducing error likelihood.
key_refs: Norman 1988 / The Design of Everyday Things
implication: MetroGraph must make query logic, graph state, and validation rules visible, not hidden in docs. Inline hints, schema visibility, and example queries reduce reliance on remembered procedures.

concept: Cascade Failure and Error Propagation in Long Workflows
definition: In multi-step tasks (e.g., 30-step agent sequences), a single error early in execution cascades and amplifies downstream, requiring complete restart. Cost of recovery grows exponentially. Intermediate checkpoints break cascades.
key_refs: CHI 2026 / When Should Users Check?
implication: MetroGraph must not force confirm-at-end for long workflows. Intermediate error visibility (at decision boundaries) prevents cascading failures and reduces total rework cost.

definition: Error feedback modality (visual, audio, haptic, textual) affects detection rates and accessibility. Multimodal feedback (redundant channels) improves detection for users with disabilities and under high cognitive load.
key_refs: arXiv 2407.08882 / Emerging Practices for Large Multimodal Model Assistance for People with Visual Impairments
implication: MetroGraph must not rely solely on visual alerts. Provide text summaries, optional audio cues for critical errors, and high-contrast visual indicators to maximize error detection across user abilities.

concept: Error Detection Patterns in Agent-Mediated Workflows
definition: Users develop heuristic error detection strategies (spot-checking outputs, verifying against known examples, monitoring for mode changes). Some errors are invisible unless explicitly searched for. Undetected consequences enable continued over-reliance.
key_refs: arXiv 2109.11690 / Discovering and Validating AI Errors With Crowdsourced Failure Reports
arXiv 2408.06546 / Misfitting With AI: How Blind People Verify and Contest AI Errors
implication: MetroGraph must make typical error patterns searchable: 'show me all rows modified by rules' enables user-driven error detection. Visible action trails reduce undetected errors.

concept: Confirmation Dialog Overuse and Modal Fatigue
definition: Confirmation dialogs prevent some errors (slips) but overuse induces dialog fatigue: users click 'yes' reflexively without reading, turning confirmations into noise. Optimal use requires high-cost actions and low-frequency triggers.
key_refs: Nielsen Norman Group 2018 / Confirmation Dialogs Can Prevent User Errors (If Not Overused)
implication: MetroGraph should reserve confirmations for truly destructive actions (delete, modify schema) and use alternatives for low-risk errors (undo, inline correction, preview).

concept: Data-Driven Error Prediction and Preemptive Correction
definition: Machine learning models trained on error patterns can flag high-risk operations before execution. Confidence bounds on predictions enable selective intervention: only interrupt when risk is high.
key_refs: arXiv 2511.18849 / Pre-Filtering Code Suggestions Using Developer Behavioral Telemetry
implication: MetroGraph can learn error patterns and proactively surface checks: 'unusual cardinality; verify this join.' Reduces false positives vs. blanket confirmations.

concept: Emotional Response to Error Feedback and Tone Design
definition: Error message tone (harsh vs. supportive) affects user emotional state and receptivity to corrections. Supportive framing reduces frustration and increases engagement with error recovery.
key_refs: arXiv 2502.16038 / Emotion-Aware Design: Modulating Valence, Arousal, and Dominance in Communication via Design
implication: MetroGraph's error messages should be neutral/supportive, not accusatory. 'Unexpected result; would you like to review?' invites correction; 'Error: invalid query!' triggers defensiveness.

definition: Misleading or cluttered visualizations (chart junk, distorted axes, omitted context) cause interpretation errors. Data-ink ratio and truthful representation are prerequisites for accurate error detection.
key_refs: Tufte 1983 / The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
implication: MetroGraph's visual representation of query results and execution logs must prioritize clarity over aesthetics. Omitted fields, hidden aggregations, or distorted cardinality cause mis-reading errors.

concept: Resilience Design Patterns for Error Recovery
definition: Software resilience patterns (circuit breaker, bulkhead, graceful degradation, retry) ensure systems fail safely and recover quickly. UI analogs include partial failures (operation succeeds for some rows), safe defaults, and fallback paths.
key_refs: arXiv 1708.07422 / Resilience Design Patterns: A Structured Approach to Resilience at Extreme Scale
implication: MetroGraph should employ bulkhead pattern: isolate risky operations to prevent cascading failures. Show partial results ('100 of 1000 rows modified; review before committing all').

concept: Habituation to System Errors and Error Blindness
definition: Repeated exposure to system errors reduces vigilance and increases error blindness: users stop noticing errors as salient. Novelty and variability in error presentation (changing location, modality, severity) maintain attention.
key_refs: arXiv 2602.05010 / Signal or 'Noise': Human Reactions to Robot Errors in the Wild
implication: MetroGraph should vary error presentation (not always center-top modal) and use escalating urgency signals. Critical errors need different visual treatment than warnings to prevent habituation.

definition: Users can accurately predict system behavior when systems are available (transparent), compact (simple rules), and aligned (matching user expectations). Complexity is not the barrier; opacity is.
key_refs: arXiv 2601.18966 / People Can Accurately Predict Behavior of Complex Algorithms That Are Available, Compact, and Aligned
implication: MetroGraph's query optimizer and schema resolution can be complex internally, but must expose simple, predictable rules to users. 'If table has column X, use X for join' is learnable; opaque optimization is not.

definition: Error detection latency (delay between error occurrence and visibility) directly affects recovery cost. Real-time feedback enables immediate correction; batch feedback delays recovery and increases downstream damage.
key_refs: PMC / Human-in-the-Loop Error Detection in an Object Organization Task with a Social Robot
implication: MetroGraph must show query execution step-by-step (not wait until end) so users can stop or redirect mid-execution. Real-time cardinality warnings prevent accidental mega-joins.

definition: Excessive system-initiated corrections (too many suggestions, too many pauses) erode perceived autonomy and increase cognitive load. Users disengage or ignore corrections entirely. Balance required between safety and autonomy.
key_refs: CHI 2026 / When Should Users Check?
implication: MetroGraph must resist over-helpfulness: not every potential error needs a suggestion. Selective intervention at true decision points (high cost, high uncertainty) preserves autonomy.
